This set of walkie talkies is a far cry from the mawkish squawk boxes of years ago. Sturdily constructed, they provide impressively clear transmissions. set p is easy,. Simply unscrew the back and insert the included batteries. there are 22 channels and 121 privacy codes which help prevent interference. One of my favorite features is the replay. It records the last 20 seconds of an incoming call so if you miss it, you can usually get the gist of the message or at least the identity of the caller. There is included the NOAA weather and emergency alert radio. This can be crucial especially in areas where the atmospheric conditions are unsettled and can change rapidly. There are customization tones for call alerts and voice activation permits hands free use. there is a battery level indicator and a flashing sos function.The walkie talkies can float and are rubberized for good grip. While not exactly fashion forward, the orange and black devices are easy to see and locate. the instruction manual is concise and easy to follow. The range is up to 37 miles.

I am very impressed with these walkie talkies. I live in a mountainous, wooded region and cell phone reception is at best spotty and unreliable. These are terrific for outdoor activities and also for outdoor jobs.The transmissions are crisp and understandable and while the mountains make it

Purchased this 4 year plan in November 2016 on a Dell Laser Printer. Thus the printer was a little over 2 years when it started doing weird things and I made a claim.

Basically ... the printer stopped printing black ... it just got lighter and lighter. I attempted to clean the heads and change the cartridges to no avail. The printer would also keep running and not stop after done doing a printer job.

I printed my receipt / invoice off Amazon to PDF. I then went to SquareTrade's website attached the receipt. I then made a claim. The claim process was pretty easy and they actually approved me for a full refund. I just needed to fill out an affidavit. I did this but a week later I still had no refund. Somehow my affidavit didn't get logged even though I got a confirmation email. I called them on the telephone and they fixed everything and were kind about it. Within 24 hours they emailed me an Amazon gift certificate (my choice) which gave me an additional 5% back. I this received a $121 refund on an $118 printer that died in its 3rd year.

I have no complaints and would purchase a square trade warranty again.

Bits of interest as I read other people's low reviews:

1) You purchase a 4 year warranty, but really, for example, it is just 3 extra years beyond the purchase's original 1 year warranty (or however long applies). If your item dies in a year, you have to go to the manufacturer for help.

2) You need to have your receipt. No biggie. Amazon is super amazing that way. I can see all my order back to when Amazon just sold books. Print the invoice / receipt to PDF and there you go. Receipt. Proof of purchase.

3) There is no paper copy of this plan. This is great. It saves trees. You would probably lose it anyway. But Amazon also kept a copy of the fact that I purchased this along with the printer. It was in my order history. There is your proof and all the telephone numbers are there. It is so easy. You don't need a stack of papers.

4) If you file a claim and get 100% of your purchase price back, you cannot file a claim for the same item again. No brainer.

5) This isn't accident insurance. If you do a dumb thing like leave your camera on top of your husband's big rig fender and it ends up in a million pieces 1/2 mile from your house ... it is NOT covered. If you think it should be ... well then ... Take out an insurance policy ... not a warranty. Those are two different things.

6) If you got a deal and paid $65 for your item, but the item now sells for $400 ... you still only paid $65 and $65 is all you are getting back. You don't make money off warranties.

We've been using an older first generation Portal and like it very much. I was not expecting to be so impressed with this one, but wow have they managed to improve almost everything about the original! It still has the very cool zoom-and-pan style camera feature that follows the subject, as well as all the fun filters and of course my kids' favorite, story time... but the polish and style of this unit is really premium. The speaker is fantastic and LOUD if you want it to be. The clarity and bass rivals my bookshelf speakers so well, sometimes the kids play music off it and I could have sworn they were using the speakers in the living room. But the biggest improvement over the previous generation is the ability to run off battery power and move around. The "portable portal" honestly makes so much sense, I wonder why the original stationary style ones came out first!
Make no mistake, it is NOT a tablet, it is not thin and won't fit in an attaché case nicely. It is wedge-shaped making it stand easily at an ideal angle, and even has a cut-out handle to pick it up and carry it to a better location for video chat. This is great for bringing it to wherever my kids happen to be congregating currently, and it can be put back up on the shelf when done to charge. Like the original Portals, it has Alexa built in and can act as an Echo for most things, however it is very tied into Facebook's ecosystem. That means that although it seems to run something akin to Android behind the scenes, this is NOT going to offer a standard App store, and even things like Youtube are not available for it (licensing issues with Google I'd suppose). However there is a browser, and you can navigate to YouTube and play it from the website just fine, although a proper app would be much easier to navigate. It does have Plex support, which I found interesting since I have a Plex server. I never thought I'd find Plex available where Youtube is not! Meanwhile, between Youtube in the browser, Amazon Music through Alexa and content on Plex, there are plenty of ways to make it a music streamer on that glorious better-than-it-should-sound speaker. And the camera works just as well if not better than the OG Portal!
Calls over FB Messenger or Whatsapp work well, and of course the camera / mic not only have a switch to toggle, but the camera has a physical cover that can slide over the lens in case you don't trust Facebook not to snoop. But that's another story.
All things considered, this is a solid product.

The Lexar 32gb 3.0 USB Thumb Drive is likely the first usb 3.0 drive that I have had that has exceeded my expectations. It's not unusual to see speeds that disappoint when a drive claims high performance but this isn't the case with this drive. In addition to that, the sliding mechanism to protect the usb connector when not in use and the aluminum housing makes this feel like a premium product that will last.

When transferring large files from a pc via usb 3.0 from an SSD I saw maximum speeds of 140 mb/s and likely an overall average of 130. I was able to copy 13.6 gb folder of diablo 3 with a mixture of smaller files and larger data files in less than 2 minutes. That is outstanding write performance for a USB thumb drive. And read speeds are just as impressive as I was able to copy that same 13.6 gb's back to the same SSD drive with read speeds averaging 300 mb/s! I'm so used to usb drives letting me down when i was hoping for so much more.

The build quality has a very premium feel to it. It slides into your pocket without catching like some usb drives that have a rubber texture. The slide mechanism also feels consistent and doesn't feel like it will fail anytime, in fact i find myself fidgeting with it because it is so well done. It's not going to come out on accident and it does require you to "mean" to open it for it to slide out. It comes with a lanyard as well but I don't plan on putting this on my keychain anytime soon but was a nice to have feature.

Overall I am completely satisfied with this Lexar Drive and I would highly recommend it over some less expensive options.

I bought this to power two small (~3"x3") 12 volt heating pads to help keep me warm while working outside at night during a Colorado winter, and for that it performs admirably. While my use case is rather atypical, it should highlight just how flexible this rechargeable power supply is--anything that needs 12 volts and less than 3 amps is good to go.

The build quality is better than I was expecting, in all honesty, and for once I applaud the use of plastic over something like aluminum because the battery pack is already a bit on the heavy side and for something portable like this, every ounce counts.

I marked it down a star for a couple reasons:
1) The documentation that accompanied it was minimal and suffered from some translation issues (though I've come to expect that for products such as this). If not for reviews/questions here on Amazon, I wouldn't have known that the Red/Green LED indicator for charging is on the charger and not the battery pack. The battery pack LED is always Blue.
2) The Li Ion Charging/Protection Circuit is contained in the "wall wart" charger that comes with it. While I understand that this saves space in the battery pack itself (and I did just make the comment about every ounce counting), it also means that if I should lose the charger, I have to get another one to continue using the battery pack (the 18650 batteries used here are unprotected, I believe). For convenience, it would be nice to be able to plug the pack into any 12 volt power supply of sufficient amperage and have it charge without exploding.

These are truly minor gripes, though, and I am overall quite happy with this battery pack and its performance. I imagine I'll find another use for it when I no longer need it to provide life-saving warmth.

Even though I have always had an interest in astronomy I was never able to work a course in this subject in my college schedule or afterwards. When I saw this telescope offered I realized that now I had both the time and the means to explore my interest a bit further. I had very little difficulty setting the scope up, and spent some time familiarizing myself with the various components. I practiced using this by checking out objects in my neighborhood, and managed to get an 'up close and personal' view of some birds in a neighbor's yard and quickly realized that this scope was powerful.

That evening I took the scope to an upstairs window to see what I could see, and despite the pesky street light was able to get a great view of the full moon (btw did you know that it sparkles a bit?). I saw details that I had only seen in photos before which was fascinating. Then I decided to take a look at Mars, which was near the Moon that evening. That is when things got complicated. The finder scope and the main scope need to be synced, and I don't know how to do this (yet). With some fiddling, and aided by Mars' close proximity to the Moon I was able to find Mars, which was exciting but for some reason it was distorted (it had a starburst appearance). My husband and I fiddled with various lenses and combinations to try to eliminate this but were unsuccessful. The experimentation was further complicated by the touchiness of the stand....it was difficult to make small, smooth adjustments and to keep the scope locked in position. Some of this is no doubt due to our in expertise, some I think is due to the equipment.

My enjoyment of this scope would have been much greater if more instructions had been provided. We discovered, more or less by accident how to lock, at least partially, the scope into place. We managed to make some focusing adjustments by trial and error. Even some rudimentary instructions in a small booklet or even a sheet or two describing how to adjust, focus and lock the scope as well as an illustration of the scope with all the components clearly labeled with a brief description of their function would have been greatly appreciated. This is a basic instrument, one that will primarily be used by beginners or novices who will not necessarily be familiar with this equipment. Basic instructions should have been included. As it is my unfamiliarity with the various aspects of the telescope make following many of the instructions I do find on-line difficult to follow.

Despite this problems I am enjoying my new toy. I found the stand to be steady, and the tray located on the stand to be a handy place to put lenses and covers. As I mentioned earlier this is a surprisingly (at least to this beginning user) powerful scope. I'm going to play around with this some more, and will probably upgrade some of the lenses and add some accessories based on my experiences. Besides star gazing I think this will be a great item to watch birds or wild life, and it is certainly portable and forgiving enough to take on a camping trip.

I do a LOT of work in front of a computer, and was getting these for when I work at home. At work, I use a Logitech 930 headset that I really like. I got these so I wouldn't yank my laptop off the desk when I get up. I got bluetooth, thinking they'd be easy to sync to my various devices. So, here's my breakdown:

Range
I can go upstairs and grab a few things or go two rooms away and I still get a signal. The range is pretty good on these.

Playback Sound
The playback sound quality is okay. Not blowing me away, but alright. I listen to music, no vocals, to block out the office noise and keep my head focused. The playback audio goes into tin-can mode when the mic is enabled. That's something I didn't realize as a limitation of how bluetooth handles the two signals. That took me a while to figure out.

Microphone
The mic is okay. It just flips me out that the playback goes into "phone mode" when the mic is enabled.

Battery
Well, I've only had these a couple of months. But, the battery seems to go at least as long as I can stand to keep them on my head. Max has been about 2 hours at a stretch before giving my head/ears a break.

Fit
I'm an adult and my head is average-sized, not large. After maybe three months these cans are still a bit tight. The cups don't quite fit entirely over my ears and get uncomfortable after maybe two hours --like, *ouch* uncomfortable.

Heat
These cans get pretty hot after maybe 45 minutes. Hot like I just got out of the shower and I need a towel in my ears hot. I don't think I've ever had sweaty ears like this before from a set of headphones.

Sync
I've easily sync'd these to Ubuntu 14.04 & 10, Windows 7, and OS X Mavericks.

Would I recommend these to a friend?
No. I like not having to carry a dongle around since bluetooth is in all of my computers (one has an $8 dongle that works just fine.) But, they get so hot, and are still not comfortable on my head and ears after maybe 100 hours of use. So, for the $50 price tag, I'd probably have to say no. If they were $25 and just to make the occasional phone call I might recommend them to a friend, but not to wear for any period of time. If they were just a bit more comfortable, and breathed a bit better, I'd change my mind. Maybe in the next revision, Photive?

A very impressive looking speaker. The unit has good heft to it and if feels sturdy and it is exceptionally well constructed. It also sounds really good. At full volume it can easily fill a decent sized room with sound, the bass is clear, with great mid range and wonderful highs.

There are white lights on the front that bounce and light up and pulse to the music. Very cool for a party, but grows old quick. I was hoping to take this camping, but I don’t want dancing lights when I’m out in the woods. I can’t seem to find a way to turn them off. The instructions are very sparse and not helpful at all.

It also is supposed to have a feature where you tap (more like hit hard) the speaker for sounds like a high hat, cymbal, and Tom Tom. when it works, it’s pretty cool, but it seemed to only work intermittently. And in order for it to sound any good at all, you have to hit it very hard.

Connecting to it is easy. You can connect through your phone’s Bluetooth or tap your phone on it, if it has NFC, for even easier connections. It also has a aux port for connecting with an aux wire. Battery lasts a long time.

Overall it’s a good sounding speaker, and it’s well made. But be warned, depending on what you want it for, this may not be for you. The lights that won’t shut off and the unit time off (even when on external power) as well as the short power cable make me not recommend it to many people.

I have had the opportunity to review many headsets and headphones over the years and without question the recent technological advancements have aided this area by leaps and bounds.

I can not recommend buying Bluetooth 5.2 enough over previous technologies if your devices support it. Nearly all devices that are Bluetooth 5.2 capable, including this one, will be backwards compatible with earlier technologies as well.

Battery life is outstanding with these headsets lasting a solid 5 hours each in all of my tests. It is easily charged using the included charging case which will allow the earbuds to be recharged several times from its one full charge. Since the earbuds can be used together for stereo sound or individually you can potentially double play time by using one at a time.

This unique charging case is powered via an included super fast standard USB to USB Type C cable. This case will allow the headsets to be recharged even when you don’t have access to electricity.

After receiving, I made sure the case was fully charged then confirmed each earbud had a full charge. After verifying full power within each earbud I followed the simple pairing instructions and had no problems whatsoever. Once the earbuds are removed from the case they first pair with each other then you simply pair with your Bluetooth device.

The design of these headset makes it so it fits securely in your ear and is relatively comfortable. As someone who has used many of these units, this design is not the most comfortable as the weight is all on the ear canal. I’ve found headsets that are worn only supported by the ear canal can end up being painful when used for extended periods.

The sound from these headphones is decent - from the rich bass notes to the vibrant midtones to the bright treble. I tested these headphones with a wide range of audio - from audiobooks to jazz, heavy metal, country, classical and blues - everything sounded reasonable.

I have listened to both music and audiobooks through these as I moved throughout my home and it will easily pick up the signal through walls up to 25’ away, and even more without obstacles. This is a decent set Bluetooth headphones.

While these are great for listening to music, how are they for calling? The sound through these headphones is absolutely outstanding - on both ends. That is not always the case. Many of the other headphones I have tested, while they sound good to the person using it - those who they are speaking to can’t hear them clearly. It is no fun having a conversation where the other person keeps saying, “huh, what did you say?” You won’t have to worry about that with this set.

If you are looking for a decent headphone set, especially one at a reasonable price, with decent sound and reception and has the power to last this is a great choice.

I have a strong interest in photography and I always keep an eye open for lights and equipment that will help me take more creative or impactful pictures. I selected this light with the intent of using it for creative photography and so far I am pleased with it. I have other LED lights that have similar functions, but this one is different in a few ways that set it apart.

This is a wand light as opposed to a square LED bank. As such, the light distribution is a bit different. It can directly cover a longer (wider) area which is handy when putting together a mock-up with miniatures. It has a couple of mounting options too, utilizing either a miniature tripod (included) or magnetically attaching to a metal surface. I do wish a clamp was included such that it could attach to the tripod horizontally, but such clamps are available if they're needed.

This light is VERY bright and can easily light a small room when at full brightness. It can be dimmed to cast a soft light too which is good. It's not exactly the most ideal light source but it will work for general lighting in a pinch.

The temperature range goes from 2500k (very warm and orange-y) to 9900k (blistering cold white) and everywhere in between. Getting the color just right is relatively easy though it does take a little patience and experimentation to get it right. Do keep in mind that because this is an LED-based light, the temperature band setting is quite narrow and presents a different light profile, one that the camera can see but the human eye cannot. In addition to "natural lighting" modes it can be set for specific colors too such as purple, red, blue and so on.

If what you're looking for is a complete backup utility, that's reasonably easy to use, this one might suit your purpose.

Installation, update, and activation are easy, similar to other Symantec programs. (This one also uses Live Update.) I do have an objection to the fact that Symantec never does a full uninstall -- they leave around stuff in the registry, as well as LiveUpdate, and it requires extra work (and some technical skill) to remove everything. I take off one star for that.

The setup is quite simple, especially if you follow their procedures. A full system backup is recommended, and the program will nag you about your system being "at risk" if you don't set up the full backup. You can in addition set up backup jobs for selectively backing up some of your files and folders. So for instance you might want to do nightly backup of your key folders, and weekly or monthly backup of the full system.

I would recommend that you use a network disk (NAS) for your backup -- there are many not-too-expensive products available, and I've been quite happy with the Buffalo products.

You can also use this program to do remote management of other computers on your network, but be aware that each computer needs its own license for the program.

One thing I don't like is that the backup files are not copies, they are in a compressed format. For daily backups I prefer to be able to make normal copies of files, so that I can go quickly to the backup folder and find a backup copy I might want. This optimizes my time and convenience over computer time and disk space, and this is how it should be. Or at least, this should at least be an option.

I take off another star for the nagging about full system backup, and the unavailability of a simple file backup or file sync (backup by copying selected files/folders directly from one disk to another).

But overall a solid program that does what it says, and does it competently. Just make sure what you want is what it wants to do. :-)

I spent months, literally, shopping for a radio for my kitchen/dining area. I had awful problems with reception with every radio I had in there, so reception was at the top of my want list. Size and cost figured in too, but reception was the key because I like listening to the radio while I work.

Every radio I researched had someone complaining about the horrible reception. Every single one. I was paralyzed with fear that I'd pick the wrong one so I just kept looking, hoping to find one where everyone said "Get it, the reception is fantastic!"

Finally I realized that reception depends on so many variables that no radio is going to work for everyone everywhere and I was able to quit shopping and actually order the Sangean CL-100. The price was good and the size was perfect for the space I had in mind.

I know you're all waiting with bated breath to hear that the reception, even in an old building where it's difficult to get good cell reception, is spectacularly good. It even picks up a lot of the smaller and more distant stations. Tuning and changing settings is relatively simple and the sound quality is good enough for a kitchen radio. It has some serious volume on it, so I can turn it up and listen while I'm making the bed or cleaning the bathroom. No the sound isn't great at that distance, but again, it's all a matter of convenience for this radio.

If you're like me and want a small, simple-to-operate radio that will (probably, no guarantee) pick up your favorite stations, give the Sangean a shot. You could spend more, but do you really need to?

As convenient as this product makes hooking up networking cables, the cheap screws that come with this wall plate make installation a nightmare.

Do yourself a favor, if you have an extra light switch plate laying around, use those screws instead. I've installed two of these ethernet wall plates into two different low voltage mounting brackets. There are no threads in these mounting brackets. You're essentially creating the threads as you go. This necessitates a greater amount of torque and the screw heads are shallow. If using hand tools, this will require immense amounts of force to prevent stripping the heads. Normally, only a small, flat blade screwdriver is all that is required. But this installation works best if you have a powered screwdriver that will provide the necessary torque.

If you can run the screws in and out prior to installation, it may prevent some headaches. I did something similar to the first low voltage mounting bracket I purchased too.

You'll also find that if you have some screws from an existing light switch plate, that they have a deeper slot and are half the length. The provided screws were much longer than necessary. I replaced the screws on the second wall plate I installed after backing out the originals with a set of pliers after the heads were damaged.

To put this into context, I have the right tools and do more DIY than most other people I know.

I received these as a free review sample eight months ago. Since there are a lot of detailed reviews I will focus on my experience with these and also compare them to other sports phones.

First, these are good quality for twenty buck phones. But do be aware that sports phones are designed for comfort more than sound quality. Not that these are marginal - they have a typical bias towards the mid range, with compressed highs and adequate bass. They are not going to win acclaim from audiophiles, but do reproduce music that is clear and perfect for background listening.

Another thing I like is comfort. I can wear these for a few hours at a time without even noticing them. For sports phones that is a major plus. These allow in a little ambient noise for safety, but it does not appreciably affect the quality of music. Volume is somewhat limited. If you like music super loud these are not going to make you happy. On the other hand, high volume defeats the purpose of sports phones since you need to be aware of ambient noise and your surroundings. I cannot emphasize strongly enough that these are NOT general purpose phones.

Finally, the specs claim about four hours of music play time. That is true with the volume at about a third. If you crank the volume to max you can cut that time in half.

[[VIDEOID:1be91bfc02339bd396543d05da1fee38]] There are SO many things about the Angel's Horn turntable that impress me. But, first, you need to be a true audiophile to appreciate the way this turntable was designed and built.

Gone are the days of the automatic turntable, where you just drop on a stack of records and walk away. Those things were the WORST! Sure, you were free to do other things for longer periods of time. But, they were very harmful to your records. A true collector would NOT even consider having one of those things.

First, the body of the turntable is ONE SOLID PIECE OF OAK! No particle board, no hollow box, no cheap crap!

Then, there is the direct one-belt drive, no multiple gears or belts. And the motor has ONE job, the turntable. Changing the records and setting the tonearm are YOUR job, as is true with any turntable worth it's status as 'top of the line' with this one.

Now, the tonearm is another factor. As we all know, too much pressure on the record (or too little) can affect the quality of the sound, not to mention the wear on the vinyl. And, vinyl is a fragile medium, revered as one of the best sources of true stereophonic sound. We vinyl fans collect the best recordings and do everything we can to preserve that quality. When we play our records, we do so with love and care. The tonearm on this turntable is built just for us. It's counterweight is perfect, allowing us to adjust the balance to a microgram. I've not found a tonearm with a more accurate adjustment as this one.

The ability to switch between input types is a nice feature. Some of us prefer to provide our own preamps, allowing us further tweaking of the sound quality. I do. Thank you.

The dust cover is great for those that have their turntable out on top. I have mine contained within my entertainment center and opted to leave it off.

I am VERY happy with my Angel's Horn turntable and very happy to give it five stars.

IMPORTANT ADVICE... do not thread the mini ball head onto anything too tightly. This stand is actually fine, it's the cheap ball head that has given me headaches. The ball head has a... I'm not sure what the technical term is for this kind of bolt, but lets call it a "dual bolt." 1/4 bolt is threaded inside a bigger bolt, I presume 1/2. I threaded a mini projector onto this thing, I guess a little too tight. When I unthreaded the projector, the 1/4 bolt was stuck, meaning it was unthreading WITH the projector. So the 1/4 bolt came off the 1/2 bolt. You would think that all it takes are some pliers, but surprisingly, pliers even with teeth, have a hard time gripping this bolt. I had to use my drill press vise to get it off.

To properly use that ball head, you want to thread it onto whatever device you're using, but don't thread it on too tight like me. Then tighten with the lower knob. You might think, this reviewer isn't using common sense. I don't think so at all. Anybody would like his/her electronics threaded securely. The amount of strength I used was reasonable. The issue lies in that inner 1/4 bolt not being secured enough inside that bigger bolt. But I fixed that. Once I was able to unthread the projector from the vise... with the 1/4 bolt now free, but secured by the vise, I then took the ball head body to the vise and threaded the bigger bolt onto the 1/4 bolt a "wee bit" tighter than the manufacturer did.

If you don't have drill press vise like I do, then you better be extra careful using this. 3-Stars.

This has solved multiple problems. having 5 HDMI inputs is a pretty sweet deal. I've only tested 3 of them so far and they work just fine. One nice feature that I didn't expect is that it doesn't appear to let you switch to an input that doesn't have a device even powered on, at least using the remote.
The picture quality is just fine. I have nothing to compare it to, but it looks no worse than it ever did.
The nice feature of my previous switch was that it did not need to be powered. The Koopman one DOES need power. It comes with the micro USB cable and power adapter, but if your TV has an open 5v usb output, that might be more convenient. I had to plug it in. It's a minor annoyance, but if you're low on outlet space, keep it in mind.
It's small and light, so I'll need to anchor it in place so it's not flying off the stand. HDMI cables like to pull things awry. It's almost inconspicuous.
Speaking of HDMI cables, it doesn't come with one. I had expected (and didn't pay attention to the product description - so MY bad) at least a short one.
The remote is tiny. This is great because it doesn't take up much space, but I KNOW I'm going to spend a bunch of events looking for it in the couch or under the footrest or because a spider dragged it into their web in the corner. The remote worked from at least 15-20 feet away (as far as I could comfortably go), BUT, the angle of reception is not very wide. It might be about 60 degrees (I did not pull out the protractor). The box itself had a button on it, so if the remote goes temporarily missing, you can still tap your way between inputs.
I'll give it some time to see how it lasts. If it does well over time, I'll possibly buy another for another TV with only one HDMI input.
One cool improvement would be if it had an audio output, even in only a 1/8" port.

I prefer a good messenger bag to a backpack most of the time. I prefer the way a messenger bag looks, how it is organized and how it provides protection to the contents of the bag most of the time, the trade-off being reduced space when compared to a regular-sized backpack. This is a nice bag and I am pleased with it. It recently came in very handy when we were traveling.

This is a large, canvas messenger bag. The canvas used is not the heaviest grade canvas I have seen but it is not the lightest or softest either. It seems to be the right balance of durability and softness as the bag is durable and holds up to abuse but is still soft and pliable enough to be workable in most spaces (like crammed behind a car seat).

Most messenger bags I have seen of late have used magnets as the closing mechanism and this one does so too. There are two leather straps on the flap that have buckles, but these buckles are strictly decorative. Attached to the main body of the bag and to the buckles are magnets and plates that work to close the back with little effort. They hold as well as metal snaps in most cases, the exception being if you overstuff the bag. There is a zipper to supplement the flap, so if you can zip the bag then you can snap it shut too.

The bag has a large main compartment that has a padded divider in the middle. This compartment is large enough to handle a smaller laptop (and I have a 10” tablet and keyboard that fits it very well) and it also is large enough to handle a couple of books. It also has a zippered pocket in the main compartment that is a good size for a phone, a calculator or a small note pad. On the front of the bag on the outside there are two small pockets that are also good for small items. This bag is about the right side for a school bag or a “go bag” with essential tools in it.

This is a good bag and I like it. It is well-made, roomy and has a good layout for the space and pockets. It’s a good choice if you need a durable and useful daily bag or even an emergency tool bag.

I will be keeping a close eye on this router, which I just purchased yesterday, because it seems too good to be true. So far, in my 24 hours of usage since purchasing it for $29 at Walmart (sorry, Amazon, I was in a hurry) I have found it to be flexible and powerful in my unusual application, which is remote and requires 100% uptime with occasional bursts of heavy usage. Mine is a factory-fresh rather than refurb unit, incidentally.

I'll admit I had some trouble believing a router this cheap could be as good as this one turned out to be (assuming it stays reliable-- but, the one I bought trumpets a lifetime guarantee on the box). I expected something dumbed-down, with seriously constrained functionality and annoying firmware. (This model's v3 hardware, although Broadcom BCM5356-based, is not compatible with alternative firmware such as DD-WRT due to its problematic NVRAM size.) It's a single-stream design, with an internalized antenna, potentially suggesting performance limitations. And it's from Netgear, which I've frankly not had great luck with before... but it's been years since I've tried one of their products, and the reviews here are generally good. Most of the negative reviews here relate to support experiences, but my networking knowledge-level is expert, so ...what the heck, did I mention it was $29? An easy roll of the dice.

Though my application requires custom configuration, I initially started the unit using its web-based wizard, which you access by connecting your computer (via cable or WiFi) and pointing your browser to 192.168.1.1. With the unit connected to my cable modem, it set itself up quickly and voila, Internet. For most people this would be good enough and the job would be done. Kudos to Netgear for delivering the product with WPA-2 encryption enabled! They provide a SSID and password on a printed label. So, you're good to go. And its default configuration is just fine for most folks' usage.

For my application, however, I needed to cable several devices including a VoIP adaptor (a la [...] and a server with several ports exposed to the Internet. The unit needed to be set to a specific IP address scheme, SSID and password. And a dynamic-DNS utility on the server needed to communicate with my DNS provider. ...To accomplish these and other advanced tasks, the browser-based configurator at 192.168.1.1 has an Advanced tab. Proceeding through the settings is straightforward and similar to other reasonably-configurable routers. The default settings established earlier by the wizard remain intact in the Advanced panes so you are starting from a known-operable configuration. All good.

So I proceeded through each of my customizations, taking care to click the Apply button after modifying any pane. Usually there's a ten-second delay during which the unit sets up the new settings; a few necessitate that the router reboot itself. Everything went smoothly.

So, for $29 I'd replicated an unusual configuration and everything was working. But how well?

Okay so my wife had to take an important international FaceTime call as I was finishing up. So, for a while there the server was downloading some massive updates, two ssh clients were talking to the server, VoIP was in use, six WiFi clients were doing whatever they were doing, a 3G microcell tower was initializing and downloading firmware updates to itself ...and FaceTime was running smoothly with a high frame-rate on her third-gen iPad. A nice acid test!

In particular, I did not feel the need to mess with the unit's default QoS settings... and additional props to Netgear for including QoS in a router this inexpensive!

So far, I'm impressed. It's hard to imagine a better value in a router. I'll update this review if there are any reliability issues, but so far, so good. So excellent, in fact.

The rooCASE Oragami Case seems to be currently at or near the top of the cases, the big advantage of this case being the number and variations of orientations, including both portrait and landscape, and at the price point, is hard to beat.  The oragami cover is ingenious, you can fold it up all sorts of ways, the iPad Air has a lot of applications that fairly beg for portrait orientation (reading a book, newspaper, etc.).  The conventional Apple case supports only landscape, as do a number of competitors (the CaseCrown Omni is one of the better conventional ones).  The Moshi and O!Case are also oragami cases, although the designs differ some.  The rooCASE has a more rubberized or grippy exterior, key because it's less likely to slip and get dropped.  Protection is generally pretty good, but the CaseCrown does a little better on edge protection, the openings on the rooCase tend to be U-shaped, the CaseCrown is more O-Shaped, but otherwise they are very similar.  The Moshi has one advantage, in that it has a back magnet, that lets it stay open better in book mode.  The rooCASE actually has magnets that keep it closed pretty well, but it lacks a back magnet.  The rooCase front cover of course folds up to support quite a number of variations or angles, which is a big advantage over conventional cases, and on a desk or table, is plenty stable.  The microfiber front interior is nice, it tends to help keep the screen clean, but it is worth noting that the orgami pattern tends to show up in the fingerprints and grease, so you do need to clean the screen from time to time.  rooCASE also shuts off the iPad Air screen when you close it, a very useful feature.  The end result is still pretty light and easy to carry, in keeping with the iPad Air design point.  Why not 5 stars?  rooCase is very close, but they could improve the edge coverage/protection, and add a back magnet (ala Moshi), and NuGuard KX probably has the better back protection (at the cost of some bulk), but at its price-point, front and back protection, oragami design that lets you pick multiple orientations and angles, the rooCASE is pretty much unbeatable, and worthy of consideration at any price.

As I am sure is the case with many, I purchased this after seeing it listed by the New York Times in their portable BT transmitter review list. It was bought specifically to allow me to transmit BT audio from my computer to my Sony WF-1000XM3 earbuds. As the Sony earbuds only support SBC with these, I wasn't expecting stellar audio quality - I usually use them for lectures or podcast-like content, or for fairly low-bitrate music anyway. I wanted to see if the advantages of true-wireless earbuds were worth the sacrifice in quality before I invested in a more expensive BT transmitter and BT receiver+high-end IEMs. As such, I do not use the receive function, and I do not use the battery on the unit - it is always plugged in via USB. I did briefly test the battery though and can confirm it lasts at least 30m.

Note: I went with this type unit, instead of USB, because I wanted to have the ability to test it in multiple environments, including while running and in the car for single-ear usage. Normally, I'd go with a USB solution for computer use in order to avoid the conversion of the audio from to and back from analog.

Initial Setup

Dead simple - I connected the Line Out on my computer to the input on the transmitter, and alternately, the HP out on my stereo receiver to the input on the transmitter. I also tried it with a Sansa Clip+ MP3 player. It worked in all cases, though with the WF-1000XM3 I had to keep the input volume on the BT transmitter under 30% and allow the headphones to do the real amplification, as otherwise the audio would distort.

BT Setup

Fairly simple. I put my earbuds into pairing mode, the transmitter into pairing mode, and they connected within 10s. Afterward, they maintained their connection for the most part, I've had to re-pair a couple times over the last three weeks, but that is mostly a learning curve. Re-pairing is easy - just hold the pairing button down for two seconds and place the receiving device in pairing mode.

Range

Unpredictable, and sensitive. If the transmitter is located on a desk, at least twelve inches away from other electronics, then the range is remarkable. I can leave the room, pass through the adjacent room, and enter into the next room - a total of maybe thirty feet, through two or three walls - and start to lose audio at the end. This is despite being only five feet from a wireless router. However, if I move the transmitter six inches over so it is next to my monitor, or a couple feet so that it is within three feet of the router, the earbuds will begin to drop out even at ten feet. So it is very sensitive to environment.

Audio Quality

Decent. Better than I expected, but I haven't used bluetooth audio in ten years. It can be hard to really gauge it, because the Sony WF-1000XM3 are true wireless earbuds and I can't A/B test them to compare BT quality to a cable. I would say that the BT audio quality is equivalent to that produced when my Sony earbuds are connected to my smartphone. While it is decent, it can't compare to wired earbuds of even fairly middling quality. You lose highs and lows. For dialogue content, lectures and the like, no issue.

Summary

Seems to be a great entry-level transmitter for the average consumer. I'm glad I bought it, because it is reliable and easy to use, and has shown me that the freedom of using wireless earbuds is definitely worth the hit to quality - I can always use my full circumaural headphones if I want to watch a movie or listen critically. Would recommend.

There's a lot to like about this kit, starting with the price. For the money, I've owned similar light kits to this before, but this one comes with batteries and chargers for wireless use as well as the AC plug adapters for constant power. Similar kits that I've owned required me to buy the Sony-style FP batteries separately. It also comes with a soft case, however I found the case very flimsy and not very protective (it comes folded up inside the box, there is no rigidity to it). BUT, I realized that the box it comes it is roughly a similar size to the case when unfolded, and sure enough it actually can fit inside the case perfectly! I'm not sure if this was on purpose, it was not obvious to me that this was the intention so maybe don't throw away that cardboard if you want to give your case some protective strength (see attached photo for carboard box inside carrying case).
As far as the lights themselves... they are pretty good. I was concerned about them being less densely populated than other LED panels I've used, however it appears that each diode puts out more light than I was expecting so overall it is a good amount of light for using with video for something like an interview setting.
Meanwhile, the colors and party mode are a bit different for me. I'm used to using light kits as a professional tool, and I think the multicolor part is a bit too gimmicky. It's cool to set a tone with a color like the way I'd gel a red light for a setting or something, but the party mode? I can't imagine a use for the strobe effect of it changing color constantly. I have DJ lights that can move to music and this has a mode for that as well, however it seems that the only option is to change color with each beat suddenly- no gradual fade or anything like that. The hard cut is kind of migraine-inducing distracting, so I'd honestly rather use a different light for party background style color changes. As a light kit, it's pretty good, but the selling point of using it as a sound-controlled DJ thing is iffy. Maybe a DJ at a bar mitzvah would find that option useful?

Slide two little metal sliders on side to remove back cover to remove battery. But you don't have to, it's in the electronic screen "Info" :)

Persons much more mechanically inclined than I will see that the door to the SIM card is on the side edge, not in the back or under the battery. I would have ruined the device trying to dig out the back compartment if my husband hadn't stopped me. He needed tweezers to get out the SIM card regardless.

This is a great, mobile, easy HotSpot device that works just like any Wi-Fi on any device with a great connection. Mobile supposedly for 10 hours, less than hour recharge.

There's only one caveat: AT&T will tell you the pre-installed SIM card it comes with, sealed in new packaging, is INVALID. AT&T will give you a good one for FREE. You simply have to replace it, or if you're like me, get someone that can. :) That simple, and you're ready for set-up. *NOTE*: Both the pre-installed SIM card *AND* the SIM card being sold by a separate seller on Amazon that is suggested as being a good companion purchase with this device are INVALID. This according to AT&T themselves. They will send you a new, free one you can use; tell them what device you have and setup a data plan.

All you need then is to add a Data plan. This device, according to AT&T, *only* works with a postpaid plan ($50.00/month for 5 G's minimum), however there's no contract. There is a credit check. It will not work with prepaid, it will not work with a lesser plan, no matter what the packaging or Amazon description says. I just spent like 20 minutes on the phone with a very helpful, patient, and knowledgeable AT&T customer service representative who also consulted another department for verification.

The one exception is if you already have an AT&T cellphone plan (I do), you can "share" your data package you already have for only $20/month. So that's what I did. It still is postpaid, and there still is no contract on that part of the plan with your new HotSpot device. You'll be given a new number that's only for the HotSpot without a cellphone (Voice) plan component.

I'm really glad I bought this great device, I was a little apprehensive because I'm not techie and I've never tried a mobile HotSpot device before. To make it simple, get AT&T to install (instore) or send you a new SIM card that they say works with this device, and then you can set up the device (supposedly) online with ease. You have to add a data plan for it. I'll update if there's a problem, but the connection to my laptop worked seamlessly and looking through the device hardware and software on the electronic screen, it's designed beautifully and is a definite winner! :) :)

ps. Oh!, and it DOES receive 4G out of the box! :) Shows right in the screen corner like a Cellphone would with the bars.

There are a lot of things I like about this smartwatch. The face is smaller than other smartwatches I've looked at and tried, about 1.09" which is perfect for me. The design of the watch is really pretty, and I like how the neutral color goes with many outfits. One thing I do wish is that the watchband was changeable so that I could change it if the band wore out or broke (or if I wanted a different style). Most of the smartwatches with changeable bands are those with the large face, a little disappointing. Battery power is good. I use the smartwatch quite often so I tend to hook it up to the battery charger twice a week. I like how I could choose from a variety of screen displays to fit what my preferences are.

The app this smartwatch uses is great, the Da Fit app. It's super easy to use, you don't have to use Bluetooth to find the watch, you just use the app to find it. I like how it has a variety of physical activity you can choose to monitor, jogging, biking, walking, etc. The sleep feature is pretty good, the biggest detractor is that it only follows typical sleeping hours. It won't work for anyone who sleeps different hours due to working night shift. Hopefully they'll update that in the app someday. The blood pressure feature seems to be pretty accurate to what the doctor tells me my blood pressure is.

Since I really don't want to put out the money for the brand name smartwatches, I am very pleased that I can still enjoy quite a few of the features for a more reasonable price. I'd recommend this watch and it would make a great gift.

Update- After a couple weeks of use, the on/off button on the side of the watch popped off and a spring came out. It's so tiny I'm unable to find it. I wasn't using it excessively, so I'm disappointed that something on the watch would break within weeks of use. It's a really nice watch, and they have great customer care so hopefully my issue is not a common problem.

Most times when I'm taking pictures I'm looking to express myself artistically rather than get a 100% accurate capture. So, color accuracy is not my primary concern - I'll play with color in post processing to get the picture to reflect what *I* want to depict, which may or may not be what others see when they look at what I'm shooting.

But, there are also times when you want the color to be 100% accurate. For those occasions, the Color Checker Passport is an excellent tool to have in your bag.

Using it is pretty straightforward if you're comfortable with working with color balancing charts and profiles. There are a variety of color samples and a white balance card that come in a sturdy plastic case. You unfold the case and include it in your shot (according to X-Rite, the chart needs to take up at least 10% of your image).

The case is well-designed so that it will stand up so it can be properly lit. Construction is solid - it will seems like it will easily survive the usual bumps and bruises of being carried around (unlike the more traditional paper MacBeth Color Checker).

The case alone would make this worthwhile to have in your bag, but the included software extends the functionality so you can create color profiles. It's pretty straightforward to use. First, convert the RAW file that includes the Passport in the shot to a DNG file. You can use Lightroom for the conversion or the Adobe DNG converter. You then load the DNG and the software creates the profile that you can use in Lightroom or Photoshop.

If you're a Lightroom user you can use the included Lightroom plug in which streamlines the workflow a bit. Lightroom will convert the RAW file to a DNG automatically, so you save a step.

You can create a profile from a single illumination (one DNG image) or from two different illuminations (2 DNG images). Using two DNG images allows you to create a more flexible profile that covers a broader range.

My first use was to take a shot of my kitchen counters so I could bring a photo to the store to pick out a coordinating paint color. The counter is ceramic tile with a number of subtle shades running through it (and, of course, I don't have any extra tiles to bring with me). The Passport ensured the shots I took were spot on accurate.

The shortcomings are few. The software seems a bit bloated in size, but that seems to be par for the course nowadays. I'd also like it if the case were just a wee bit bigger. Yes, the compact size is a plus, but I think X-Rite was a bit too focused on getting this to be about the size of a passport (which I'm guessing is the genesis of the name).

Excellent addition to your tool chest, especially if you do a lot of production shooting under controlled conditions.

Most of the places I have lived have been reasonably safe, so I have never felt any pressing need to add a camera security system to my home. I already have an alarm system, which is useful, but no camera system. I decided that it would be good to be able to see people at the main entrances to my home/property and this convinced me to add the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System to my house.

Setting this security system up is simple enough. You have to mount the included 2 cameras and it doesn’t take much time to complete this step. I placed one of them by my front door and the other one just outside my garage, facing the driveway. The gated entrance to my backyard is right there, and I usually leave my car in the driveway and not the garage, so this seemed like a good place.

There are many things to like about this security camera system, like the wide angle of view that is good for seeing from my backyard gate to the end of my driveway. You can even speak back and forth with someone at your front door and this can prove useful when you want to avoid talking directly, face to face, with solicitors.

With the image quality, although it isn’t as sharp as I expected, it seems sufficient to me. I haven’t experienced any intruders thus far- knock on wood- so I haven’t necessarily needed to get crystal clear details. One limitation I have is that I haven’t owned a camera security system before. This is a first for me, so I don’t have any point of comparison. Still, the picture quality seems good. And I like the notification system. Any motion detection is set up to record, so you can see what is going on and you know quickly.

The app itself is user- friendly enough but one thing to keep in mind is that the Arlo Smart Servive and cloud recording are free for only the first year. After that, you have to pay for a subscription. I will wait to see if the system is worth my while, then decide whether to subscribe. A year of free usage time should be sufficient to make the call.

Security is important and the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System is a good way to keep safe. Two cameras are definitely better than one because I am able to secure the two areas of my property where an unwanted individual is most likely to show up. I find the app and picture quality good and the system as a whole has enough positive points to recommend.

The user interface revolves around the books and videos that you bought from Amazon. With a considerable amount of work, you may be able to replace the user interface with a more standard Android launcher that focuses on your apps and files. Realistically, the performance of this tablet clunky enough that I don't recommend it unless you are mostly using it for e-books and videos, so maybe changing the user interface is not worth the effort.

You should also ask yourself if you are using the tablet for mostly e-books and videos, do you really need a 10 inch screen? The 8 inch Kindle Fire tablet has similar performance and a much lower price and is also lighter weight and less bulky, making it easier to use in many situations.

I have tested and reviewed several WiFi extenders and this one works nearly as well as one that cost over six times as much and was far easier to set up.

I set this up simply using the WPS pairing method with the extender being plugged in next to my primary router. It paired perfectly in just over a minute and I was able to unplug it and move it to an outlet farther away where it would then repeat my signal for greater range into my shop in my back yard. This worked perfectly.

Here are a few tips for getting the most out of this or any similar device.

1. Understand this will only extend the coverage you already have. If you are not satisfied with your current speed when located close to your current router this type of device will not help. In this instance you will need to improve your internet service, modem or router.
2. An extender / repeater must be placed close enough to receive an optimal signal that it then repeats - if it is too far away, it can only transmit what it picks up - if this signal is weakened due to distance from your primary router the end result will be a reduced signal. It can only work with the signal it is receiving.
3. When placing any extender / repeater pay attention to what is between it and your primary router - keep in mind interior walls tend to not have insulation and are thus easier to penetrate than exterior walls, metal objects deflect signals more than other materials as do especially dense materials.
4. Optimally a primary router should be placed in a centralized location within a home and where the bulk of the time is spent. Extenders / repeaters can then be utilized between that and where you have found weak signal points.
5. In some instances, such as within Mesh WiFi networks extenders / repeaters can slow down the entire network and are thus not advised. A lot of this depends on advanced settings.

I found myself needing to teach from home, like most US teachers, because of covid-19. Using zoom and whiteboard software locally, I would attempt to maintain some of the same methods I use in class, but also knew I'd need to do a lot more "showing" for that low ratio of students showing up for conferences sessions. It meant I could write (doing math work) in the whiteboard software without trying to do it with a mouse or fumble equations in real time with an equation editor or giving too much away using Geogebra.
I'm also a lefty, so that proved annoying quickly. It defaults to right handed mode, and the body that holds the electronics gets in the way. So I HAD to find drivers. Thankfully at Github (search Linux driver for Veikk-brand digitizers ) there is a driver. Installing was not too bad (had to compile myself - and had to find a fix for something getting in the compile way, search ""FATAL: Module veikk not found in directory" and a potential fix" at github).
Viola! The touch sensitivity works just fine and I can rotate the orientation, by manually editing parameters in /sys/module/veikk/parameters
Great, but then I had to find the GUI, because it kept resetting my orientation setting any time I rebooted. Search "Configuration tool for the VEIKK Linux driver" at github for the gui installer. It gave me hassles to install, but somehow I got it installed. Idon't use it much, but somehow it also keeps my orientation setting correct on reboots, and that's what I cared most about. I could change button configs and the sensitivity curve, but I'm not there yet.
Openboard (foss whiteboard) actually works with the touch sensitivity, but Activinspire doesn't. No big deal. Gimp doesn't until you set it to in device settings. Krita didn't need to be told what to do and works wonderfully.

My complaints:
The PITA driver installation isn't one really. They don't officially support linux - THAT is worthy of a complaint though. For those using linux, I'm going to guess, still, many are used to dealing with this.
The placement of the USB cord is annoying when in lefty (108 deg orientation), as the cord comes in your direction.
The drawing surface isn't huge, but that's a given. The challenge is that the sensitive area goes very close to the edge, making it hard to draw on the edges if you are not using this on a regular flat surface. I'm using it on my lap, most of the time.
The pen is also thick! 7/16" or 11mm diameter. Not super comfy. My hands aren't small. It makes using the buttons a little less than optimal, but I don't use them much yet anyway. I'm sure as I do more art with it than math, I'll want to customize that. I have an older wacom stylus I'll try to locate and see if it magically works. It was a far better fit.
All said and done, I do recommend this. I might even buy one of the larger ones.

My hat size is 6-7/8 (man's small), to give you some perspective on how these fit. With the headphones adjusted to their most compact size, they fit me perfectly, so there is plenty of expansion room for larger heads. They might be too large for a younger child, however, and I know some children are into gaming. So keep that in mind.

Installation is straightforward, and you should definitely download the THX software to get the full benefit of these headphones. An icon for it was not automatically added to my desktop, but I was able to find the software in the Creative folder (it's not the Alchemy one; I don't know what that is). The software allows you to adjust and save equalizer settings as well as game-enhancing features under the TruStudio Pro tab: crystalizer, surround, bass, dialog plus, and smart volume. Each of these can be adjusted in percentage increments, so you can tweak them to be just perfect for whatever game you are playing. Clicking the play button on this tab loops a sample video with sound to allow for experimentation. A VoiceFX tab allows you to morph the sound of your voice using a bunch of presets so you can freak your friends out! I like using the Deep Voice preset, because I sound like a man when I answer my Skype phone.

The ear-surrounding cups cradle my ears for an immersive sound experience and are not too heavy, so (except for the cord attached to a USB port) I can forget I am wearing them. How I'd love to have a wireless pair of headphones that sound this good! If the ambient air is hot, the headphones can feel too hot, but I don't have that problem most of the time.

The adjustible microphone piece is detachable, and all sound input is muted when it is removed. For online conversations, the sound through the mic is sharp and clear, and the piece is flexible enough that you can put it just about anywhere. I've already lost the little foam mic cover, though, because it slips off a little too easily.

As far as attaching to your computer goes, you have a USB plug-in with a small rectangular THX TruSoundPro module attached. Your headphones, with separate (thankfully color-coded) mic and headphone plugs, plug into this module. When I forget I am wired and walk away from my computer (as I too often do), the headphone plugs pull out of the module first, leaving the USB plug in my computer, still sensing the headphones are plugged in. That's a boon. Volume adjustment wheel, mute switch, and a handy shirt clip are built into the cord, which appears to be of a decent length. (I've left my cord bundled and tied because it's plenty long for desktop use without undoing it.)

The sound and fatigue level (or lack of it) have surprised me with these headphones. My hearing has always been sensitive and I have to keep my volume turned really low to be able to wear headphones for any length of time. With most headphones, turning the volume down that low means I don't get shooting pains in my ears but the sound is tinny and practically inaudible. With these, I can turn the volume down quite low and still hear the nuances of music while still being able to hear voices clearly. Best of all, I can wear them for hours without fatigue and NO hearing-loss-signaling pain. Often, I will suddenly realize I have on the headphones and that people in the room with me cannot hear what I'm hearing. It sounds like the sound is filling the room and not coming through the headphones.

First of all, the signal quality is great over my 300' of CAT5e cable going from my entertainment system in front of my room to my projector around the back (cable goes behind walls and snakes around furnishings to get where it needs to go). It is fast and responsive, and the lag seems minimal if any. I love that it can also be used as a pass through, and that it only requires power on ONE side! My old HDMI extender required a power adapter on both the tx and rx side, but this can actually send power over the network cable (PoE) so that the other side does not need its own adapter. Now THAT's awesome!
This is one of the primary reasons I was interested in this, as there are two times I use such an adapter: When I use my projector instead of my TV for movies, and when moving a camera around at an event that I want to send a live feed back to a screen or streaming box for. Currently I have to supply power at both ends of the network cable, but I imagined ONLY needing power on the receiver, and having THAT power the transmitter. For example, in the case of the camera, I could have the screen receiving the signal send power to the transmitter by the camera using PoE and be somewhat more free of tethered power on that side. Also, when using the projector, I could turn on the outlet controlling the projector via remote and have it power on the transmitter behind the TV as well. Less wires and outlet spaces where already difficult / congested is good! THE PROBLEM, however, is that this thing misses its potential by only sending power from the TRANSMITTER! In other words, I can send power from the tx with PoE to the rx side, but the RECEIVER can't power the transmitter! It only goes the same direction as the HDMI signal. This, to me, was disappointing as that's the side I wanted to save from having more wires to plug in. Not the receiving side. That side is never an issue to supply power.
So I was a little upset about that. But otherwise, it is a solid product that seems to do what it claims to, and so far seems more reliable than my previous setup. If it could send power using EITHER side, it would be perfect! So close this time!

This weird little tripod is a useful addition to the gear of any amateur or hobby photographer with a DSLR and the inspiration to take breath-taking and/or unusual photographs. (I'm using it with a Nikon D7000)

Pros:

1. Light and portable. If you don't have a side pocket on your camera bag, just wrap it around a strap or loop.
2. Flexible. As advertised, the legs can be bent into loops and angles for getting shots from weird angles. It can also be wrapped around posts, tree branches, bench rails etc.
3. Convenient. An easy way to get shots requiring a stable camera almost level with ledges or sideways attached to a tree. However, you can only shoot in landscape format unless you get the accessory BH1 ball head. Naturally, with its little legs, you'll be pretty close to the ground if there's nothing available for wrapping around, but you'll be sure to get great camera angles from a worm's eye view.

Cons:

1. Attaching your camera to the tripod is a bit of a pain, requiring a coin (any currency) or a strong fingernail. A better bet is to get the accessory Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level and attach the quick release clip to your camera beforehand.
2. You need to practice with it a bit to get the stability right, and if you have the legs in an unbalanced position, or on a smooth surface, you can get sagging and camera movement.
3. Trying to get the camera level without the ball head can be quite challenging, and you may well miss the shot. (Of course you can always do the straightening with software, but it's better to get it right the first time.)
4. Can't shoot in portrait format unless you get the ball head.
5. Hard to get the legs back straight with all the segments in line.

Note: It comes with a 1/4-to-3/8-inch adapter attached to the mounting screw, so you have to remove this to attach the camera or accessory ball head.

Recommended (with the [[ASIN:B002CVU4G0 Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level for Joby GP3 SLR-Zoom Gorillapods]]) for photo walks, theme parks or general walk-abouts where that prize-winning shot may be just a Gorillapod away.

Amanda Richards, January 10, 2012

THE GOOD:
--------------
* Very easy to set-up, app is intuitive to use and follow.
* This is for a smaller home with just the hub, 2 entry sensors, 1 motion sensor, 1 yard sign, and 3 window decals.
* Hub is not obtrusive size-wise. It has a control panel at the top. I have it next to an Amazon Echo for size reference.
* Sensors work really well. Anytime you open the door where you've installed a sensor, there is a chime that goes off on the hub. You can disable this chime if you wish.
* For those who are not sure yet how much security they need, but do know that they at least one something as a deterrent, then this no subscription required DIY system is perfect.
* You can turn on system once outside your house via the app. You can also turn it off via the app before entering your home, or turn it off at the hub during the "entry delay."

THE BAD:
------------
* The sensor and the magnet has to be half an inch or less apart. Installation will be tricky for those who have a door frame with a raised decorative trim. You'll need to put the sensor at a strange angle, or come up with a better solution yourself. Raised, or irregular door trims is something ADT should have thought about, and should have included for us adapters, spacers, etc.
* If you choose not to subscribe, then the system is nothing more than a deterrent.
* The instructions assumes we all know the industry lingo. For example, "Entry or exit delays." I had to search online for more info. It's basically the time the system allows for you to properly turn off the alarm before it goes off. That's my understand from YT videos.
* Whenever you arm the system, it takes forever, like 60 to 90 seconds, and during this time, there is a CHIME that's counting down with the seconds. There doesn't seem to be a way to mute this. This means if you arm the system late at night while people are sleeping, the chimes may wake them up. I will update review if I can find more info on this. There has to be a way you can mute this.
* Although the yard sign is great, the window decals are small compared to others I've seen.

Overall, I'll rate this 4-Stars for now.

This is without a doubt the best looking soundbar I’ve come across so far. The shape is more than just aesthetics – if you have a TV on a table stand the low profile of the soundbar doesn’t get in the way of the screen. Granted, I’m sure there’s a TV out there that sits low enough that the soundbar will get in the way, but if it does it will be minimal. Even if you have a wall-mounted screen, the soundbar shape is still something that can be appreciated.

No complaints either with regard to the build quality. This feels as solid as it looks. I had high expectations given the price point, and I was not disappointed. The remote is also well-done with a straightforward design that makes it simple to use.

A few years ago I ran wiring for my main TV for a 7.1 speaker setup. It took many hours, and gave me a new appreciation as to why electricians charge so much for fishing wire through walls. So, the fact that I was able to get this set up and running in about an hour (including the unpacking and calibration time) was a real treat. I would rate the setup ease, and the included instructions, as excellent.

There are a number of great features, the main one for me being the detachable side speakers. It gives more flexibility than the usual sound bar in that you can position them for rear sound if you want that immersive feel, but also use them as standalone speakers for other devices. I had no problems pairing one to a tablet. One potential negative is the internal battery. While the run time is fine – I ran it for a good four hours continuously without a problem – I’ve had enough devices with internal batteries go bad (e.g., the battery will no longer take much of a charge) that I always am wary of internal batteries.

The sound quality was both good and bad, and in an unexpected way. I was expecting that this soundbar would be left in the dust by my wired system at high volume. While it was bested (especially with bass given the slim subwoofer) it was a far closer horse race than I thought it would be. This soundbar can put out a healthy amount of volume and still remain in control of sound quality.

Where it fell short is when it was not pushed hard. Soft passages were weak; dialog was unclear at times. Running this at a soft volume (such as at night when others are sleeping in the house) was not enjoyable – I ended up having to turn on subtitles since I could not make out the dialog clearly. Now, this issue could be exacerbated by my aging ears, but others in the house, who are younger, also found it weak and unimpressive at low volume.

I think most people who get this will be looking to have “big” sound in a simple to set up, simple to use system. On that end, the Philips soundbar delivers. It misses somewhat on the soft end of the spectrum, but the build quality, looks, and flexibility warrant a five-star rating even at this rather lofty price point.

Note: the 4K term is marketing, just about all consumer devices are UHD (2160p). So I'm going to use the UHD term, feel free to translate to "format commonly referred to as 4K" if you prefer.

I tested this cable on my newest UHD tv, with streaming UHD video from multiple sources, and then with a UHD nature documentary on a bluray player. I'd been using a very good 18Gb ("4K") cable before, so possibly a side-by-side test wouldn't show any difference. But I did immediately notice how sharp and bright the picture was in both cases, so I can at least say that this makes a very good video cable for UHD.

The cable is well made and feels sturdy, with a nice grab handle at each end, and inserts just the way it should into HDMI ports, with neither wiggle nor overmuch tightness. I didn't notice any minor flaws that might make me concerned about build quality, and I would expect it to last, at least until it becomes obsolete.

What should you buy if you don't have any so-called 8K media or devices, like most of us, and don't see them in your immediate future? In that case I'd just go with very good "4K" or "8K" cables, but without paying premium prices. The product description might say "Premium High Speed HDMI Cable" (18Gbps) or "Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable" (48Gbps). The first corresponds to the HDMI 2.0b standard, the second to HDMI 2.1.
