I've been working in video production for over 2 decades now, and bought my first teleprompter for infomercial style videos back in the early 2000s. Let's just say, much like camera tech has gotten smaller and more efficient, so has teleprompting!
The concept is pretty simple and hasn't changed- angle a piece of glass in front of the lens with a black drop material behind it to create a sort of 2-way-mirror, then reflect text in reverse (you know, because mirror?) and your subject appears to read their script off your lens while the camera doesn't see the text at all.
Things that are still true from back then:
- Your text has to be reversed. My old one came with PC software to do this, and since iPads weren't really a thing yet, we used laptops that could fold all the way backwards (Thinkpads mostly). This, surprisingly does not come with software. But no matter, there are some free ones out there, and my personal favorite is just using powerpoint. We reverse the images and make a slide show that the subject can advance with a standard presenter remote. I will not regurgitate the product specs since they are not only complete, but have been validated by more than a few previous reviews. I'll stick to some key observations about the review sample that I received and why I think this light deserves five stars.

The main reason why I love this light is price and performance. I own a few other music stand lights and they either perform on par with this one, but are priced twenty-five percent (or more higher), or they are not as well made.

Features are also more than I expected for a twenty buck light. For one thing you can easily get seven hours of continuous use on a single charge. I did a rundown test on mine and it remained illuminated for a little over seven hours before it started dimming, That was with both LEDS in each head switched on. I ended the test when it started appreciably dimming, but even at seven hours this is more than adequate since I actually do use this as a music stand light and the longest performances are less than three hours.

Another feature that I love is the LED indicator in the USB A end of the charging cable. It will be red until the light fully charges, then it will turn green.

Note: there are two things that I do not care for: (1) the charging end is a barrel connector instead of a micro USB connector, so if you lose of damage the included cable you are going to have difficulty replacing it, and (2) the barrel connector does not completely seat into the charging port. It charges, but I would be hesitant of using this light in a studio where you wanted to suppress all electrical interference. I am not sure there is any from this light, but the fact that a conducting connector is partially exposed gives me pause.

Bottom line: for stage performances this light is better and brighter than most other two-LED models and illuminates sufficiently to read music or lyrics. It holds firm when clamped to my music stand, and the flexible arms allow me to position the lamp heads for optimum reading while staying put.

I bought a ZuneHD 32GB as a replacement for my iPod Video. I still have the iPod but I don't particularly care for it (never really did) so I decided to search for a better MP3 player. After digging online for a while I decided on the ZuneHD which has proven to be far and away better. It is not a perfect device but it's excellent for my needs.

Looking a lot like a small smart phone, the ZuneHD is a sleek and attractive device with a nice touch screen and a brushed metal back. Having never before used one of these I was a little confused at first on how it worked but the learning curve is easy and it took little time to get used to it. It works a lot like a tablet, actually. The screen is very responsive and navigation is simple.

I confess that I never used the ear buds. Instead, I use a set of really nice noise-canceling head phones and the sound coming out of the Zune is excellent. My music of choice is usually techno-trance stuff so there is a lot of base and a lot of synthesizer, and by default the sound is well-balanced and clear.

So, my main use for an MP3 player is to connect it to my car. My car has voice-controlled everything and I wanted to be able to listen to my music collection in the car without fiddling with the player directly. When I used the iPod I found that the system frequently got confused and the player would often select the wrong song. If it got confused enough, it would hang the voice activation for controlling the MP3 player for weeks at a time, so I gave up and put my Zune in the car instead. So far, the Zune and the car work together nearly flawlessly. As a bonus, the car keeps the Zune charged up.

The only drawback I have found with the Zune is that there is no way to expand the storage capacity. It would be nice to have the ability to add a MicroSD card in to expand the capacity.

I am exceptionally satisfied with my Zune. I likely will never buy another iPod again, now that I know how much better an MP3 player can be.

UPDATE: I noticed that my setup would start displaying an incorrectly sized and formatted hdmi feed (instead of 1920x1080, it was a squashed 960x1080 with incorrect colors). If I turned the whole system off and wait a few minutes before turning back on, it would sometimes go away but it is very strange. I thought it was either the player or projector connected to it for months now, but I just did some testing and realized it has been this HDMI extender! A monitor plugged into the source displayed fine, and plugged into this receiver had the same 960x1080 w/ mixed up colors that my projector did. The good news is that the transmitter has a reset button and that seems to fix it when it happens. But it sometimes comes back when I reboot or start up from everything being off. It is annoying that I have to go find the little reset button because the transmitter is hidden in a cabinet, and it seems like a completely unnecessary step to take every time I boot up. Hoping Sabrent can offer a solution- if so I'll update my review back to 5 stars because otherwise this is excellent.
These things are a great way to reliably reach farther than an HDMI cable, but you need to still understand the limitations. Video requires a lot of bandwidth, so the quality and length of your cable is directly related to how realistic it is to reach the maximum resolution and frame rate.
I already have an older one of these from a different brand, which I bought a couple of years ago for a projector in the back of the room (switch between TV and projector, but entertainment system is in front of room and projector is in back, hence the need for a long run of cable). That older one claimed to work at 1080/60p, and in my initial tests it did. But once I ran the long cable, I was able to only get 720/60p or 1080 at only 24p. 1080 at 60 was just too much bandwidth and the adapter just couldn't handle it over a longer cable run.

UPDATE #1:

I am changing my rating from 4 stars to 1 star. DO NOT BUY THIS DRIVE (or anything else from VisionTek).

Reason: several weeks ago, my drive simply stopped working at USB 3.0 speeds when plugged into USB 3.0 ports. I spent a couple of hours on the phone with Dell's professional support seeing if my Dell T1700 was the cause: no dice. Indeed, I eventually got my hands on another USB 3.0 device (an external hard drive), and verified that my USB 3.0 ports work at high speed. So the problem must be with this flash drive.

Even worse, after I emailed VisionTek, it took days before I got a response. They wanted to know how I was doing the benchmarking. This was stupid: my original email gave them enough details to know that the USB 2.0 speeds I was seeing could not be due to benchmarking flaws. Nevertheless, I gave them another detailed answer. ORIGINAL REVIEW:

I ordered this drive a couple of months ago, and have been using it steady ever since.

I wanted a thumb drive that is really an SSD. In particular, that uses a proper controller, as opposed to the crap el cheapo controllers in almost all thumb drives. This VisionTek drive is one of the very few that fits the bill. I bought it instead of Corsair's because it is slightly physically smaller. The review that best informed my judgement was this one:
[...]

Overall, I am pleased with this drive.

It has been, and remains, reasonably fast for an SSD drive in this form factor. For example, using the freeware benchmarking program AS SSD just now, I measured:

sequential read speed = 156.91 MB/s
sequential writes as 101.43 MB/s
4k random read = 16.74 MB/s
4k random write= 63.26 MB/s
4k-64 thread random read = 16.76 MB/s
4k-64 thread random write= 72.84 MB/s
read access time = 0.155 ms
write access time = 0.347 ms

(The above was measured in the drive's first partition, which is a 8 GB FAT32 partition that I have strictly for backwards compatibility with certain software or operating systems that require it, such as GParted or Clonezilla live images. I do most of my storage in the second partition, which is all the remaining space formatted in NTFS with 4K block size.)

My device gets warm, but NOT HOT (where I define the start of hot as when it becomes uncomfortable to touch).

I love the fact that it has a cap, and that the cap can be put on the back when plugged in. My previous thumb drive was a Sandisk Extreme Pro slider which eventually broke; never want a slider again.

I have 3 moderate complaints that prevent me from rating it at 5 stars. First, it is bigger than I would like. Sure, it is still small enough that you can still carry it around in your pocket, and I do, all day long, but I would like it to be smaller if possible. Second, the case, while made of high quality metal, has some edges and corners that are sharper than they out to be. Third, the paint has started to chip in places (like those sharp points).

Overall, this is the best thumb drive currently shipping that I am aware of, but it could be improved. VisionTek: I hope that you are reading this review.

I bought the Manfrotto 808RC4 along with their 190XPROB Pro Tripod and the Manfrotto MB MSTRAP-1 Tripod Carrying Strap. All at Amazon. Here's why:

This head gives you unlimited control in all directions. The large knurled handles allow you to grip and adjust the tension on the pivot points to any degree you want. I use it to pan video, I use it to do off center composure and metering. I love how rock steady this thing is when I am shooting my 60and 120 second exposures with my 300MM lens. Rock steady. And the rotation is greased smooth, nary a glitch.

With a bubble level and two straight levels you always know where you are. And gradients to indicate -30 to +90 tilt for replication. Great for panning video or shooting stills for a panorama. There are two "softening springs" to slow the movement of the tilts as you reach either end. You can disengage them if you wish.

I have friends that went with the ball heads. And regret it. They are fast, but not accurate, especially with a long lens. With this head you can adjust the tension and just ease the camera around without having to adjust it again.

Now hear me on this. I see other reviewers not so happy with the way the shoe is a little tricky. Let me say that by practicing with the shoe mounted to your camera and paying close attention snap it onto the head three times and you know all you need to know. You may have to practice a few more times to get it in the dark but I tell you that you are going to love it. When you snap the camera onto the head it automatically engages and you have no worries. The double safety has stopped me from dropping my camera twice. Lesson learned at no cost.

As to the tripod - sturdy is the word that comes to mind. And NOT overly weighty. Together the head and tripod are 7 lbs. With the strap - which I did not buy at first - this rig is rock solid and you won't even know you are carrying it. I don't even notice the combo. I hike several hours at a time and have been know to stop in a panic on the way out and feel on my back to see if the whole thing is still there! I think a big part of the "weight" issue is how it is carried. In your hands it feels hefty. On your hips, 7 lbs feels weighty. Across your shoulder diagonally, head down? It ain't even there!

The tripod has a wonderfully steady center column assembly that comes up and tilts over to the horizontal - great for macro shots or simply needing to place the camera where you aren't. The legs are sturdy and the snap retainers have just the right tension - not too hard to snap open or closed, not so loose that you worry whether one might slide. I also like that the center column is not attached to the legs with the typical arms of lesser well made tripods. Makes for very easy folding and stowing. I love the leg angle presets - easy to use and not worried about them slipping. The rubber grips on two of the legs are a hand saver in chilly weather. Nice touch.

So, in case you haven't figured it out, I love this rig. If I were going trekking across country for days I might want a little less weight, but for day long trips, portraiture or car trips this is the ticket.

Very nice high quality item, but you're sort of left in the wind to figure things out yourself. Here are some things to note, so you don't encounter the same issues as I did.

-The app to download is called PRINT MASTER. You'll naturally want to download Phomemo app, but you'll soon realize it won't connect with your printer. Then you'll notice there is a specific Phomemo 110 app, so you download that as well. But after installing this app, a pop up says "we are discontinuing this app, please download PRINT MASTER." There, I saved you from the run-around I encountered. LOL!

-You are given a starter roll of labels, but to use the templates in the Print Master app, you'll need to choose the proper dimension. It would be nice if this info was given in the manual, but the manual doesn't even mention the free roll. Everything is in mm, but I happened to have a mm ruler and measured the labels to be 40x30mm.

-Lastly, the most important advice you need to know is you need to turn on AUTOMATIC. You might ask AUTOMATIC what? My reply is.. EXACTLY. LOL! You see, once you go to print your label. There is a setting called AUTOMATIC. There is no explanation as to what this means. The default is WHITE, which is OFF. What it means is where it will stop after it prints your label. If it's OFF, it will NOT stop. It will continue spitting out blank labels. I saw a YT reviewer who had this issue, and I didn't think anything of it, until it happened to me. LOL! You need to turn this to GRAY, which is ON. It will then automatically stop after it prints your label. Why in the world is the default set to continuously print blanks? We all tend to use default settings because we trust the manufacture knows what's best for us. I mean why would you turn something on if you don't know what it does? So I can see why many make this mistake. But now you know. Turn it on! Even if you need multiple copies, for example 5 copies. You still need to turn it on, so that it will stop after 5 labels. I would love for someone experience with these things, or the seller, to comment below what that setting is for, and why is the default off?

I've learned a lot about surveillance systems recently, having researched, selected, installed, and tweaked both this and a LaView model with four cameras and eight channels. This Defender model has a price tag more than double the LaView, but its specs clearly justify that. But although this is an excellent product, having experience with another brand shows me neither are perfect:

Overall. The Defender comes with a more solid looking DVR and a couple extra cables (i.e., Ethernet and HDMI), making it appear more premium right out of the box. However, the AAA batteries (worst kind of batteries anything could take price/power-wise) for the remote came DOA which was totally lame. Both units come with very cheap mice, rectifiers, remotes, and cables.

-Most people into this kind of stuff have extra of these things around anyway, so it's not a big deal.
-The cables look and work fine, but they are not actually coax in the shielding/cladding sense. After cutting the ends off mine during installation anyway, I'd recommend planning to buy your coax on a roll (especially when you have some runs >60') and maybe getting a boxed power supply rather than using multiple awkward rectifier packs.
-The Defender had issues pushing HDMI output past 25', which the LaView did not, which could be an issue if you're planning to view your output on your TV far from your Telecom Closet (TC).

DVR. The LaView has D1 cameras, but only the first two channels can record D1@30fps, while the other channels can do CIF@30fps or D1@6fps (bogus). The Defender can record all four channels WD1@30fps.

Using NTSC in N. America, WD1 is 960x480 resolution. This is also referred to as 960H. Or, more accurately, one is a capability of the other, but I'm trying to keep this simple. D1 is 720x480, so basically, WD1 is "Wide D1". The TV Lines (TVL) spec you see is independent of the previously mentioned spec from what I understand, but my full understanding is still a little fuzzy. Suffice to say, higher TVL is better.

But the Defender is missing these features that the LaView possess:

-USB port in front for easy mouse or backup HD access, convenient IF you have the DVR pointed forward (I have mine pointed backward in my TC for cable access).
-IR extender port, which should be great if you have your device pointed backward in a TC or if you want to view this on your TV in a different room. I haven't gotten mine to work, but I haven't researched it much yet, so I'm not sure who's fault that is.
-Alarm inputs, which you can set to turn on cameras when something triggers an external alarm you set up.
-Controls. The LaView has buttons on the front of the DVR while the Defender does not.

It should be noted that the only way to control either of these devices fully and easily is with the included mouse or through their remote viewing software. I attached a little mouse holder to the inside of my TC door so it is available when needed.

Remote Viewing. I could immediately pick up the LaView from my home networked computers. The first one immediately gave me full functionality while the next three gave me limited functionality. I think the difference may have to do with the newest Internet Explorer not working as well, but compatibility mode does not give greater functionality. I had to mess around a little bit to get the Defender working right away, but you basically have to push it to the IP address and then port 5000, but then it was still less easy to get my computer to install what it needed to install (the 1step thing included didn't work for me, and I tend to think they know it will never be one step, they just want to motivate you to go through the process).

But, once I got it running, I like the full featured remote viewing software of the Defender better. For viewing off your local network, both needed port forwarding set up on your router. This can be quirky if you're using a home-type router rather than a commercial router. I'm a network guy, but I believe this is just the reality of the situation.

The local software is great on both devices. They have about the same features, and both are intuitive to use. The LaView software is easier to read on my TV from far away, and the Defender's software looks a bit more like a computer program. The Defender has PIP and PIPx2 options that are really cool.

Cameras. These Defender cameras, with their better specs - are clearly superior, but they are also a lot bigger, which is a small disappointment (as I really don't want to flaunt my extreme paranoia to the neighborhood). You can't hide it either way, but small cameras are a good thing. Anyway, side-by-side, it's hard to get a firm grasp on the resolution difference because the LaView cameras are almost zoomed out further so you see more anyway, but the wider resolution of the Defender is theoretically fantastic because you get more off to the sides (given a same zoom to start with) and less toward the sky. For example, on my porch, the LaView covers it just fine, but you see some of the ceiling. The wide Defender cameras can get more of the yard to the side of the porch while getting the same amount of ceiling. Oddly, it's not as much more crisp as you might think, but lighting and everything plays a roll in this. But at night, the Defender cameras really shine because the night vision is truly excellent and then the lines are much more crisp and detailed. This is especially important in very dark settings (less important when you have city street lights around).

Personal Gripe: I'm looking for a way to record into my gun safe or into a locally remote hidden area, but turning the SATA HD into an eSATA HD does not transmit very far. Neither device records on the fly over USB (maybe this could be done with USB3.0?). I know I can push this to a web server or to a NAS device, but I like simpler methods in addition to those, because they are always more reliable. Please comment if you have some ideas on this.

Anyway, this is a great system that I'm very happy with. I'd recommend it for most basic installs, and I'd probably recommend the other Defender models for those needing more cameras and channels. If you have a problem with any of the minor issues I mentioned above, then look elsewhere.

But $2200 Buckaroos are a long way from $300 and I did get the tv at a great bargain price, so cheap instead of expensive became the call of war.
For what I got this soundbar does everything I wanted done. It was very easy to install through the optical option, and even though the first unit I purchased had troubles pairing with the subwoofer and was returned immediately, the second was the charm and now it works very nicely with the added plus that it certainly did not require a Kamikaze investment. Works very well and it adds a great sound capability to the living room in our home which was the intended site. Some shows are better than others but even the subwoofer does its magic and is a lot of fun to crank it up once in a while, specially for the internet type movie sites (like Netflix, Amazon, Vudu, etc.) that come with the smart tv and required some sort of subscription. Their sound, specially amazon and netflix, was way below average and even at maximum volume on the tv it was very sad. I could hear it but one of the members of the tribe is a little more than a little hard of hearing and was always having trouble (probably the main reason why I decided on a sound bar in the first place).
Needless to say this soundbar delivered what was expected of the product and now my living room is one loud area and when the subwoofer is doing its thing you can feel it kind of in the furniture itself, like some of the controllers in PS3 with the added vibration. Minor thing but rather invigorating, for the whole room now sounds like a mini theater without having had to add several speakers coupled with tedious connections, which certainly I am not qualified or inclined to want to do myself. I just put the sound bar in the same table in which the television rest and the subwoofer about 6 feet away and voila! Just waiting for the neighbors to reassure me as to the loudness, kind of like its baptism when they finally complain (makes you feel a little bit proud that you are putting enough noise to draw the attention of nearby houses, silly but what can you do sometimes?), so for now I am very happy with the purchase and glad that when necessary I have the equipment to raise the noise way higher than it was capable before. 4 very solid Stars!

I wanted a set of speakers to use mainly for my Kindle Fire and MP3 player, but also as my computer speakers. Due to space constraints, a 2.0 system was my only option, since a subwoofer (regardless of the size) would be problematic.

So the search began. There were several speakers that sounded great, including the Creative Gigaworks, M Audio and Audioengine. However, they lacked the convenience features I wanted such as ease of connecting/disconnecting a tablet and volume control without having to reach out and touch the speaker.

The Bose Companion 20 initially caught my eye because of the control pod. That was a great solution to my problems since I could control the volume right on my desk plus have the ability to plug in/unplug a tablet very easily. The sound quality sealed the deal - everyone who hears these speakers think they are a 2.1 set due to the ample bass. But, the bass is not at the expense of clear mid and upper ranges.

I use these 60% for music and 40% for video, and for both applications, the sound quality has been just wonderful. I'm also impressed that they sound just as good with the volume dialed way down as they do at moderate or blast-out-the-walls loud.

The control pod is very well made. It has a nice weight to it and a non-skid backing so it stays put. The volume control works very smoothly with a solid feel. I'm especially fond of being able to turn the speakers on and off by just touching the control pod.

You can connect it to the PC and to an aux device (such as a tablet) and use both at the same time. That's important since I want to listen to music or a video from my Fire, but still want to hear a chime when an email arrives.

My complaints are that the control pod cable is a bit too short for my needs. It's about 5 foot long, which is ample if you have the speakers next to your PC, but I have my speakers on a shelf above my desk. I was able to arrange things to make it work, but another foot or two of cable (or the ability to purchase an extension) would have been nice. It's a custom cable, so an off-the-shelf extension is not possible.

My other complaint is the price. I was able to get a used pair for half of the regular price. I think these are a bit overpriced at the regular price. But, Bose hit a really unique niche - the ability to have great sound without any compromise in convenience. If you want both, there's a high cost for admission.

If the price is not an issue, these very much deserve a hard look if you're in the market for a great sounding pair of 2.0 speakers. Highly recommend.

I am super happy with this computer. It's really a work of art, and I say this as a guy who has an Alienware 17 from a few years ago.

Even counting for inflation (i.e., the fact that specs and hardware have gotten better in the years since the A17), I think the specs are dead on with what you get out of an Alienware. But while the build quality is just as good - and just as impressive - it is so much lighter and more portable (not that I really care, mind you, as I don't travel with my home laptop). But you really don't lose anything - besides weight - because the Asus is a strong machine with everything you could want (including the space for an extra HDD, which until now I had not seen outside of the Alienware...of course now that you can just get chips for ROM, this is becoming more normal).

I love the tactile feel and the fact that it is still a real laptop that can be upgraded easily. I don't want a slick tablet that won't come apart for serious computing and gaming. I want a real laptop. I want this. They keyboard is probably the best built-in I've ever used (which is even more impressive when Surface Pro-type keyboards are becoming more and more common).

And the touchpad. Oh, the beautiful touchpad with it's real buttons. How anyone could want a tap-to-click-only touchpad is beyond me. And you know what - right out of the box - I didn't even change the configuration of the touchpad to keep it from doing obnoxious things to me like clicking all over the screen with my palms. This is probably one of the reasons that this was the quickest setup-to-acceptable laptop I've ever had:

Usually, I spend a week not wanting to deal with a new computer and getting everything configured right, and then a whole day complaining about all the crapware I have to get rid of and trying to find stuff and get it set up right (typically exacerbated since Windows 10 is still sort of annoying when all you want is Win7 back...). And then it's another week until I finally work up the muster to go fix the touchpad settings. I cursed less with this laptop than any other, ever. And after just an hour or two installing the must-haves, it's all ready to go, and works fantastically.

Install Windows Classic Shell right away if you want to avoid as much of the Windows 10 garbage as you can. Don't do an "online account". Remove onedrive and the other MS crap that tries to get you to always be online and buy their stuff and treat you like you're using a tablet (this is a Windows problem, not that of the Asus). Remove included Macafe (now is a good time since it never wants to allow the software I will next install) Then get rid of the one Asus program that is like a store. Now just add the software you actually do want and you have a darn near perfect computer. Really nothing to annoy me. And it is as perfectly responsive as anything you could ever want.

Keyboard is awesome, like I said. Most tactile keyboard ever on a laptop. I couldn't find any software on the machine to change colors and stuff (I may have deleted it immediately while trying to get rid of minimal bloatware, but I don't think I did). So I downloaded ROG aura (and a different Aura program that did NOT work right) and then you have your full keyboard color controls. It seemed like that other program was for syncing with other light-up devices, but it would not allow me to control all four sections of the keyboard independently (even though I think it was supposed to).

I'm getting a full 60 frames + on every one of my new games I run on this. It reminds me why a specialized rig like this is better than consoles. 1080p is still amazing, even (and especially) thrown onto my Sony TV. No problem with any of my controllers or accessories. Bluetooth setup is so mature nowadays.

I was going to wait until I actually had truly tested and used this before I wrote a review.  I got this free as a review unit.  The problem is that I can't use it without spending some money for cables, as it does not come with cables.  StarTech says that's on purpose since people have different cable needs, especially different lengths. The cables that StarTech has available for it are over $21 each, which comes up to well over $60 for my 3 computers, almost the price of the switch.  With 4 computers connected, the price would be even more.  Okay, so they don't provide cables, but for the price of the switch, maybe they should at least give you a coupon or a voucher for one or two cables or a discount on the cables.  Interestingly the 2-port version does include cables; the 4-port does not.  StarTech's cables are nice, as they combine the needed USB with the VGA cable; otherwise you have to run two completely separate cables (one VGA cable for monitor and a USB cable for keyboard and mouse).  If you have USB cables as most people do, you can easily purchase the needed VGA cables inexpensively.  This brings me to the first real issue I have with this switch.  The master monitor connection is a female connector, which is standard.  Unfortunately the 4 computer monitor connectors are all male connections, so you can't use a standard male to male VGA cable that you would normally use from a computer to a monitor.  You have to get male to female VGA cables (which are typically called extension cables).  Why they would use this non-standard method of connecting monitors is puzzling.  A couple of reviewers were also concerned that this switch does not come with a power supply.  That's usually not a big deal as I found out that a power supply is not necessary, as the switch gets it's power from the USB connections.  There is no explanation as to why it has a place to plug in a power supply, although in some cases if you have a lot of USB devices connected to your PC, you might need additional power that a power supply would provide, so I assume it is for supplemental power.  It's good that they provide a way to add additional power, if you need it, even if not the actual power supply.  The next issue I encountered was trying to determine whether or not you could switch between computers with a hotkey sequence on your keyboard or whether you actually had to reach over to the switch and press the button for the computer you wanted.  Apparently there is no keyboard switching or if there is, no one seems to know what keys are used.  I read the manual for the setup and was concerned that it states that for PC to get the switch to work properly, a couple of BIOS settings for PC need to be changed.  I am not even sure that my computers have those particular settings, especially my older computers that sometimes have more limited BIOS settings available.  I have had 3 other KVM switches and none of them needed a change to BIOS settings.  Given the problems that others have had with this switch in that it doesn't always work flawlessly, I am not sure that I want to take time to test it right, since I already have a nicely working KVM switch.  I still have to buy cables.  On the plus side, this switch appears to be well built with a metal case; not cheap plastic.  It appears to be nice and solid and just heavy enough.  If the issues I mentioned are not a deal-breaker for you, I think this is worth trying.  I will update my review and add or subtract stars once I have a chance to test this in actual operation.

I bought a Garmin 60CSx GPS receiver as a replacement for a Garmin eTrex Legend for the purpose of geocaching. My eTrex Legend has served me well (and continues to do so) but I wanted a GPSr with more functionality, better operation under heavy cover and expanded map coverage for hiking and road navigation. Researching GPSrs led me to this unit, and I have been very pleased with it. There are a couple of minor negatives that I have found, but these can probably be overlooked.

I am very pleased with the appearance of the screen when the unit is powered on. The display is bright and colorful, and easy to read in the light. This is true of the daytime display. The night display is not as pleasant, with a hard-to-see color scheme. Backlighting the night scheme makes it a lot easier to read but it is still less than ideal.

The unit's software is very intuitive, a menu- and icon-driven interface giving access to all of the features. I have found little need for the user manual since I fist started working with this device, as everything is clear and easy to find. Buttons on the unit make it easy to find the menus and to navigate without too much hassle.

The base map is nothing special but it is adequate for basic navigation. We have used it to follow our path down the interstate. It shows the major roads and also any waypoints that are close by.

The best feature of this unit, in my opinion, is its ability to navigate under heavy canopy. With my eTrex Legend there were times when my unit would simply not be able to get a lock. The 60CSx has yet to lose signal, even inside my living room. The accuracy does drop when there is sufficient cover but the important thing is that it doesn't drop completely.

One thing troubles me a bit about the 60CSx. The accuracy rarely gets any better than 10-12 feet, whereas my eTrex Legend - a unit costing a third as much - routinely can get down to 6 feet. I do not understand why this is the case. I would choose ability to hold a signal over pinpoint accuracy every time, but why can't I have both?

The 60CSx has a Micro-SD card inside and the unit will take a card up to 2GB inside. That's enough room for a whole US street map. This is a nice thing to have available, as it means not having to decide what section of map to load. Load the whole map and be on your way.

The waypoint management functions are acceptable for my needs, which up to this point has meant managing geocaching waypoints. I like being able to mark a point as "found" and then being asked if I want to go to the next closest point. I have noticed, though, that if I am navigating to a point and leave the navigation menus, the point is marked as found anyway. It would be nice to have the ability to specify "not found" without having to go through the menus to locate the point again, just to change the status.

The Garmin 60CSx is a very nice handheld GPS that will serve you well. It is not perfect, but for general use it is plenty close enough.

I tried 2 other antennas at this location and was less than thrilled by the results. One was an amplified unit that I purchased years ago that had two vertical antennas that could be independently positioned forward or backward up to a ~45 degree angle from a straight, vertical position with a rotating base. I don't recall it's brand, but it worked fairly well most of the time, but I found myself going back to the old method of adding aluminum foil to get the best reception. The second antenna I tried was an RCA amplified bar antenna. It picked up most channels, but I had to change its direction back and forth depending on whether I wanted the CBS or the NBC affiliate; I could receive most all other channels with either direction. I returned that unit to WalMart.

According to AntennaWeb.org, I should receive 27 channels from 13 stations; the government site stated that I should receive 8 stations with a strong signal, 1 station with a weak signal, and that I would not be able to receive 1 station in the area. With this antenna, my TV found 49 channels this morning when I re-ran the scan, including all the channels listed on both sites that I mentioned previously. The first night that I ran the scan, I was able to pick up over 50 channels, including Channel 5 from Nashville! It was very cloudy that night, and I assume that reception was due to a propagation anomaly since I have not been able to receive that channel since then.

I highly recommend this antenna. For the record, I ran this test 11 floors up in a high-rise apartment building in downtown Louisville. As others have noted, very slight changes in the orientation of the antenna significantly affects reception of some stations. My antenna is currently attach to a window on one side and bends around the frame and attaches to the wall on the other side of the antenna. (I recommend getting some of the 3M replacement strips to attach the antenna so that you can re-arrange it as needed.)

The main thing about this radio that I really DO NOT like is that it has a permanent battery that must be charged via a USB cable. The cable must be connected to a computer or to a special adapter that can be plugged into any regular household outlet in order to charge it. The fact that the battery can only be charged and not easily replaced as in AA batteries to me, defeats the whole purpose of having such a radio. I consider the ability to listen to shortwave from an emergency aspect, such as if the power grid went down or for some other catastrophic reason. It should work for a while but when the battery dies, so does your ability to get news and information about your local area as well as other parts of the world, unless you have a way to charge it. And if the battery totally dies (I let mine completely expire), you will lose all of your settings including time and date.

I also don't have any use for the recording function, iPod player, and e-reader. They are nice extras but not necessary for a shortwave radio. Most people probably buy shortwave radios for their ability to pick up shortwave radio signals from around the world and not for it's recording function. If you should need it in the event of an emergency of some sort, will you be wasting it's precious battery energy listening to your iPod? And no one takes a radio like this to a pool anymore....they use their iPod, iPhone or whatever for all of their listening needs. Personally, I consider these types of radios to be stored away and used when things look ominous outside or other unfortunate global events are happening.

The owner's manual was not easy to understand, and the radio itself is NOT intuitive at all. If you don't have the poorly written manual to go by you will be spending a LOT of time trying to figure out how to work the controls on this radio. It was a lot of work just to get a few stations programmed into it, and somehow I still managed to delete them all. One aspect that I DO like is that it is very easy to turn it on. No need to fumble around looking for the on/off switch. Just push any button or turn the tuning knob and the screen lights up with the time and date. However, you must then proceed to use one of the functions for it to remain on. It only stays lit for exactly 3 seconds.

It's certainly better than no radio, but it's not very practical and there are better ones out there. It looks nice, has a decent overall sound quality for a small radio, is a easy size to deal with and comes with a black pouch to carry it in, but good looks can only get you so far. It's what's inside that counts. Also, for what it's worth, the black tuning knob on my radio fell off. I was able to get it back on, but what if I lost it in the dark and couldn't find it and a hurricane was coming towards my area?!!!

Setting up/pairing the device is pretty easy. Press the button for 4 seconds or so and you’ll hear a pleasant female voice say, “Hello”. This means the power is on. Continue holding the button and the device will enter pairing mode. You’ll hear the voice say, “Ready to pair.” When pairing is complete, you’ll hear the device say, “You’re connected” and tell you how much charge the battery has. So far, all I’ve heard is, “Battery full.” I have no idea what other battery indications the voice will give – perhaps only at 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4? Or maybe percentages?

The buttons are the biggest drawback with this device. Actually, it's really just one multi-function button on the right earpiece. The button functionality is not like any Bluetooth headset I've used before - very non-intuitive. The button has no label at all and the tactile feedback is nonexistent at times - I press the button sometimes and there's no "click" feeling. If a song is playing, it doesn't seem to matter where I press, the song stops if it is playing. When I press again, anywhere, it starts playing again.

There is no volume control on the headphones at all. You’ll have to adjust the volume from your phone/audio player. There is a bare bones EQ function. You control this by clicking the multi-function button 3 times in rapid succession. Each time you do this, the device advances to the next of 3 EQ setting – balanced, bass boost and JLab signature. The “balanced” setting seems to sound just like what it’s named – balanced or equal high, mid and low tones. The bass boos is decent – not overbearing. Not sure what the last one is, but if the pictograms in the manual are any indication, it boost the high and low ends. The EQ function does provide audible feedback – the voice announces each setting by name.

There's a next track function, but no function for going to the previous track. The next track function requires holding down the multi-function button for 2 seconds. There's no audible feedback for this function (other than a very short moment of silence). When you hear the silence, let go IMMEDIATELY. If you hold the button down for too long the Bluetooth connection will be severed and you'll have to reconnect.

Apparently, there's no ability to fast forward or rewind within a song or audio book. You'll have to do this on your phone/audio player. Pretty poor design if you ask me. BTW – I use this only with my audio player, so I did not test the phone/mic functions, but I’d be surprised if they were robust.

The instructions are minimal at best. The manual is one piece of paper printed on 2 sides. Unfolded, it's about the size of 2 business cards - about 4"x4.5" (10.16cm x 11.43cm). One side has instructions and the other is all promotions/disclaimers, etc. That's it.

Sound quality is acceptable - decent bass and stereo separation is good. I’m no audiophile though. The product description says it has "Noise Isolation", which is marketing speak used by all on-ear headphone manufacturers. It simply means the ambient noise is slightly reduced because the headphones cover your ears. Bottom line - there's no tech/function in this device that does any active noise cancellation.

The headphones are a little snug/tight, but not so much to be uncomfortable - at least that's my opinion after an hour+ of testing. Not sure if this will be true for something like a 3-4 hour flight. I’ll test this out in the near future and will update this review, if possible.

The charging cable that comes with the item is 9” long (22.86cm). Not very useful at all, but better than nothing.

On the plus side, the manufacturer did provide an extra set of foam earpiece covers - the set that comes on the headphones is orange. The extra set is black.

Bottom line, for $15 I wasn't expecting a lot - well maybe better button functionality, but hey, what can you do? As my granddad used to say, “You pays your money and you takes your chances.”

Yes, the UI and apps are very clearly Android. No, it isn't a mini tablet.
Players like this are an interesting market that is hard to pin the audience down for. There are music players that are cheap on the market for those that would rather have a dedicated player (ie, not their phone). However the user interface tends to be wonky and slow, and newer generation features like bluetooth 5+ and streaming are often a mixed bag, if even available.
The idea behind players like this one, is that it is based on a supported operating system (Android, in this case) so it can play almost any format you throw at it, has plenty of support for popular streaming apps and features, as well as a familiar user interface that is already so polished, it seems silly to reinvent the wheel like the super cheap older media players.
Is it a mini tablet or phone without service? Not exactly. This is not a Google certified device, it does not have the play store or any Google apps on it. Unlike some other Android based players, I couldn't even get sideloaded apk files to install (it kept throwing errors at me). It seems like this device was purposely locked down to keep it an mp3 player. That's good in some ways, my kids aren't allowed unlimited screen time and their schools don't want them bringing smartphones around, so this is a strictly music-player oriented device (especially once you remove things like the browser for them, which it allows you to do). But I also know there are more capable players out there, some of which have quad DAC audio chips. Also, what happens when an app gets updated and goes out-of-date? Sometimes streaming services make changes and updated clients are required for it to work, however you are largely stuck with the version that this came with unless they issue a firmware update or something.
This is still cheaper than the higher end mp3 players that support high end DAC and app updates, but not by much. It seems to be a sort of in-between product. If you have a use for something like this, it could be a pretty good option. But if you're expecting a handheld tablet or alternative concept to an ipod touch, it is not exactly that.

I love my laptop. It is so handy and easy to type on, but one thing has a tendency to drive me crazy- the touchpad. Although I like some of the features on the touchpad, it has a tendency to make so many mistakes or tracking errors that I often want to throw it out the window.

When I was given an opportunity to review and rate the Logitech Wireless Marathon Mouse 750, I was skeptical, but willing to try it.

I do not do well with most mice. They hurt my wrists and make me so frustrated that I prefer using my desktop keyboard touchpad which is perfect- has been for over 10 years.

I was so frustrated with my touchpad on my laptop, however, that I decided to give it a try anyway. What I discovered was so exciting that I actually LOVE using a mouse with my laptop.

WHAT DOES THIS MOUSE COME WITH?
Although the mouse comes with a CD with drivers and program on it, I downloaded it from the Logitech site finding it to be more current. There are two AA batteries that come with it and they are easy to put in the mouse. There is also a short instruction sheet, and a tiny little USB wireless antenna that plugs into the laptop USB.

HOW WELL DOES THIS MOUSE WORK?
I am very impressed with this mouse. I use my Kindle case to run the mouse on, but it will work with many surfaces. Tracking is very accurate and can be adjusted through the program. Plugging in was easy and the mouse worked instantly with no problems. The ergonomic mouse is the most comfortable mouse I have used. There is an ON OFF button and a side button for going forward and backward on web pages.

I can not comment on battery longevity as I have only had it for a month. This is supposed to last for three years. Only time will tell.

All in all, despite the fact that it is an extra piece to stuff in my laptop case, I really like this mouse. It is very comfortable, easy to use, and excellent in tracking performance. The buttons work well and the center wheel will magnify or reduce the size of the screen- internet pages are esp handy this way. You press once, and then a magnifier comes up. Clicking the wheel one direction will enlarge, and the other direction would decrease the size. Clicking again locks it into place.

The center wheel will also scroll the page down incrementally, or really fast if you spin it, making it much easier to control the page views. Two buttons on the left hand side will forward or reverse pages on the browser very easily using the thumb. There is a little button just below the center wheel which I have not figured out yet.

There is a press point right where the thumb rests which reduces windows allowing you to pick the application you want to use- you click on the window you want to change to.

You can completely change the settings on your mouse any way you want to, however so that you can have it the way you like it.

FINAL COMMENTS
I really love this mouse- and I can not stand most mice for computers- they really get to me. This one is so comfortable and easy to use, it has changed my opinion of mice- at least this one.

I first bought this GPS several months ago when Costco had it on sale but ended up returning it because I was not pleased with the time it took to recognize my location. More specifically, I would be on the Capital Beltway surrounding DC and the stern female voice would repeatedly tell me to make a U-turn. Impossible. I then used a friend's hand-me-down Magellan which would not hold a charge, not recognize the location and simply needed to be retired. Enter Amazon and their great price for the Navigon 2100 max. Since I'd read that the device was improved with the Fresh Maps update, I purchased Fresh Maps and I highly recommend you do the same if you're contemplating this beautifully sleek GPS.

If you have a PC, you are able to upgrade by connecting the GPS directly to your computer. If you have a Mac, then it's a little more complicated but so worth the effort. You need to remove the SD card from the GPS and transfer the downloaded software to the SD card with a card reader/writer and then reinsert the card into the GPS. I kept a backup of the original software on my hard drive just in case, but have had no need since the upgrade immediately worked. Now on to what I really like about this system.

The 4.3 inch screen is easier to view than the 3.5, particularly if you have many of the POI's selected for display. I first chose them all, then realized they obstructed my map because I'm in the DC metro area. Mine connects with a satellite in only a few seconds each time and reroutes immediately if I change my route. Previously, it would announce that it was rerouting, but it no longer does that, just does the work. Three choices for trip planning are fine enough for me, I tend to choose the Optimal Route. I love being able to select different destinations, too, if I'm going to different places. The address book is easy to access and locations are easier to save. Traffic support is a great asset and now comes free with this device -- I've been saved from many a jam and not have to be tuned into the radio for traffic reports on the 8's. I have the screen set to automatically change from day to night and have had no problem viewing the screen at any time. With the new software, you are able to turn off the GPS from the touchscreen in addition to the usual power button at the upper right hand edge. I love the 2D/3D view, especially when I'm approaching a multi-lane area and I'm unsure as to which lane I need to take. Two voice selections are fine for my needs, Dagmar is more pleasant, but the higher pitched Sarah gives the text to speech option (TTS), so that's the one I've selected. She's not very pushy, either, as some voices I've heard on GPS systems. In the pre-update version, her voice sounded more Germanic, I assume from its origin of Germany, but it's not as odd now. For me, this GPS is intuitive to use and I can make any adjustments from the touchscreen very quickly. I've yet to have a freeze of the system and it has always known where I was with one exception when I was off road on a gravel trail.

This is not a true coconut water, but a drink that contains coconut water, nata de coco (a gel made from fermented coconut water), and flavoring among the ingredients. I love it because it's refreshing, especially on humid days, and uses real sugar instead of substitutes that I try to avoid.

Each eight ounce serving contains 70 calories with 18 grams of carbs (16 of which are from sugars). Contrast that with the same serving of Classic Coke, which comes in at 95 calories and 26.4 grams of carbs (all of which are from sugars) and this wins from a nutritional perspective. This drink is much lighter than most sodas and I have personally found it to be good for suppressing my appetite as well.

While it does quench thirst, it does not have the sodium content to be ideal for rehydration. Gatorade, for example, contains roughly 100mg of sodium for the same serving size, which is significantly more than the 15mg this drink contains. Moreover, this drink is missing potassium, which is also recommended for rehydration. I am mentioning this because there are coconut waters that are formulated for rehydration, but this one is more of a beverage.

The main ingredient is mineral water, followed by nata de coco, organic cane sugar, coconut water, calcium lactate, citric acid, sodium citrate, gellan gum and grapefruid seed extract.

Bottom line for me: I consume about sixteen ounces of this per day, and during exceptionally hot and humid days about twice that. Although this is no substitute for a rehydration drink, it does quench my thirst and the sugar gives me a boost without causing cramps in my fingers and toes like a soda does.

I happen to use a D-Link DIR 1360 as my internet router at home, and while it does a decent job broadcasting signal around me, it is located at one corner of our home which means the opposite corner of the house has too many barriers for a fast signal. And if I want to take my laptop out to the porch? No reliability at all!
But with this placed a few rooms over from the router, it has greatly extended my network and the speed of things nearby it. It was super simple to set up, too! I'm not sure if that's just because I happen to have a D-Link router, but all I had to do was press the setup button on the router and extender while plugged in next to it, then once setup I could unplug and move it wherever I wanted to extend to. No app or IT knowledge required! Literally press the button, wait a few minutes for the lights to turn green, and good to go! The access point matches the original name of my router, so it is all completely invisible to the user. The device picks whichever device is closer / stronger and automatically connects to it without any user intervention, much like a cell phone. Now, this is only possible because my router supports this mesh-style setup. Otherwise you'll have to do one of those alternative SSID things where the device sees two networks and has to decide which one to connect to. The first was is preferable obviously, and just works better in addition to being cleaner.

With my laptop in my living room (on the other side of the house from my router), I used to get somewhere between 20-40mbps in my speed tests downloading. That's not terrible, but I'm paying for 300mbps service! But with this plugged in the middle of my home, that jumped to 80-90mbps reliably! Still not the 200+ speeds I get if only a room or two away from the router, but definitely an improvement by almost 2x... and spots outside on the porch that rarely had coverage before now do.

HOWEVER, like any extender, this WILL introduce some lag to your network. This is the part I was warning about in the headline, as most people think extenders will improve your performance across the board, which isn't true. While my download and upload speed improved, my Ping time degraded from 8ms to 14 (lower is better). That extra hop from the extender back to the router has a cost. Now, that difference shouldn't make a huge difference in most things, 14ms is still pretty respectable, however a larger ping lag can effect real-time performance like lag in multiplayer games and video call performance. Arguably, in those cases, a lower ping is more important than higher speeds. So if I'm having trouble with gaming lag or video call echo, I'd probably unplug this and go with the original weaker signal to the router directly. But if I'm going outside, or just streaming Netflix etc, than the download performance is more important than the ping. So, make your decisions wisely... I've seen too many people running multiple zoom devices over lockdown and think a wireless extender is going to solve their problems, but in fact just made everyone's zoom calls worse! But this isn't the fault of the device, that's inherent of how all extenders work. So, I'm still giving this 5 stars for being an excellent instance of what it should be: a way to boost transfer speeds and extend range that's dead simple to set up.

The prices on big-screen smart tvs are in free-fall these days; projectors are always a bit of a project. But you're sure you want a projector, right? If so this is a great choice. Easy set up, great image, amazing keystoning (more on THAT in a moment), powerful internal speakers, and a decent price point (under $900 currently.)

Setup could scarcely be easier - provided you have your screen and the (not included) input cables/stick - or a wireless dongle. As I already had a projection screen and an HDMI cable for my laptop, all I had to do was switch on the projector, adjust the lens, run the start utility to keystone for the projector being offset from the center of the screen, connect the cable from laptop to projector, then allow the device to find the video source - the device finds the input in a few seconds and is soon streaming video and audio.

The projector's own audio is surprisingly good - and loud. Response to the remote is... a little slow, depending how close you are to the projector. The projector's own audio is great, and as we have it closer to the screen than we sit, I haven't felt the need to connect speakers. Persons with more demanding tastes in audio will of course differ, but the device's own speakers do a solid job.

Video quality is OUTSTANDING. Colors are vibrant and although a light source placed near the screen washes them out, the image is still clearly visible. With a light source more than 10 feet away and even with natural light through windows (at the opposite end of a 25-foot room) the image is perfectly clear; even though as I'm using a white screen the blacks are clear and dark. There was one strange exception to this with a streaming video (Extant) where the darks were warmer in the projection than on the laptop, but we have run other video and also had a DVR player (hooked up via the triple cables), and run DVRS with perfect light levels. I recently got an Amazon Fire Stick, and actually set it up on the projector - setup was easy and there have been no adjustments needed for the streaming video.

The keystoning is an amazing, but somewhat tedious, feature; you can offset the device and still get an excellent image. Using the keystoning feature on the remote, some tweaking gives you a near-perfect image. I say near perfect because when we had the projector placed eight feet back and some feet down to the left of the screen, the upper right-hand corner of the image frame bent inwards - although the cast image itself was clear and undistorted. This was apparently because the projector was not on a perfectly horizontal surface. The real issue was that when the projector was moved back in front of the screen, I had to redo the keystoning manually; holding down the OK key was supposed to reset it, but this didn't work for me.

The projector is relatively light and easy to move around. The feet are easy to unscrew to manipulate the image, but for the afore-mentioned keystoning issue, it was necessary to adjust the surface the projector was resting on; this would obviously be a whole different matter if ceiling-mounted.

I think it's a great projector. So really it all boils down to whether you WANT a projector - the VERY big picture and/or the portability, eh? You don't care about having to control light levels, positioning the device itself (and the associated transmitting device,) maintaining a screen, dealing with multiple interfaces... You're not the complete couch potato, surfing the channels via remote... Not to go on and on - this is a projector, not a tv. You can hook it up to a tv, or a laptop, streaming stick, etc, but - a projector is always going to be more complicated. This, however, is an amazingly uncomplicated projector!

I wanted a wired connection in a far room out of reach of my router. This works perfectly for that by allowing me to use any power outlet in my condo as a way to extend my wired network.

I tested my upload and download speeds with a network cable plugged from my laptop directly into my router and compared it to a wired connection with the Netgear Powerline Outlet. There was no discernible difference either positive or negative. I even ran video under both scenarios and I detected no difference in performance.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the router, my ping was 12 ms, download was 17.08 Mbps, upload was 5.17 Mbps.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the Powerline using my electrical house wiring, my ping was 12 ms, download was 16.63 Mbps, upload was 5.20 Mbps.

Although these speeds are not great, that is the performance I usually get with the router and service provider I have. Based on my results, this works as designed. Below is a list of what comes in the package and the PROS and CONS.

The package includes two Netgear Powerline 1200 Outlets each with an extra outlet and one Gigabit Ethernet port, two 6.5 foot Ethernet cables, and a quick start guide. For the initial installation of these units, both outlets have to be used because one Powerline must be plugged into an outlet near the router so that the Ethernet cable from the Powerline can plug into the router. The other Powerline can be plugged into an outlet anywhere else in the home. The other Ethernet cable is then plugged into this unit on one end and an Ethernet-enabled device such as a laptop, SmartTV, etc. on the other. If additional Powerlines are purchased then both units can be used for two additional wired connections.

PROS
- The LEDs on the Powerline enable the user to diagnose if there's power, Ethernet connectivity, or the ability to "Pick A Plug" (a.k.a. electrical outlet) with the strongest performance.

- There's an extra outlet on each Powerline. This unit covers the second outlet if it's plugged into the top outlet of a two-outlet receptacle. However, I do not see that as a problem for two reasons. First, there's an extra outlet on the unit. Therefore, I am still getting the ability to plug in two items like I would have had I not been using the Powerline. (In this case the Powerline is one item and a light is another.) If I want to turn my outlet into a three outlet receptacle, then all I have to do is plug it into the lower outlet. This would allow me, for instance, to plug in a lamp in the top receptacle, the Powerline in the bottom receptacle, and another item into the extra outlet on the Powerline.

- According to the manual, the network can be secured by pressing the security button for two seconds and then pressing the security button on one of the other adapters in the existing network. If additional adapters are added throughout the house when security is already enabled, then ALL the adapters should be factory reset. To re-enable security, all that has to be done is press the security button for two seconds on one adapter and then select any ONE other adapter (it's not necessary to do all adapters) and press that security button for two seconds. Both security buttons have to be pressed within two minutes time.

- There's a 1 year warranty plus 90 days basic customer support.

CONS

- I see none at this time.

I will write Netgear to find out what is meant by security with these security buttons. Up to 16 adapters can be installed in a home. I know if I were to install another set of these, I would actually be able to use both Powerlines for extra wired connections, thereby increasing my wired connections to three from one. It's only for the first installation that the extra Powerline is lost because that is used to connect to the router.

In summary, I feel this Netgear works as designed with no discernible difference in speed over a wired connection whether I was plugged directly into the router or the Powerline. Installation was simple and turning any one of my electrical outlets into a wired connection was practically instantaneous.

UPDATE April 27, 2015 - I contacted Netgear for an explanation of why there's a security feature on these adapters and exactly what that means to me. Below is Oleg Fishel's (of customer support) response which I slightly paraphrased.

The security refers to encryption between each of the Powerline adapters on my network. A random key is generated and shared among the adapters when the security setup button is used. All traffic is then encrypted using the highly secure 128 bit AES encryption protocol that prevents any unauthorized person from accessing the communication on my network. The reason enabling this security is recommended is to prevent someone from coming into my home with another Powerline adapter and connecting directly into my network to get information or for free Internet access. Although this scenario might be rare, this may be a concern with apartment buildings and offices where electrical circuits might be shared and in the case of homes that have outdoor electrical sockets. In summary, it is best to enable security. It is especially important when the Powerline is on a shared electrical circuit where someone can come along and plug one of these adapters in and piggyback off the network.

In regard to another question I had regarding the use and installation of 16 adapters all at once, he said "The HomePlug standard (HPAV2) used by the PL1200 supports up to 16 adapters on the network working together simultaneously. So if you purchased 7 kits (14 units) in addition to the original kit, you could have a 16 node network."

The Lensbaby Edge 80 Optic is one of Lensbaby's "swappable" optics for its line of lenses. It has a focal length of 80mm and features a 12-blade aperture with a range from f/2.8 through f/22. It can function as a regular 80mm f/2.8 lens when facing forward on your camera, but this optic's special feature is that it allows you to employ the usual Lensbaby bend and tilt to reposition your plane of focus along any point not parallel with your camera's sensor plane.

The usual Lensbaby lens tilt allows you to place the point of focus (with varying diffusion all around that point) but did not allow you to change the plane of focus itself. With this optic you can put a "slice of focus" through your image in creative ways. For example, you can highlight a certain aspect of the photo (such as producing a portrait where the eyes are in sharpest focus and everything else is softly blurred), or you can create the "false miniature" effect where the objects photographed take on the appearance of miniature scale models. The optic also has a close focus mode that will allow a close focus distance of 17".

There is a bit of learning curve for this optic. Expect to play around for bit before you get the hang of it. There are some good video tutorials on the Lensbaby site. I included a couple of example photos with this review.

You don't need to swap lenses to get back to "normal." As I mentioned earlier, the Edge 80 behaves like a normal 80mm lens when you aren't employing any of its tilt features. The aperture ring on the optic adjusts smoothly, and focusing and tilt occurs on the lens body itself. The shift from regular focus mode to close focus mode is a little tight -- you have to firmly pull the front edge of the optic outward. But, I imagine that's as it should be to avoid it shifting by itself.

My one source of frustration so far is in detaching the optic from the lens itself. Suffice to say you will need to review Lensbaby's instructions for this, and practice several times before you can successfully detach the optic. My first try took almost half an hour, which is not a delay you would want to experience in the field. I did get better with practice, but it's still a bit of tricky. Older hands might suffer more than younger hands. I've found in practice you can get by with swapping out other Lensbaby optics from the lens without detaching the lens from your camera, but with the Edge 80 optic, you really need to detach the whole lens first in order to get the optic out of the lens. That will allow you to get the best grip on the components when performing the detach maneuver.

Note that the optic in this product listing is not sold with a lens. The Edge 80 only works with the latest line of Lensbaby Lenses (NOT the 1.0, 2.0 or 3G). You need at least one of the current Lensbaby Lenses to use this optic. The optic works with the Muse, Composer, Control Freak and Scout lenses; it can also work with the Composer with Tilt Transformer, but you need to buy the Macro Converters in order to use the Edge 80 optic with that lens. Note too that if you want true macro capability, you will need to buy the Macro Converters anyway, regardless of which Lensbaby lens you have (their earlier Macro accessories will not work with this optic).

Normal in-lens tilt-shift lens are expensive ($1200-$2500). While the Edge 80 does not give you all the features of such a dedicated lens, it is a highly affordable alternative that provides enough capability for many tilt/shift needs. It's a great way to get into this type of photography without breaking the bank. Highly recommend.

This is a flawless tablet. Everything you'd expect. There are a few things that don't feel comfortable or might feel jarring, but then you are here because you want a huge tablet, so they should be expected.

The screen if gorgeous! And Samsung has done a great job of making the icons proportional to the screen. Because at this super high resolution, if you left the icons to the normal size, they would be TINY. That said, be prepared to see -huge- icons since they are proportionally bigger than, say, even a huge Note 3 phone. Still the ratio isn't one to one from a tiny tablet, there is room for a couple of more icons per row.

Weight: This is light and feels great... for a tablet its size. That said, be prepared to always have to put it or your hands on something if you are using it more than a couple of minutes. While it is solid & light enough to hold it in one hand by a corner and use, your hand will be cramping in no time.

Look and feel: Just awesome. I don't get professional reviewers issue with "faux leather", it looks and feels awesome! Even though it's bigger than all the rest, this is still a tablet, as I said above, you can brag and pick it up by a corner without feeling like you are putting too much force on a corner or anything of the nature. But its dimensions do mean you have to lean your arm on something or put it down for using more than reading a single email, even then...

The large dimensions also mean awkward reading in bed unless you are sitting up with your legs or a pillow under it. If you are laying on the ground or on your bed faxing down with it flat and reading websites or an online book with the tablet in portrait format (as one would tend to read long things), then the top is too far away and an angle, as would a tall magazine be.

This can easily be fixed with a little something to prop the end away from you up of course, but just making sure you realize that you will get what you are asking for, a gorgeous, great feeling tablet that is the largest on the market, but you are also getting something rather large, and all that comes with that, so expect it. I read all professional reviews saying pretty much that and I figured they were just complaining to have something to write about... nope, it really is a bit hard to wield.

The Good:
-They sound good. They're not audiophile speakers, of course, but they sound much better than some of the other outdoor speakers I've heard, and better than any other outdoor speaker I auditioned in this price range.
-They're rugged, which you really need in an outdoor speaker. It's not just rain, after all; an outdoor speaker has to contend with errant footballs, rough handling, curious animals, etc, any of which would break a normal indoor speaker. These have a metal grill and very sturdy build and should stand up to almost anything.
-I like the mounting system; very flexible and well-engineered.

The Bad (and these are minor)
-Very cramped, awkward space for the binding posts. I use banana plugs because I need a quick, easy way to hook them up (standing on a ladder, fumbling around behind the speaker) and there's not enough room back there for normal banana plugs. I wound up buying some right-angle plugs (I got the Monoprice), and those resolved this for me.
-Sound quality is good for an outdoor speaker in this price range but if you don't need a rugged speaker, you can get much better sound for the price. As I'm writing this review, the ELAC Debut 2.0 B6.2 is on sale for about the same price as these Atriums, and the ELAC has much better sound. Of course, the ELAC probably wouldn't survive a night on my patio.

Over the last year, I've tried various hdmi capture devices and this one is the lowest priced and best of them. The most common problem with capture cards are their drivers. Custom drivers either introduce too much lag or are simply unsupported by various software.

The PACOXI HDMI capture bypasses ALL of those driver problems by showing up as a simple USB webcam. Without the need to install any drivers, the built-in Windows 10 camera app immediately recognizes the device and shows the signal. OBS, of course, fully supports this product and VLC can open capture device successfully . Turn off buffering in OBS or VLC and you get near real-time performance.

I've tested this capture device with FireTV and Nintendo Switch and both worked well.

I've even connected this to my phone through a USB-A to USB-C connector. On Android, it is necessary to download a "usb camera" app, but I can say that with the right software, this device will work.

In the last week, I've been using this for my Zoom calls. Plugging in the HDMI output from my mirrorless camera, I used a shallow focus lens and got a great image with beautiful bokeh (blurry background) without the weird cutout effect that you'd normally get when zoom tries to do it for you. At 1080p, the image in zoom is simply flawless.

At this low price, I'm thinking about getting more than one so that OBS can cut between multiple cameras or inputs.

I'm a huge fan of Microsoft keyboards. Never been much of a fan of their office productivity software, but when it comes to keyboards, Microsoft fits my needs to a T. I'm using the Microsoft Digital Media Pro keyboard which (I believe) was discontinued years ago. A shame, since it has so many useful features.

But out with the old and in with the new. I tried and did not care for the previous generation of ergonomic split keyboards from Microsoft. At first glance the Sculpt looked to be a better design. The divide between the two sets of keys did not appear to be as pronounced, and my hands seemed to fit the keyboard very well. Love the feel of the pad on the wrist rest area!

Installation was straightforward, although getting the items out of the box was a challenge. I was happy to see that the necessary batteries were included - nothing worse than having to go hunt for batteries before you can start to use a new device.

The keyboard feel strongly reminded me of a laptop. For some, that may be a good feature. For me it is not. The flat keys and shorter throw makes typing feel "unnatural." I know that sounds vague, but it's the best way I can describe it.

This odd feel translated itself into a much slower typing speed - cut my throughput by about half. Since I write reports for a living, that's a rather big issue.

I also could not come to grips with the function key placement, size and meager supply of ancillary keys. That's a feature I love with my current Media Pro keyboard in that I can map pretty much any of the ample number of multimedia keys to any function I choose, or even a URL. For example, to start SPSS, Excel and WP I press one key. Another single keypress also opens my browser and my Amazon cart URL (and yes, the lettering on that particular key is pretty much worn completely off from use).

Still, if I was forced to, I could live with the keyboard. I could not, under any circumstances, live with the mouse in this set. Feels poor, lacks refinement, and far less versatile than my Logitech M500. I tried my best to get used to the Sculpt mouse, but just grew to hate it the longer I used it.

Now, my opinions are certainly affected by my current choices in keyboards and mice since I've been using them for years and years. I've changed PCs at least three times, but have retained the same keyboard and mouse since they have worked so well. If you have less keyboard/mouse "muscle memory" perhaps the Sculpt will fit the bill. The build quality seems decent, and if they are as reliable as other Microsoft keyboards, it will continue to work for some time. But for me, I just can't move the approval meter past "meh" for the keyboard and "dud" for the mouse. Three stars.
