The sleek and totally elegant Vizio VBR220 is promising on so many levels. The sleek elegant design is pure eye candy. The touch screen "buttons" on the front are fascinating and fun to play with, the internet apps and included wireless connectivity works well when it works, and DVD playback is wonderful. Menu is elegant and well designed, the remote is a bit cheap feeling.

This unit comes with internet apps like Netflix, which works wonderfully and streams in HD pretty well, along with Vudu apps and three free Vudu rentals. This is nice, though VUDU has trouble with streaming the same quality as netflix does on slower internet connections like DSL. YOu have to have a scorching fast home connection to stream in 1080.

But when it comes to doing what the product was meant to do, play Blu Rays, this product fails on so many levels. Actually there is a good chance that it will not work right out of the box. My device would not play any Blu Rays. I tried two new blu rays, Dinner with the Schmucks, and Avatar. Neither would load and only a complete reboot of the machine would solve the problem.

After looking at online it is a common problem. There are quite a few of these devices that will not work out of the box and only returning for a new one will solve the problem. Unlike some other units, like the VBR100 there is no firmware update to solve blu ray issues.

Overall, this unit shows promise. It is beautiful, with some interesting design features, the menus are well laid out and attractive, and internet streaming, though can be a bit stubborn at times, works well.

I would hold off on this purchase until they solve the blu ray issues with a new product built. Then and only then will I think this device will stand up to standard bearer, Sony.

It is comfortable to grip, the scroll wheel is smooth and easy to turn, and the buttons are easy to press without being hyper-sensitive. Ergonomics are this mouse's strongest attribute.

In use, the mouse is on par with other Microsoft mice I have used. It is accurate. Unlike some of the comments by other reviewers here, I have had no issue with it being too sensitive or too precise. The performance has, in my opinion, been average. This is not a bad thing - Microsoft mice are usually very consistent and this one fits the norm.

Where I ran into difficulty with this mouse was in charging it. I read a lot of other reviews on this mouse beforehand so I was prepared for issues with charging. That said, I was still having issues getting the mouse to charge the battery until I cut part of a 3x5 index card, folded it up and crammed it into the battery compartment with the battery. There have been enough other people that have had to do similarly odd things to rule out the possibility of this being an isolated case.

The battery can be put into a normal charger, but that defeats the purpose.

This is not a bad mouse. It's actually quite good and I would recommend it except for the recharging issue. As a wireless mouse it is fine, but as a recharging mouse it needs a design revisit.

Disclaimer - I've only had these for about a week so far and these are the very first Truly Wireless Earbuds that I have ever owned.

I purchased these earbuds on a great sale while waiting for another more expensive brand to get restocked, and honestly didn't expect to much from these. First impressions were that they were quite cheap however after using them for a little while now, I've come to appreciate them even more. Even though these are my very first Truly Wireless Earbuds, I feel that after tons of research and watching reviews, I know what to look for in sound and quality. There are so many budget wireless earbuds on the market right now with so many more on Indigogo (which from comments and reviews I've seen and read, I will NEVER buy from). This makes it quite hard to know what to buy. For me, I have been waiting for that perfect very small and discreet Truly Wireless Earbud with amazing sound. The Iyesku YK-T02 TWS Sport Earbuds didn't hit that mark for me but at the price I paid, I honestly can't complain.
Pros:
1. Bluetooth 5.0 - This was one of my main requirements when searching and the YK-T02 has it.
2. Easy to pair (I am using the Samsung Note 8) and pairing was very easy. Once the buds are initially paired, they connect super fast once you pull them out of the charging case.
3. No loss of connectivity to either earbud. I've seen a bunch of reviews where this is an issue with MANY other wireless earbuds on the market. Even some of the more spendy ones.
4. Fit is very comfortable and seem to be very secure though I have not put them through the test of running nor exercise. However I don't think this would be an issue at all.
5. Sound quality is decent. More about this in the Cons.
6. Tons of ear tip options. Most earbuds come with a few extra sizes but these come with a plethora, for that perfect custom fit.
7. Quite small and discreet.
8. Small pocketable charging case.

Cons:
1. Sound. As I stated in the Pros these sound "good" (for the money) but the Highs are quite loud (Mids and Bass are not) and almost hurt when the volume is turned all the way up. Mids are not to bad but the bass is nearly non existent which was a huge let down. HOWEVER let me say, once I played with the ear tips and found the right fit, Highs, Mids, and Bass are much better, but still not what I would have hoped for but again these aren't "High end" earbuds right?
2. Because the volume of these buds are quite low, Audio books are hard to hear when in a loud environment.
3. No satisfying magnet to hold the buds in the charging case like many others on the market. (The case does click shut to ensure the buds wont be falling out.)
4. Speaking of the case, my first impression was that the case felt very nice and lightweight, but it does feel cheap.

Final thoughts:
Like I said earlier in this review, if you can get these from Amazon on a lightning deal or with a coupon, I would say grab you a pair, but just don't expect these to compete with higher end buds. These would be great for the kids and anyone that just wants a good pair of Truly Wireless Earbuds that wont break the bank.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

Personally I really like the flood light security cameras. Flood lights are a natural deterrent for criminal activity - when the light comes on it startles the person trying to sneak around and having the light almost guarantees that you will receive a clear image.

I have tested and reviewed several similar floodlight camera systems. As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

In terms of this particular floodlight WiFi camera by FREECAM it comes with a 16GB SD card but while the manufacturer claims the camera can accept up to 64GB, I’ve been unable to get mine to accept anything but the included 16GB.

The app, while certainly not the worst I’ve used, is far from the best. It is not particularly user friendly and support is non existent. I was able to achieve a reasonable reliability in terms of video capture although the alert system is not reliable.

The bulbs are bright - 1400 Lumen and while they are not replaceable being LED, they should last a long time.

Installation was as straightforward as installing any floodlight and required around 15 minutes.

In terms of WiFi flood light cameras, I’m disappointed with not being able to get anything but the included 16GB SD card to work - this tends to point to the company trying to force buyers into their cloud services. I have carefully monitored all traffic and if the camera was attempting to access the internet independently - my internet blocks will prevent this but I have not detected anything in my testing thus far.

The app is not dependable nor is it user friendly.

All around this is a product I would avoid.

I wrote this review with a heavy dose of input from my husband, who is a retired IT professional.

We had a problem with the router supplied by our internet provider. It was causing all the devices on the network to lose their connection multiple times per day. The provider sent us a new router, but it was a "black box" device that did not allow for configuration by the user or even the provider's tech support personnel. So we decided to buy our own router. After quite a bit of research, we picked this one.

PROS

-Good speed at 600Mbps for the 2.4GHz band and 1300Mbps for the 5GHz band.
-It is configurable by the user. I can sign on to the admin page via my browser and change settings. The setting we most wanted to change was the default DHCP server lease time setting. For a home network such as ours that always has the same devices using it, there is no need to have short (i.e., hours long) DHCP lease time setting. The constant renewing of the lease can cause connection issues for the devices. At least, that has been our experience.
-The device seems very stable. Since swapping it in for the internet provider's router, we have had no dropping connections whatsoever. We are quite pleased with this router.
-2 year warranty.

CONS

-The maximum DHCP lease time setting was only a couple of days, unlike a previous router I had, which allowed you to go up to 30. But this is not really a big disadvantage. I have not noticed a problem with it.

Now this station comes in crystal clear, loud, and strong. Note that I decided to mount this antenna on the side of my house, just beneath the peak of my low roof facing the back yard. I had a quantity of twin 300 ohm cable which I wanted to use. Using a 300ohm/75ohm converter, I simply attached the end of the cable to the two 300ohm screws, protecting the connection with electrical tape. I measured and fabricated a wood mounting plate (see photo) and then screwed the mast bracket to it from the back. The wooden support board was then lag screwed, in turn, to the outside of my house just below the peak using 5" long screws. I then installed the antenna and mast, after reversing it. It now extends upwards vertically yet does not interfere with the roof line. The versatility of the mast permitted me to accomplish that.

Assembly tips:

- Both curved antenna segments are secured to the antenna cross bar with the supplied hardware.
- The ends of one (bottom) segment are held in place with two phillips head screws. First, remove the curved metal clamp. line up the holes in the segment and, maintaining hand pressure on each segment end to ensure that it is seated firmly into it's curved metal seat, insert each screw and secure. Do not over tighten these fasteners. This is the "bottom" of the antenna, opposite the 75 ohm connector side. Attach one leg of the segment at a time.
- The ends of the second (top) segment are held in place with two hex head nuts. You will note that each nut is topped with a rubber 'O' ring. This is used to keep the nuts from threading off until assembly. Do not attempt to re-use these as they are not spacers or washers.
- Again, seat the ends of the antenna segment firmly in place, aligning the holes over the studs. Holding down the segment, install each nut. Do not over tighten these nuts.
- The closed loop ends of each antenna segment may now be gently guided in front of the black plastic locking clips. Once the looped ends are in position, firmly, yet carefully snap them into place. GOOD STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX Bi323-U
--It's a decent piece of gear... at least for now. I'll be back if it fouls up later on. The memory and hard drive installation couldn't be easier.
--Once you install an OS, it boots into the software very quickly.
--Windows 7, 8.x and so on install well.
--Debian 8.4.x installs on this unit as well. It takes some tinkering and it finally installs.
--I installed Win 7 Pro, and then removed it and installed Debian. Just wanted to see how easy it is to do that. Notes about Debian are at the end.
--For a very low end item, this isn't a bad choice so long as you're willing to set aside a few hours to set it up and are willing to put up with a poorly designed manufacturer/seller website, and poor customer service.
--For my purposes it was an okay choice. I had a few extra SSDs around as well as memory that were compatible with this unit, so this was a cheap solution to add an extra computer.

NOT SO GREAT STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX-Bi323-U
--BE SURE TO SCAN EVERYTHING FROM THE ZOTAC SITE AND THE CD/DVD THAT COMES WITH THE UNIT
--The documentation is really thin, almost useless.
--At first boot, the BIOS screen appears and you may (likely will) have to change some settings. It's best if you're familiar with what the settings do and what they effect. TIP: the Legacy Boot seems the most reliable. Complete the settings, save and exit.
--The BIOS (after adjusting settings) looks for an OS on the hard drive or CD/DVD. It does not look at USB thumb drives or SD cards. Have the external CD/DVD attached with install disc inserted.
--How to get back to the BIOS or BOOT SEQUENCE settings DOES NOT appear on any boot screens after the first power on, as it does with most other systems. How to access the BIOS settings IS NOT included in the docs. You have to press F8 for the bios or Delete for boot sequence settings. Found it on the web.
--Zotac site uses a squeeze page to get your info before you can access anything useful.
--The combination SD reader/USB port is just weird. You cannot use this port for both at once.

About Linux (Debian 8.4.x)
--I installed this successfully after several attempts. Zotac's site shows Linux drivers, but they download only the Win 7 drivers. You don't really need them for a Linux install. Set the bios for Legacy Boot or it won't boot into Linux after an install. ISO DVD 1 is the only file you need for the install. Graphical install is the only option that worked out.
--DO NOT TRY AND CONNECT WITH DEBIAN MIRRORS FOR NEWER APPS, it fails on all. Later use terminal to upgrade.
--After a successful install, the Zotac restarts and you end up at the Debian login screen for you user id and password. The password is rejected. --Power off with the power button. Power back on and this time you can login with the credentials supplied at install.
AFTER LOGGING IN, your user ID won't be in SUDOERS. Use terminal, SU into root. After that, use apt-get update followed by apt-get upgrade.

I did figure out that the initial way I had them in my ears was upside down when I went to test the calling features. The microphone needs to be pointed towards your mouth for best audio reception and sound quality improves a bit in this position.

It would have been helpful if the manufacturer put a different texture in that area so you could feel it with your finger to locate it.

While the manufacturers claims these last for 12 hours I found it was closer to 8 under normal use - still excellent. And the case will charge them without it having to be plugged back in which is always a nice feature.

These earbuds excelled in all of my tests showing that they are a high quality, dependable product.

This is a set I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend.

Somewhere there is an ancient marketing survey that identifies teen-age boys as a prime segment of the gaming market and that says they really like bright, flashing lights. So manufacturers who want to sell to the gaming market still think they have to add flashy lighting to all their products. Well, the gaming universe is much larger than teen boys these days and bright, flashing lights have nothing to do with playing a game. With that pet peeve off my chest let me add a couple of things to give this review some context. First, I do spend a lot of time online playing an MMO but I'm very much a casual player, not a hardcore competitive one. Second, I am not an audiophile. High end stereo gear is wasted on me as the music coming from most any clock radio is good enough for me.

To my non-audiophile ears, the sound from this speaker is fine. It provides a nice range without being too heavy on the bass end or too shrill on the high end. Whether gaming, streaming videos, or listening to music and audiobooks, this speaker holds its own nicely. Though, like the flashy lighting, the sound quality really doesn't make any significant difference while I'm playing in my MMO world. The ambient noise, NPC chatter, battle music and such, all come through nicely but that's a perk, not something that particularly improves my game play.

The under the monitor design of this speaker really doesn't save me any desk space. The mini speakers I was using before were much smaller and were out of the way on the side of the monitor. This space bar basically sits in front of my monitor and takes up more room than other speakers. One strong plus to me for this speaker is the fact that it really is plug and play. I had it up and running in just a few minutes. Other "gaming" gear I've tried with flashy lighting systems require software to control the lighting and sometimes getting that software to install and run properly can be a major, frustrating effort. So I really, really like that this product lives up to its "plug and play" claim.

There is one last negative point to mention. a minor one. The volume and other controls are flat buttons on the side of the soundbar. So to adjust the volume, change the lighting, etc, you need to move the soundbar to look at the side of it so you can see what you are doing. I call that a minor issue because my keyboard has mute and volume control buttons on it and I can just use those to adjust the sound as needed.

The bottom line of all this for me is that I wouldn't buy this speaker as a "gaming speaker" but simply as a nice mid-range speaker who's sound quality I like, one that is easy to set up and use. Oh, and lest I sound too much like a Grinch, the lights really are pretty, the way Christmas lights are. It's just that they have nothing to do with gaming. :)

Most of the USB cables I have are either 3' cables or are really short ones that come with electronic devices. Sometimes a longer cable is really handy, especially when the immediate area surrounding a work space is cramped. I looked to these 10' cables to help alleviate one such issue and I learned a few things. One of those things is that a cable can be too long in some cases, though this is a failure in organization, not in the cable.

These are flat USB cables. Flat cables are less likely to tangle than their round counterparts, but I will confess to preferring round cables anyway (it’s a personal preference, not a technical preference). These are shielded in woven nylon which is great; the nylon is stronger than soft plastic shielding and gives the cable a little more stiffness but does not make the cable so stiff that it’s awkward to run. The connectors are interesting - two-tone plastic that is different than anything else on my desk which makes it a lot easier to determine where both ends of the cable are plugged in. I tried stressing the cable ends at the connectors by trying to pull out the shielding from the plugs and they held firm.

I tried one of these with my phone and it worked just fine, I was able to charge the phone and move data between it and my laptop. I did not attempt a speed test.

There is a big difference between 3' cables, 6' cables and 10' cables. If you need a 6' cable, a 10' cable will leave you trying to figure out what to do with the extra 4' of cable. In my case this meant having to use a twist tie to bunch the cable up in the middle. This is not a criticism but rather a suggestion - get a cable that’s the right length for the job. If you need a 10' cable, these have worked great for me.

These are nice USB cables. They seem to be made well and they work as expected. If you need a really long cable, this is a good choice.

This is a very complete kit and does contain everything you need to setup a Raspberry Pi 3. Yes, the op system installs easily and, with luck, you can be up and running in less than an hour. So, why the 2 stars?

It gets 2 stars because the Raspberry Pi is probably one of the most frustrating devices I've ever tried to put to any real use. For example, I wanted to set it up so I could use a VNC server on the Pi and a VNC client on my Mac (OS X El Capitan). After three days of almost non-stop failures, I'm sick of this thing. Researching how to get this task done leads you down a black hole of internet articles and posts on the Raspberry Pi site, most of that give different instructions, use different commands, tell you which files to edit and what to put in them, and almost none work, period!

The core problem rests squarely on the Raspberry Pi organization. Their own website is full of conflicting posts on how to do just about anything beyond a basic setup. Few, if any posts state which model of Pi is being referenced, and many bear no date. All in all, it's a very frustrating experience and, while I like to tinker with these things, a little success is required once in a while to keep me chugging along. I think I'm done with this thing. I had hoped it would finally be a Linux for the rest of us. Unfortunately, it's just as convoluted and difficult to use as any version of Linux out there (my opinion).

However, if you're looking to explore the Pi, this kit has everything you need to do a basic setup of Linux. And, should you want to use it as a web server, file server, media server, you're really on your own. Drink lots of coffee and plan to pull our lots of hair.

I received a review sample of this cord and charger combination and have been testing it thoroughly. The most striking feature is the three meter cable, which is the longest I have seen for any iPhone (or Android phone for that matter.)

My first inclination was to test the cable for failures because the length seemed excessive. It performed every data transfer and synching operation flawlessly. It also fast-charges like an Apple OEM cable. I was a bit surprised that this and the charger were not MFi certified (Made for iPhone/iPod/iPad). Other cables and chargers that I have received from the manufacturer were, but this is indistinguishable from the MFi and Apple OEM cables that I have tested - both visually and from a performance perspective.

The contacts on both the USB and Lightning connector ends are precision made and mate perfectly to the ports to which they were designed to connect. The outer jacket is thick, but not too stiff to make handling it a problem. There are strain reliefs on both ends to ensure a long service life.

This set includes a bonus wall charger with folding prongs. This has the same well made construction, and also puts out a steady 2.1A for fast charging. This charger is perfect for iPads too because of the output rating. If I had one wish it would have a second 1.0A port for those of us who want to simultaneously charge a phone and tablet - perhaps the next generation of this product will have that feature.

Bottom line: when size (in the form of cable length) matters this is one of the very few on the market that is a full three meters long. Add in the fact that this one is made to perform like an Apple OEM cable and the value should be apparent.

If you've been using a "free" router provided by your ISP, this Linksys router will give you some interesting additional features not found in the freebies. A guest mode lets you create a separate network with a separate password and access to the internet, but not to other devices on your network. A USB port lets you connect a hard driver or printer that can be accessed by any device on your network. Parental controls let you limit access based on time of day or web address.

There are supposedly performance optimizations based on media prioritization and beam forming, but I have no way to test whether those actually work or not. I had no problems with connectivity and performance, though my home is not really large. Media prioritization supposedly allows you to give higher priority to selected devices on your network, which could be useful if for example you want to allocate a lot of bandwidth to streaming video and less to other uses.

Setup and configuration is always an issue with network devices. Make sure you access is using a generic DNS setup or you will confuse the setup process. Once I figured that out, the setup went smoothly. The setup makes you create a Linksys account to manage your router remotely. Network control is nice since you can login from anywhere to manipulate your router settings; but if someone hacks into the Linksys server, you could be in trouble. There is an option to disable network access in the settings.

The main issue I have with this device is that the configuration software is too simple. Simplicity is good for people with only basic computer skills, but it also leaves out a lot of things that more advanced uses will want to do. For example, the guest SSID is your main SSID with "-guest" appended; there is no way to create a custom SSID for guests. Also, the USB port sometimes work for me and sometimes not. Rebooting usually got it to work, but that is a big hassle. This is a cheap way to store music and videos on a central hard drive, then play them on any computer on your network.

Wow, these inexpensive fitness tracker watches have really come a long way! I've used WearOS, Fitbit, Galaxy and Amazfit brand watches, and usually find the cheap ones are cute for my kids but not very accurate or full of mostly gimmicky features.
This one actually looks and acts a lot like a cheaper version of my current Amazfit GTS3 watch. The way the menu works, the way the app works... it's all very familiar. Granted, this watch does not have the high resolution OLED display that my Amazfit does, but the display is capable of vivid colors and looks great!

The accuracy is surprisingly spot on, I even tested my heart rate with this and other smartwatches I own since usually there's a lot of discrepancy, and it often lined up exactly. Steps were interesting- most smartwatches don't count steps unless you move for more than a few steps at a time (disregarding a step here or there as an error). This one goes a step further and actually refused to count steps I made unless I was WEARING THE WATCH! I'm not sure if this is a attempt to prevent cheaters from shaking their watch or something, but I noticed it would not count any of my steps when I held it in my fingers, but when I put it on my wrist, it counted! Perhaps there is a proximity sensor on the back of the watch, I'm not sure. This might be a problem for those who occasionally put the watch in a pocket or something to get steps if, for example, pushing a shopping cart (since your wrist doesn't move, pushing strollers and carts tend to not count anyway- one workaround is to put the watch in a pocket but that might not work now).

Another thing I wish it had is a better notification system. Certain apps which aren't in their list of known notifications won't work correctly (Google Voice, for example). But that's true of all cheap tracker watches. It also can't install apps or extend functionality like the more expensive ones. There is definitely a reason my regular watch costs 5-6x as much as this one, but for what it is on a budget, honestly, it's pretty amazing!

I've become somewhat dependent on the sight of this bright blue radio. Every morning I stumble, groggy-eyed, into my bathroom. Having this clear-sounding radio, blasting my favorite music, is a nice pick-me-up as I shower. But does the design offer me anything more than what I would expect from a typical shower radio?

PROS: It's cleverly designed to mimic the shape of a shampoo. It melds easily into the background. My initial fear was that I would accidentally grab it instead of the real thing, but so far that hasn't happened.

PROS: The sound quality is tinny but quite decent for a shower radio.

PROS: The radio offers a "store" function where you can bookmark your favorite radio stations and get to them fast by using a "recall" button. This is a feature common to most clock radios but I don't spend enough time in the bathroom to use it. I basically stick to one station while showering and can't see myself using the "store" function unless I'm taking a long bath. Still, nice to have that option.

PROS: Great battery life! I used my AA batteries for this and it has been running for months with no problem.

CONS: It's not that easy to see the buttons. They're located on the sides of the device but the positions are not intuitive. I always have to squint a little to see the print above the buttons because the buttons do not stick out.

CONS: "Light up" function. The time display is very clear and easy to read as-is. Since it's not a bedtime clock radio that benefits from having a glow-in-the-dark function, this feature feels extraneous to me. Perhaps it's best for someone who likes to take a bath with candles all around.

CONS: Not space saving. I used to have a shower radio that could be hooked over the showerhead. While the radio is not huge, I still had to move my shampoo and conditioner bottles to make room for it.

Overall it is a decent radio and I have been using it since I got it with no problems.

First time using a GMRS system and this was exactly what I needed for how I'm using it. My off-road group has switched from CB to GMRS and this was the model I went with to make sure we could all keep comms up. With no modifications or aftermarket purchases, I was able to keep up 2-way comms with vehicles out to at least 2 miles away from inside my Jeep (never got further than that). It was all very clear transmissions and having the 2 button PTT option was nice for a private conversation to one other driver.

I can't speak to the battery too much but having it on and using it 2 days in a row, while keeping it off during the night, I never showed less than the 3/3 bars on the battery. That was even after resting it at night in below freezing temps. Very impressed with the life so I don't have to carry a separate charger or extra battery.

Setup for basic usage was very easy although getting into more advanced functions is fairly complex. Being able to switch between channel and ferq mode is simple, just turn it on/off while holding a single button. Also, I like that you can turn on high power with a single button push. Anything more than those adjustments and setting a frequency is complex however. Its possible to access the menu on the unit but its really to small to display a lot of text so you need the manual in front of you to really be able to make any useful changes. Not a huge issue for me as I don't need to do much more than set a channel and go, but for those that want to really dive into how the unit operates, its going to be somewhat of a chore.

Overall highly recommend the unit for anyone wheeling in a group that needs a simple comms setup and doesn't want to deal with mounting a more permeant unit. Don't forget to get your callsign to stay legal!

I have had 2 Tom Tom-Go GPS units and have been reasonably happy with this brand. My first Tom Tom Go lasted less than a year at which point it lost its "mind" in the LL Bean parking lot, uttering, "Turn, turn, turn." The 2nd Tom Tom lasted 2 years when it suffered screen damage. When both units worked, they were reliable and paid for themselves many times over in gas savings.
I decided to invest in the 1350 Nuvi refurbished Garmin to try out a new brand, to be reassured of having up-dated maps and to receive a 1-year warranty on this refurbished product whereas Tom Tom provides only a 6-month warranty on its refurbished GPS. I also liked the prospect of using the GPS for walking tours of NYC, Philadelphia, Boston, etc.
My Garmin 1350 arrived quickly and in perfect condition. It could be used right out of the box.I was impressed by the sturdiness of the case and by how well the suction gripped the windshield. The unit seemed to turn on a bit more slowly than my Tom Toms but the route planning may be somewhat faster. I liked having the points of interest scroll down the screen. There appear to be many more POI choices on the Garmin than the Tom Tom. The categories are intuitive and it is helpful to quickly see both map location and contact information. Since my cell phone is paired with my car, I did not use to Blue Tooth feature to call up the store via the GPS unit, but this would be very helpful.
I don't think that the default setting gives as much screen detail; e.g., providing names for all the streets. I have found the greater visual detail of the Tom Tom helpful when driving at night, but it is probably a needless distraction most of the time. It is very helpful to have the streets spoken at turns. The volume was perhaps even better than that of the Tom Tom. This surprised me, having read numerous complaints about Garmin being inaudible. I even had to turn down the volume to 80%. The pronunciations were reliably clear with only a few oddities; e.g., the town of St. Davids was spoken as "Street Davids."
Route corrections were made more quickly than I experienced with Tom Tom and it is helpful to know which side of the street the destination is on.
In making comparisons with the Tom Tom Go, there is a feature which I miss: the IQ routing. My Tom Toms had an uncanny knowledge of different routes and respective drive times at various times of the day. Quite fequently, the return route would differ from the original Also-- and more importantly-- the drive time was extremely accurate.
In contrast Garmin seems clumsy and mechanical. Perhaps, this is because I am stil getting used to the Garmin? So far, I am extremely frustrated by Garmin's under-estimation of drive times. Even when I go 4 miles above the posted speed limits, I am seldom able to catch up with the predicted drive time.There seems to be no allowance for stopping at lights. The greater the distance, the more this discrepancy.This is surprising given the Garmin's close attention to changing speed limits.
Also, I do not think that Garmin provides a warning about toll roads and the option to avoid them. I found this a very helpful Tom Tom feature.
The option of adding a memory card to the Garmin provides increased flexibility. I am yet to download additional points of interest to the card from the various on-line web-sites which provide such information free. I also look forward to trying out pedestrian information for NYC, including (I hope) public transportation details. Had I known that Garmins with MP3 players are needed for auditory tours, I might have chosen such a model.
A convenient feature is that the Garmin turns off automatically less than a minute after the car engine is stopped.The unit comes off the windshield readily for toting.
While a manual is available at the Garmin web-site, the curious user will find various hints and tips on-line.
I e-mailed 2 questions to Customer Service and received a helpful response within a couple of days-- even on a weekend!
I am still exploring so have not firmed up my opinion as to which brand is the better choice. I am tilting toward Tom Tom because of the IQ routing, but then I would not want to give up the more detailed points of interest given on the Garmin.

This Surface Laptop 4 model from Microsoft is an excellent premium grade laptop. My prior laptop is an older 17" Lenovo. This one is smaller (obviously), but much, much quicker.

The aluminum chassis is thin, lightweight and solid. The display is looks great- colors are detailed rich and vibrant, and the touchscreen is effective and appropriately responsive. I find myself simply reaching for the button on a given sites screen, rather than maneuvering the cursor and tapping. (Although, the TouchPad is certainly responsive, too). The keyboard is comfortable and responsive - the surface around the keys and track pad has a texture that makes it seem sort of "soft" (even though it's not). Sound is rich and full. Very nice!

Very few ports - only what you need and not much else. A USB Type-A and Type-C, a headphone jack, and the chargers connector. (Or you can charge using the USB Type-C port).

Set up is straightforward, I loaded in some software (Wordperfect suite) and everything just fell right in place and all worked as it should without issue)

5.) The keyboard is good. It’s not the best, a little spongier than the MacBook Pro 16’s, with a slower rebound, but still among the “good” keyboards on the market, - reasonably tactile. It has physical F-keys, something I wish I had on the MacBook Pro 16. I think the TouchBar is one of the worst things to happen to MacBooks (inadvertent touches are the worst!), so I hope Apple reverts to physical keys this coming year on their flagship system. Rumor has it they will.

6.) Ergonomics are decent, though it’s actually a bit tricky to open the laptop as there’s no indent where you’re meant to flip the screen up, - a peculiar oversight. Bezels are a little large for 2021, but far from offensive.

7.) Sound quality is not bad, but a far cry from the bass that the MacBook Pro 16 is able to generate. You could certainly listen to music here, but headphones would be preferred.

8.) Battery life and thermals are absolutely fantastic, decimating the MacBook Pro for general usage, which is just a portable toaster. The laptop just runs remarkably cool with this AMD setup. That said, when the fans kick in, they kick in with a WHOOSH, which can be a bit disconcerting. Battery life is superb, easily giving me 8-11 hours for general web usage, a good 40% longer than my MacBook Pro doing the exact same things at a comparable brightness.

  9.) The SSD is nothing too special. While yes, any SSD is faster than not-an-SSD, this is on the lower end of the spectrum in terms of NVMe performance.

Overall, I really enjoy the Surface Laptop 4, but it’s not hard to see where Microsoft could make some massive improvements and solidify the Surface line as THE Windows 10 systems to buy.

4 out of 5. A worthy alternative to high-end laptops, but not yet at the top of its game.

Q- see 12 camera security system is a nice way to protect a home or business from threats. Install the cameras in different sections of the home or company and then access from home, online, etc. for top level security.

This security system seems much more complicated than it really is and the reason, I think, is due to the number of cameras. Looking at all of those cameras, out of the box, is a little bit intimidating and it leads one to believe that setup will take days and even weeks to complete. But it is actually much simpler than it looks and there is no need to install all 12. Just use the number of cameras you feel is necessary and store the rest for later use.

With this security system in place, you can access the live feed through the internet and even on your mobile phone via the Q- See applications. This is great for convenience and its one of the security systems best features. Other security systems have this feature as well, so it’s nothing unique. But it is very easy to use and it lets you monitor specific places on a property, for maximum security. Wherever you might be, home or away, you can take a look at what’s going on by pulling the mobile phone from your pocket. It doesn’t get much easier than that.

The one issue I have with this system is the same one others have complained about, and that is the wires. In the modern world in which we live, we expect wireless technology more and more. This system is wired and it could present some problems as you try to tape wires and otherwise conceal them from view. If this was a wireless system and I could place the cameras anyplace I like, then I would be hard pressed to find much wrong with this product. But I know many people who would likely reject this product immediately for this reason alone.

I have been learning more about photography and as time has permitted I have been improving my skill as an amateur photographer. I have worked with other types of filters, in particular CPL and FL-D filters, but before now I have never worked with ND filters. I have been able to achieve good results with it and so far I am pleased with this filter though I know I have more to learn about it.

A neutral-density filter is used to reduce light reaching the aperture without fiddling too much with the colors. This allows one to get creative with shutter speeds. This particular filter is adjustable and turns on the lens body face, allowing the photographer to increase or decrease the amount of filtering done. At the lowest setting the filter does very little filtering; when turned up to the maximum filtering level very little light gets through and a moire pattern appears so I do not recommend turning up the filter to this level.

To get a feel for how well this filter works I took my camera outside as a big thunderstorm approached and took some pictures of one of the cloud formations. I selected two pictures from that set, one where I did not use the filter and one where I did use it on about 1/4 strength. Although the filter evenly reduced light levels, the color contrast in the filtered image is much more pronounced and obvious.

The most common use for this kind of filter is to reduce the light levels, then take an extended exposure for a scene with motion, such as a waterfall.

This is a very nice filter and I could not be happier with it. It is very easy to use and it really works well.

I was able to fix it once by unpairing the speaker from my tablet, and then pairing it again. On another occasion I went into the Nexus 7 settings to disconnect and then reconnect the speaker (as opposed to fully unpairing/pairing it) to get the audio to play smoothly. I spend a great deal of time in a computer lab where there is literally over 1,000 running systems. In this environment, ear protection isn't absolutely necessary but without it there's some discomfort with which to deal because of all the fans in these systems and the requisite air handling units. I already have a pair of Bose QC-15 headphones but I am not a huge fan, so I recently purchased a pair of Sennheiser PXC-450 headphones for use in this environment. After an initial break-in period, I have come to really appreciate them.

This is going to be a comparative review, though primarily about the Sennheiser phones. Bose is generally regarded as the gold standard when it comes to ANC headphones, so matching the Sennheisers to the Bose is a good match-up. I'll break it all down into categories: Noise Canceling, Comfort, Sound Quality and Build Quality.

Noise Canceling:
Active noise canceling is THE primary feature of these phones and each has its strengths. Bose is, without question, the more capable ANC set when it comes to removing noise. This supremacy comes at a price though - because of the aggressiveness of their ANC, the wearer often feels a "pressure" on the ears when using the phones, something not present with the Sennheiser set which is close to Bose's level of canceling. Where Bose went to extremes to eliminate noise, Sennheiser went with the thought of "good enough for most". To be sure, both sets do a nice job of eliminating low frequency noise, enough to make air travel more pleasant if you dislike the rumble of plane engines.

They work in the car too (if you're not driving). I tried both sets in a moving vehicle and all do a fine job of eliminating road and engine noise. In fact, it was quiet to the point of eerie in the car. So, if you're a passenger on a long trip, either of these will work to suit your needs.

For the Sennheisers, you don't have to use ANC to listen to music as they provide the ability to override ANC and work like normal headphones. Bose, on the other hand, is an all-or-nothing deal and requires ANC to be on when listening to anything at all.

And that brings up a nice little feature on the Sennheisers - the "talk-thru" function, which allows a listener to cut off all sound and turn on a small microphone so that one can carry on a conversation without having to remove the headphones. No other headset I have ever used has this feature and it has already proven to be a handy tool.

Both sets require a single AAA battery to provide ANC. The battery life is definitely better with the Bose - mine last about a week between needing new batteries, whereas the Sennheiser set needs a new battery every other day.

Comfort:
The Sennheisers are the most comfortable headphones I have ever worn - period. The padding is buttery soft and they fit over my ears with no issue. Other reviewers have said that it seems like they just melt into your head, and that's a very accurate way to describe them. The Bose are nearly as comfortable, though they are slightly smaller.

Where the Sennheisers have a slight comfort disadvantage is actually in their size. These are big headphones and when they are worn around the neck instead of on the ears, they tend to rub on the neck and sometimes (depending on what you're doing) they can get in the way. If you take them off, or don't wear them around your neck, there's nothing about which to complain.

Sound Quality:
Sennheiser has always had premium sound, and the PXC-450 headphones demonstrate why they are the champs when it comes to quality sound. Though not audiophile phones, the PXC-450 brings awesome sound quality even at low volumes, with very full midrange and decent bass. The Bose sound great, except that the bass is too rich and without an equalizer in the mix the bass is enough to give me a headache over extended periods.

Build Quality:
I have not had the Sennheiser set very long but so far I have had no trouble with them. They feel rugged and sturdy, though they are mostly plastic so they do scratch and twist easily. The cord is heavy gauge wire, a welcome improvement over the cabling on Sennheiser sets I have worn in the past. The Bose set is a little more flimsy, with lesser gauge wire.

In summary, I find that the Sennheiser PXC-450 headphones are a better product than the Bose QC-15 headphones. They sound great, feel comfortable and they do a fine job of canceling noise. Bose does have better ANC and if that is the main thing you need and you don't mind the sensation of pressure they put on the ears then Bose is a better choice, but in almost every other aspect the Sennheisers bring more to the table.

Our AV department bought a BDP-300 so we could release our HD video content on Blu-ray. We bought the expensive Blu-ray burner for the computer, we bought the expensive authoring software, we bought a bunch of expensive BD-R and BD-RW recordable disks and we bought the expensive Sony BDP-300 player, with an eye toward buying a bunch more for our conference rooms if the system worked. It didn't.

We found that the BDP-300 will not play back BD-R or BD-RW discs. Though it might have been possible to be upgraded via a firmware update (like its REALLY expensive big brother can be firmware upgraded) it most likely never will. Thanks a lot, Sony. Way to make an integrated system. No wonder Blu-ray has been so slow to catch on. Thus we as a very large company cannot commit to Blu-ray because we can't play the recorded Blu-ray disks back on even a $400 player. Sigh.

Secondly, if you connect to a digital display that only has DVI-in via an HDMI/DVI adapter or an HDMI/DVI cable adapter, the player doesn't work. I suspect the problem is connected to copy protection schemes built into the multiple HDMI standards.

So, if you have an older HD display that only has DVI-in, forget this "reasonably priced" Blu-ray player. You'll most likely need to use the analog YRB (component) outputs, which is an inferior signal to the digital HDMI output. I did a component/HDMI comparison for my wife and she definitely picked the HDMI as the superior output picture.

There is a workaround that allows the HDMI/DVI to work, but it's a pain: First, connect both the HDMI and component cables to their respective inputs on the display. Now, before powering the player on, manually disconnect the HDMI cable from the back of the player while leaving the component cables connected to the display. Then power up the player and switch the display to the analog "component" input. You can now see the menus and the Blu-ray disk will be able to be played. After you get the movie running, manually plug the HDMI/DVI cable into the back of the player and switch the display to the digital DVI input. The Blu-ray disk now works and allows the menus and other overlaid controls to function normally. As different HDMI copy protection schemes get adopted this trick might fail.

If you have HDMI-in on your display, the player might work, but no guarantees. Bear in mind that the HDMI standard is constantly changing. I think they're up to at least HDMI 1.3 so far, and counting. And a totally new plug protocol is on its way for computer monitors, too, called DisplayPort, which might make it to TV sets, but who knows?

After this little problem was overcome, I finally got to see the picture. It was very nice, especially after I got to see it via my HDMI-DVI workaround. Definitely better than the analog component feed.

The overlaid menus allow you to access the menu anytime, without leaving the movie. Pretty cool. The menus are also more animated and better integrated.

Audio quality is fabulous. Both Dolby and DTS sound great because with all the storage capacity on the disk, the signals don't have to be compressed as much as they are for a standard DVD.

If you want the very, very best audio, though, you can select "uncompressed" and route the RCA audio outputs directly into your amp's dedicated preamp inputs. This takes the Dolby and DTS compression systems out of the picture altogether. So you are hearing multiple uncompressed audio tracks sent directly to your amp.

The worst part of the Blu-ray player is the time it takes to "boot" up. It's really a dedicated computer running an operating system. Java, at least, and maybe more. Thus it takes a full two minutes to fire up. You press the power button and nothing happens. After about ten seconds, you get a display that says "power on." After about 90 seconds, the machine is finally ready to play your disk. Give it a lot of time to fire up, especially the very first time you plug it in. After the initial plug-in/power-on sequence, the manual says it will be subsequently faster. But not by much. And the system can "crash," requiring you to turn it off and reboot. It happened several times to me as I moved too quickly between menu selections.

Overall, this player can put out a great picture, eventually, and after learning a bunch of quirks. I don't think it's ready for prime time, though. For the price it should be much better: faster boot up and with the ability to play back recorded Blu-ray disks.

Buy the BDP-300 knowing you will be replacing it for some reason in a year or two.

It crashed the player. Think "Blue Screen of Death" but without the blue screen and a longer boot sequence. I repeated the process six times.

I was about to flame this inop player when here on Amazon it was suggested to update to Firmware 4.20.

I went to Sony's site and found even newer 4.30 firmware. You download the exe and click on it to uncompress it. This creates an ISO disk image. You burn this to a new CD as an image (very important--an IMAGE, not a data disk.) Turn on the player and stick the CD in. It took 13 minutes for the update to install. One of my favorite Nikon lenses is an old 16mm fisheye from about 1977, I think. It has two problems: it is a fisheye and curves straight lines at the edges and it's a non-CPU lens, like many of my aged old Nikon lenses. Non-CPU means I have to remember to select it from my list of non-CPU lenses using that menu feature of the D800, and that there is no focus assist. It's full frame, however, and now that we're back to shooting full FX 24x36 sensor, the old lenses are making a comeback.

That 16mm fisheye costs a pretty penny today and the 14-24mm Nikon f/2.8 zoom is even more. And I'm sure they are both fine lenses.

So I bought a Samyang/Rokinon 800mm f/8 mirror lens for two bills and said, "that ought to be fun, even if it's not that great a lens for such little money." Funny thing: it's a pretty good lens.

That good purchase experience allowed me to select this 14mm Rokinon f/2.8. It is surprisingly good considering it's one third the cost of its Nikon equivalent. Even wide open at 1.5 feet, it is tack sharp.

The main difference between this and the Nikon is that this Rokinon is a fully manual focus lens while the 14mm Nikon is auto focus, although I'm not sure how accurately a 14mm lens can focus automatically. I've often simply estimated the distance and set the lens to that distance using the barrel markings. The focus ring is a pleasant long throw, with the ring rotating about 270 degrees around the lens from infinity to .28 meters (less than 1 foot). Focus drag feels silky smooth. Focus happens internally -- the front element does not rotate.

This Rokinon has a clickstop f/stop diaphragm. It also has a chip in it, giving it enough smarts to qualify as an AI-S lens. To use it on a D800, you have to set it to minimum aperture (f/22) or you get the flashing "fee" in the viewfinder. Ah, takes me back....

Setting it to f/22 (marked in orange) tells the camera what f/stop the lens is working at and allows control of the f/stop from the front selector wheel on the D800. The focus indicator in the eyepiece also works -- you see the left/right arrows and the little ball that verifies it's in focus. It also automatically records f/stop and focal length data in the metadata with the shot. In other words, it's a real lens, just without auto focus, for one third the cost. Old Nikon AI-S lenses have a little lock that holds the f/stop ring at minimum aperture that's not present on this lens, but the click stops are secure and the f/stop ring stays where you set it.

The front element is radically curved and is protected somewhat by the flower petal shaped built-in lens shade. Be careful: that front element is really exposed to the weather.

The front lens cap is terrific and very well designed. It's a durable hard plastic unit that slips over the flower petal lens shade and snaps securely in place against detents in the the lens shade. You have to squeeze both plastic flush-mount buttons on the front edge of the cap to release it. It won't fall off by accident under any circumstances. Only drawback it that it's about 1-3/8" deep and 3-5/8" diameter, so it doesn't exactly slip into a back pocket when it's off the lens.

The cosmetics of the lens are appealing. Even has a brass/gold colored band around the front that mimics real Nikon lenses. The focus ring rubber grip is good and the the body of the lens, minus the front element, is about the size of a 50mm f/1.4 lens. Focus distances in feet and meters are clearly engraved. One nice thing it has that I wish all lenses had is the focal length clearly and largely printed on the side of the lens so you can tell at a glance what it is. Nice. The mount is precision machined and fits the camera like it should. There are five little electrical contacts that interface with the camera body to communicate exposure info. For transport, it comes with an unpadded velour drawstring pouch. May want something a bit more padded if it's bouncing around inside a camera bag against other gear. But the bag's adequate, folds flat when not in use and is compact.

As for performance, I'm not going to go into lines/per millimeter sharpness. What I can say is that it's great for architectural interiors and wide, WIDE rectilinear shots. And in analyzing a snap of my dog I pushed in on his eye as far as I could looking at the D800's rear screen and could see the finest of eyelashes, showing off both the resolution of the lens and the remarkable resolution of the D800's 36 megapixel sensor. The lens distinguishes itself from all the wide/medium wide 24mm/35mm lenses out there. Do I really need to have a heavy, giant, hyper-expensive zoom lens that zooms 10 whole millimeters from 14mm all the way to 24mm? Not hardly. If I need serious wide angle this 14mm will fill the bill nicely, even wide open.

No filters for it, of course, because the front element is so deeply curved.

I'm particularly interested in using the 14mm for video shoots, which I use the D800 for more than for still photography. I'll be able to see the whole world with this lens, even in the most cramped of situations.

This will be a fun lens. Highly recommended.

I own a DJI Ronin S which I use with my Sony A7 series cameras (an A7S and A7Rii). It worked well enough, but after trying this Crane 3 Lab, I'm blown away and ready to sell my Ronin for this.
For starters, I love the ergonomics of the extra handle. Being able to hold onto it with 2 hands and shift from the handle to the pistol grip makes using this thing far more stable than trying holding just the pistol with both hands. It also makes it easy to pass and shift to a low angle mode, as well as seamlessly pass it to another person easily for those really impossible looking tracking shots (thought a window, down a staircase, etc). I'm also really impressed with the buttons and controls- if you've got a USB cable controlling your camera, there's a lot more you can easily access right from the gimbal without touching the camera than you can with the DJI Ronin S. With the Sony cameras, unfortunately, you can't control the focus motor of an automatic lens with the follow focus wheel... that's a limitation of the camera since Sony doesn't have that protocol in their USB remote interface. Other features work perfectly, however, and I've been told that other cameras like Canon and Nikon work with the focus control as well (this is something I'm hoping Sony changes in the future, but for now I'll just rely on auto-focus during gimbal shots).
Another HUGE improvement over other stabilizers is the ability to LOCK the axis motors in place. This is a fantastic tool to help when balancing (you can lock the other 2 axis and work on balancing them one by one, rather than holding the other positions in place as you work backwards like on the Ronin), and its also great to lock it in place when you are powered down and carrying it around- I've found that when taking a break with my Ronin, it is always awkward to walk around with it since the camera can flop and swing around as I walk. The Crane 3 doesn't have that problem if you just lock the motors in place with a little red switch.
Honestly, I wish I would have waited just a little bit longer before buying my Ronin S so that I could see how much better this is. The app is honestly just OK, I've heard people say they like the DJI app better and I would probably have to agree with that, but this just does everything else so much better that it I'd still say it is worth it in the end. The crane 2 is easier to balance in my experience, more forgiving (less crazy vibrating when the gimbals shifts out of balance), has better features and ergonomics and overall just seems to do a better job.
I STRONGLY recommend it if you are shopping around between those two options.

KEY RESPONSE

ON LAP

MULTIPLE

This is a fantastic split keyboard. If I could change anything to make it absolutely perfect, it would be to have the wrist pad not be abrasive and the mouse built into the keyboard as a mouse pad.

MY RATING
I still give this FIVE STARS. I love how I can use this at a downward angle on my lap and type just as fast or faster than on a desktop. I will probably be using this for my laptop as well as my desktop.

THIS REVIEW

I have several of the Logitech M510, and think this is the best general purpose mouse you can buy. It's comfortable in the hand -- I have a large hand, some in the family have larger hands, some have smaller hands, but everyone finds the mouse comfortable to use. It's precise, easy to configure, and I'm very fond of the tiny usb adapter.

I particularly like the fact that you only need use one usb adapter for multiple devices (the "unifying receiver"). In fact you can switch between different Logitech mice if you need to do so (e.g., for a portable).

As for the keyboard, I was a little wary of the "wave" shape, not having used one before, and having some mild carpal tunnel issues. But to my relief, the keyboard is really comfortable to use, the wrist rest is well placed, provides support just where I need it. The keys have a nice touch, not too light, not too heavy, so perfect for me. There are a number of programmable buttons on the keyboard, most of which I tend to use only occasionally, mostly because I forget I have them. But the volume control is very useful, as is the button to bring up the calculator.

Do make sure you install the Logitech SetPoint software (you can download from their website) to properly configure the devices. You'll need that to make good use of the unifying receiver, among other things.

So if you're looking for a good mouse keyboard combo, I can happily recommend this set. If you just want one or the other, I still recommend the M510 mouse, and one of the many Logitech wireless keyboards that you can buy separately. (For instance, I also have the K270 keyboard, and find it to be quite good.)

I was in the market for a hard drive-based music player and didn't want to go the normal iPxx route, so I began checking into different brands. I had a list of criteria that the player had to meet:

-EXCELLENT SOUND. This is critical. A SnR (Signal to Noise Ratio) of 95db or better

-Excellent battery life. At least 15 hours

-At least 20 GB

-A color screen

-Sturdy build

-As little touch-sensitive controlling as possible. Click wheels are inaccurate and bothersome.

-Ease of use. Drag and drop is preferred.

-AC adapter for charging on the road or from an AC converter in a car

This player meets all of those needs. The SnR is 97db, I've gotten 18 hours out of the battery (remember that increased settings like equalizers and higher bitrates mean lower battery life for ALL players), the case is solid and brushed aluminum, the screen is pretty and quite sharp, only one touch-sensitive control is present, the player CAN drag and drop through Win XP, and it comes with a wall adapter.

I love the powerful sound this puts out and it can drive my big headphones with no problem. It can, like most HDD players, set aside a partition for storage. It has a good FM tuner, recording of FM and a little mic for voice notes. It can even sync with Outlook for contacts and other info. The hard disk seems fast and

Now for the drawbacks:

-You can't watch 15fps video on a tiny screen and reduce your battery life by 67%

-The USB cable is proprietary...no mini USB!

-The wall charger cable plugs into the USB cable...this means two cables for recharging from the wall

-Looking at photos and playing music at the same time is not possible

-Creative software is always iffy. Thankfully, in Win XP, you can open the player from My Computer and access its contents directly with non-DRM music and photos.

-Battery is NON-USER REPLACEABLE. This is odd for Creative.

-No mention of this on the Creative website. Thankfully, updated drivers ARE available from support.

This player would have been state-of-the-art about a year ago, but has been eclipsed by its bigger brother the Zen Vision with 30 and 60GB drives and video...however, if you're not buying into the "kill your eyes with tiny video on tiny screens" and just want a SOLID and RELIABLE player with booming sound, this is it!!! You can tell it's custom-made for Windows (it's MTP, not UMS for any computer), but if you're running XP, then it's a solid choice because you can skip the Creative software and just load music on it.

If you can get it on sale like I did, snatch it up. This is a little gem of a player!

The AC power adapter then gets plugged into your home outlet and the cable end goes into the jack marked DC power on the right speaker. On the back of the right speaker, plug another device into the AUX IN to listen to a different audio device.

I have had good success with Kingston products (in particular their SSD storage) so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this encrypted thumb drive. It has a lot of promise and it works better than other encrypted drives I have used. There is one drawback, at least for me - it does not support Linux (if it does, I haven't figured out how yet).

I have the 16GB version, and the thing is built like a tank. It has a metal casing around the inner workings and it can handle some abuse. That's good news if you keep these things in a briefcase or loose in a bookbag.

Setup is easy. When it is plugged into a Windows machine (I do not have access to a Mac so I cannot speak to that use case), the software is available and can be used to set up the drive with a password. That's pretty straightforward. If you forget your password, you can wipe the drive and start over but you cannot recover your data. So, choose your password wisely.

Copy rates seem to be decent - a little slower than similar-sized drives I have that aren't encrypted but not prohibitively so. It's a trade-off, and a small one at that.

When I popped this drive into my Linux machine, the kernel saw it immediately. However, all it could see was the setup partition which is approximately 100mb, a far cry from 16 GB. The drive is smart enough to hide its data from foreign OS-based systems so your data is safe. Linux is gaining users though, and being able to access the data from a Linux system would be good, even if there was a tedious process to get to the partition but still requiring a password. This is better than other encrypted drives I have used in the past which made the data scrambled but was still accessible. However, not being able to use this drive under Linux is a problem for me.

To be fair, it is not advertised as compatible with Linux.

This is a good drive and from what testing I have done it works well. That said, it does not support Linux and that is a negative for me. Hopefully Kingston will release a Linux-based version (or a software layer) for it in the future; for now it's only usable for me under Windows.

This LEATHER LAPTOP MESSENGER BAG FOR MEN (by Leather Centric) is made of real leather--animal hide, NOT the man-made “pleather” stuff that’s often marketed on Amazon as “real leather” or “genuine leather”. That’s a big plus, but the bag itself has a lot of minuses.

First, the bag’s styling is so old-fashioned, it makes the bag look cheap. You have to really love the 1950s “retro” look, to like the overall appearance. The bag definitely looks handmade, but it also looks crudely rustic.

Second, although the bag has lots of zippered compartments (inside and outside), it is only 3” deep. It has no expansion gussets, so the total capacity is one laptop or one very thick sheaf of documents. Internal zipper compartments are relatively useless if a bag can’t expand to hold the things added to the compartments.

Third, the bag is difficult to open. It opens with two metal clasps--these are hidden beneath the purely decorative buckled front straps. You have to pull up on both clasps at once to lift the flap, and you can’t do this easily without laying the bag flat on one side, or holding it on your lap. The leather flap itself is very stiff (at least when the bag is new), and this adds to the opening difficulty.

Fourth, the bag has no locking mechanism. Not that it is easy to open (see previous paragraph).

Fifth, the brass fittings must tarnish very easily, because the bag arrives with every single exposed brass piece wrapped tightly in thin plastic wrap. It takes something very sharp to cut the plastic, and you must be careful not to scratch the fittings. (I succeeded in removing the wrappings without damaging the bag, but I punctured my left wrist with an Olfa knife in the process.)

The bag is reasonably priced (about $90 on Amazon). It comes with a snap-on shoulder carrying strap, and has a sturdy, permanently attached satchel handle. The handle is very comfortable. The bag leather is already distressed, so you needn’t worry about scratches. This is a truly rugged laptop bag.

A power inverter for your car is a very handy device to have. It plugs into the car's power outlet (which I still call the cigarette lighter) and gives you the ability to plug in an AC powered item. There are limitations, of course - you're not going to be able to plug in your refrigerator, but for low power demand items, it can be very helpful for power when you're traveling or for when the lights go out at home.

I'm very pleased with the Sabrent. It offers a decent amount of power - 300 watts - which makes it far more useful for the things I'd like to use it for than the lower powered inverters. However, the larger capacity comes with a larger size. The unit is about 3 inches wide, 5 inches long, and 1.5 inches thick. It weighs a hefty one pound. Not a small and inconspicuous device by any means.

All the controls and ports are located on one end, which makes it easier to deal with the large size. There's an on/off rocker switch. I wish it had a more solid "click" to it - it has a rather soft touch, so it can be inadvertently switched on/off when moving it if you grab it the wrong way. It has a single 3-prong female outlet to power an AC device, and 2 USB outlets. The USB outlets are a nice addition, since it can be used to charge phones, tablets, etc. without having to unplug the inverter and plug in a conventional car USB adapter.

The housing is plastic but appears pretty sturdy. The plug that goes into the cigarette lighter is decent. Works fine, but feels a little on the flimsy side compared with the overall unit. The cord could also be a bit thicker for greater durability or, ideally, coiled so it does not get tangled. But quite workable as-is and MUCH easier to deal with than an inverter that does not have a cord and plugs directly into the car power outlet.

Performance is very good. I had no problems running a 60 watt cooler using the inverter. Power delivery seemed fine and steady. I don't have test equipment to measure the power quality, but the cooler ran at a steady pace.

The inverter does get pretty warm in use, and has an internal fan that kicks on to keep things cool. The fan can be heard, but the sound is not what I'd consider to be noisy.

It's important to know the power demand of whatever you're plugging in, plus keep in mind that some devices, such as coolers, have an initial surge demand. For example, a 60watt cooler may use 60 watts when running, but will pull 100+ watts when it starts up. If you try to run something that attempts to pull more than the inverter can supply, the inverter will shut down for safety (both for itself and the item attached). According to the specs, this can handle a surge of 350 watts, but I'll keep any surge loads I put on it at not more than 300 watts to be safe.

Although 300 watts won't go far, this is a handy item to keep on hand not only for power on the road, but also to serve as a power source (albeit limited) when the household power goes out. While there are some faults with the unit, overall it is a good performer and a decent value for the price. 4.5 stars rounded to 5.

I tried the first generation Kindle but didn't really care all that much for it. While I loved the screen, it just didn't feel right, and remember thinking this would be perfect if it had a touchscreen.

When the Touch was announced I ordered this along with a Fire with the thought that the Fire would be for me, and I'd give the Touch as a gift. The Touch got here this morning and I opened it up just to make sure it was OK. It looked so nice that I carefully peeled off the plastic just to try it out for a few minutes. After all, one wouldn't want to give a gift that didn't work, right? Well, it's now been a few hours and several chapters of a few books later. I'm keeping it. A second one will be on order for Christmas giving.

Why keep the Touch when I also have a Fire? If you skip over the obvious answer (I just love electronic gadgets) the e-ink on the Touch is much better in terms of clarity and lack of glare. Not that the Fire is bad. It has a very clear screen, but there is some glare. The Touch is better for reading under all lighting situations, and remains highly readable in direct sun. I can't imagine getting better screen clarity than this for black and white text.

I also tried reading it while on a treadmill (a situation that usually gives me a headache when I tried it using the kindle app on my Touchpad) and it was quite pleasant. Best of all is that I can zoom up the text size so I can read it while it is on the treadmill reading stand (it's too far away for me to read hard copy unless it's in HUGE type. Getting old is _not_ fun).

But the strength of the Touch is also it's biggest problem for me - black and white. I read several magazines each month and reading them in B/W is lackluster at best. Magazines are more enjoyable on the Fire, especially publications such as Wired.

The touch interface is great. So far its been very smooth and glitch free. Love the feel of the screen - has a bit of texture to it. I have to say, however, that I am a bit concerned about the screen longevity. The Touch overall feels a bit fragile and less "solid" than the Fire. I'm not deducting any stars for that since it's just an impression, but it will be interesting to see if the durability of the Touch screen is better/worse/same as the Fire (and vice versa). I'll be getting a case for it for sure since it's going to be getting bumped about.

I'll be using the Fire mainly at home and for reading material that works best in color (and, of course, video - need to relax the mind with mindless entertainment as well!). The Touch will be living in my briefcase for reading while commuting (I take the bus and subway, so lots of time to read) and for killing time prior to an appointment. The longer battery life and smaller size makes it a better traveling companion than the Fire. I don't have the Touch 3G version, so I'll have to make sure I keep a few books on my to-be-read stack so I don't run out when I'm out of wi-fi range.

Granted, if I could only have one device, I'd stay with the Fire since that offers more entertainment options, albeit at twice the price. But the cost is not excessive, so I treated myself to both. With a Fire and a Touch I've got all bases covered (until, of course, the next glittery gee-whiz piece of electronics comes out...).
