I also have an Alienware 17 with GTX 880M GPU. Comparisons are somewhat unfair considering the nearly $1000 price difference, but I believe they may be helpful to a prospective buyer:

You can look at specs and framerate comparisons of the GPUs all over the web, but my experience is that both deliver seamless perfection in the newest games. If I'm dropping some frames with either, I don't notice, but I often like to play on my TV, and I know I lose something there. I am also not obsessed with gaming like some, so I'll concentrate on some of the other factors.

The displays themselves are both fantastic, and I cannot distinguish a huge difference there.

The GTX970M included with this machine does make a noticeable difference in terms of power consumption, as this machine is much thinner and lighter than the AW. At the same time, it feels slightly less robust because the entire chassis is not metal.

I don't like the CD drive placement on this machine, as I keep popping the slot open from time to time.

USB 3.0 is on only one side of the machine (2.0 port and card reader on the other side). AW has two ports on each side.

What I really like about the AW is that it has a second full size HDD slot for added versatility. It's the only laptop I've ever seen with that.

There are no obvious annoyances with the touchpad or keyboard as far as accidental hitting a key or something not working correctly, which I've seen with other laptops. I am not thrilled with the placement of the delete key on this laptop, and I don't really like the fact that the arrow keys are scrunched up with the numbers and other keys, either. By contrast, I believe AW got their layout perfect, including their four programmable keys.

Lights. The keyboard by itself may actually look cooler on the Apache because the lights are in the height of the keys. BUT, there are only three zones, compared to AW's four, plus multiple chassis zones. I really love the light-up touchpad on the AW. What really annoys me about the lights on this keyboard is that despite the controller software that allows lots of per-key and per-game customization, there is no setting that allows the keyboard to turn off at the same time that the screen goes blank (or any time for that matter; you have to wait until the computer goes to sleep). I have it rigged to change from one profile to a dark profile when I press the special command button, but that's not seamless.

Windows 10. Actually, I love that I got the AW at the time when they were still loading Win7 (Win 8.1 was out, but nobody wanted it). I'm still not thrilled with Win10 due to their moving some settings out of control panel and into settings, getting rid of other settings altogether, still having a ridiculous start menu, and wanting to control your life as if you're some dumb tablet/phone user. I installed Classic Shell to get my start menu back, messed with the control panel and settings for a long time, turned off everything they were "offering" me, and I have this working just about as good as a Win7 machine. Oh yeah, and I ditched MS Edge; God, what was wrong with Explorer? Anyway, if we're stuck with it, may as well make the best of it.

Very little crapware on this machine. On most computers, I disable even the proprietary controls since most of them do nothing. This machine has a System Control Manager that doesn't do anything that Windows Power settings cannot do, but it confuses things and messes up my settings, so it will be turned off. The other stuff seems harmless so far.

I was telling someone that computers like this are a status symbol to some people (like cars are to some people). And it came with a key fob, like a car... Oh yeah, this and the AW both come in fancy packaging, including a suitcase-style box that you'll be tempted to keep, but practicality keeps me from doing so. However, you may want it if you frequently transport your machine. Also comes with the largest - but not softest - microfiber cloth I've ever seen (the size of the screen).

In conclusion, you can see that there are a few minor things I prefer about the AW. Are they worth an extra thousand bucks? No. This is an impressive machine that can handle anything I throw at it. It should definitely be on your consideration list.

I am having a love hate relationship w/these ear buds.

What I like about these ear buds was first the price...these are much more affordable than some other name brand blue tooth earbuds, but the performance also explains the price differences.

The sound: These do sound really good.

Noise Cancelling: Very good for earbuds, maybe even a little too good. I run w/these and still want to be able to hear road noise.

Fit: These fit me very well and stay put while running. To me this is probably the best part. I have not had good luck w/earbuds staying put while running or lifting hard. These do that. I find myself checking them often, out of habit, and they are tightly in place.

Battery Life: I've not had an occasion where the batteries have run dead. I use them, put them back in their case and they are ready for my next workout.
Telephone calls: Works well while making and taking phone calls.

The not so good:

The functions: Too many. On/Off, pair, pause, really are the only things I need.

Pairing: I can only get these to pair to one item. If I pair to my phone, I cannot pair to my watch. The first time out of the case they automatically paired to my phone. When I tried to also pair them to my watch, following the very complicated pairing sequence of button pushing, I could not get it to pair. I had to completely unpair these from my phone to get them to pair to my watch. Then I could not get the earbuds to pair back to my phone.

I also get a lot of static and drop off while in these. It's not on common for one of the ears to lose sound while out running or walking. I also get a static sound pretty frequently which requires me to pause and restart playing music.

In the end, I do not think I would buy these again unless they come out w/a better version. If they could make earbuds with this fit and work like some others, they would be perfect. Until then I'll use these until they die and probably not replace them w/more SkullCandy earbuds unless some improvements are made.

When I first purchased my 3 TB MBL some time ago I was quite pleased. Network access, remote access, even an android app. In short, everything my DLink had plus the app and a nicer look on the shelf. I used it extensively for pulling up photos on my cell phone when I was bored as well as to store my most important files. I didn't back them up, a back-up drive is something I kept saying I would add later...

14 months later (note the 12 month warranty had just expired) the drive stopped being accessible over the network. I spent a week and at least 40 hours of my time going back and forth with tech support by e-mail and trying every option they could offer, and the result was that they deemed the unit broken. They said that the unit can not be opened because that would break the drive inside, and they said that they can't fix it. They "kindly" offered me a referral to one of several companies that give them a kick back for data recovery services. Incidentally, I asked two for pricing by e-mail and they didn't respond.

So I took the unit apart and bought a new unit and took that one apart and swapped the drives. Neither one worked. After talking to support again it turns out that WD didn't want these to be upgradable because if they were upgradable you could buy a cheap drive instead of a new unit so they code each board to the drive that will be in it. TO make matters worse, they encoded the drive in a Linux format that no known version of Linux can translate. Attaching it to my Linux system I couldn't mount it using any utility. Several Linux recovery programs couldn't do anything either.

Okay, having told you why I will never buy a WD NAS again, I should now tell you how to fix this if you have the same problem that I do: DiskInternals makes a program called Linux Reader. That's right, Linux can't read the drive but a program designed to read Linux drives from within Windows can! Recovering the data to a drive is time consuming though. I tried it all at once but that froze after a few days. Then I tried one major directory at a time and that worked better. But recovering nearly 3 TB of data has taken a very long time! I'm about 3 MONTHS into the recovery effort and I have about 400 GB remaining. After starting on my wife's computer because mine is a laptop and causing a few crashes and a lot of delays I finally had to pull out an older computer and set it up just to run this program.

If anyone has the same problem and can't get this solution to work, I'll do my best to help if you simply reply to this review and give me all the details. If anyone is considering buying a WD NAS, I want to encourage you to buy a DLink model 323 (I think the 325 is the current version but it is missing some features so I'd get an older one) instead. I've had that thing running for 5 years without a glitch!

I was looking for a good strap and found one from this company, but it is leather. It is great to use when I need a sturdy strap, but for storing in my case, the strap is too stiff. I got this one as an alternative.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes wrapped in a cardboard stuck in a tube. I took photos to show you so you can get an idea. It is quite smart because you always know where it is.

COLOR
This is a really attractive light gray color.

HOW TO ATTACH
This has a great loop system which loops into the camera rings. The cord loops are attached to a snap on piece which locks into place on the strap. The strap comes with two of these so you can swap it between cameras.

PERFORMANCE
I really love to use my leather strap, but for storage, I prefer to have the nylon strap on the camera. If I need a quick change I can, but both straps easily interchange because they are from the same company.

BACK OF STRAP
The strap has silicone bars on the neck area to keep it from sliding around. Sometimes I like it and sometimes I am not as fond of it. It is great for use around the house as I take a lot of photos of products and jewelry.

IS IT ADJUSTABLE?
This is adjustable which is another feature I like. I am not locked into one length like with the leather one.

SECURE CONNECTION?
I find that so far the connectors snap in well and are secure. Over time, I am not sure how they will wear, but for now they are working well.

PLASTIC OR METAL?
When I looked at the photos for this listing, I thought the connectors were metal, but they are gray metallic colored plastic/nylon.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This neck strap fits my camera and I am glad to have it. It stores well in my camera case and is easy to disconnect and swap with my other strap from the same company.

Small, solid and nice looking. But the instructions have zero help and had multiple spelling errors like "white corn, green corn" instead of cord.
As for the install, this is what I did on my 2011 Altima:
1. Removed the lining of the trunk lid. Removed the license plate shade where the lights sits. Drilled a hole where I was going to mount the camera. Drilled a second hole thru the trunk body to the interior of the trunk.
2. Ran the cord from the camera thru both holes and screwed the camera in place with the locking washer. I taped this cord to the other cords that ran thru to the trunk interior.
3. Unplugged the main wiring harness from the taillight. Used a multimeter to test each pin in the wiring harness. You can go to a shop like PepBoys and ask to test it, it only takes a minute. First I turned the car on and tested each pin while it was running, all lights off, and marked down the numbers. Then I pulled the emergency brake and put the car in reverse and tested each pin again to see which wire was the reverse relay wire as that is the wire I tapped for the red power wire. In my car the white cord was constant power, purple was the reverse relay. I used a simple quick splice to tap the red power wire into the reverse wire. The black wire I grounded to a nearby bolt.
4. Ran the longest cord under the trim pieces along the driver's side and up under the steering column to the stereo.
5. Connected the rca cords and the camera cord. Covered all with electrical tape. And put some silicone around the wire where it entered the trunk to keep it sealed.

Overall, it's a decent camera. I just found the instructions lacking and unhelpful. The diagram wasn't easy to follow either. So it goes Camera to short RCA cord. Red & black wire from that RCA need to tap to the reverse light and ground. Then the short yellow RCA into the long RCA then into the stereo system. The two really short red wires were unused. Hopefully that helps some people.

The Philips GoGear Raga is the first exposure I have had to Philips' line of mp3 players and I was unsure of what I should expect of it. The price is comparable to other mp3 players of similar capacity so I expected it to be in the ballpark with them. For the most part I was correct, though there are a few things about which one should be aware when using this particular offering. It's a good product, but it has its quirks.

Setting up the Raga is easy. In the package is a USB cable that allows one to connect to a PC (packaging does not indicate if MacOS supports the Raga), and upon connecting Philips Songbird downloads and installs automatically. The installation is painless and does not take long, and a few clicks of the mouse along the way and the software loads up.

The first thing I tried to do was load music into the Raga, and once I got the music into Songbird the Raga disappeared from the available devices list. I am not sure what happened. I unplugged it and shut down Songbird, plugged the Raga back in and everything was as it should be, so I dragged 67 songs to the Raga for transfer. I saw two problems. First, the user has to know to drag and drop - there is no "transfer to..." option that I could find in any of the menus. The bigger problem, though, is that the transfer speed is abysmal and it took close to 2 minutes to transfer 67 songs that average 5MB in size. With my old iPod and with my ZuneHD, transfer speeds are appreciably faster. This doesn't make the Raga a piece of junk, of course, as the problem may be Songbird itself, but the transfer speed is something of which to be aware, especially if transferring large amounts of music.

Navigating to the newly transferred music is simple. For that matter, navigating the Raga is simple, period. Anyone with even slight familiarity with music players will have no problem finding and playing music on the Raga.

For comparison, I matched the Raga against my ZuneHD for playback. Of course, the Zune HD produced a more natural and clear sound, but only slightly. For the difference in price, I would have expected the ZuneHD to REALLY outperform the Raga, but this was not the case. In fact, when playing with the built in equalizers in both, I was able to get the Raga to get very close to the ZuneHD for sound quality. The difference was more pronounced with higher end ANC headphones, but this is unlikely to matter to the large majority of users.

The Raga has a tiny screen (the package says it's 1" diagonally) so this is not the kind of player one would want if frequently messing with settings and searching through. That said, the Raga is designed as a player to be worn with the included arm band, suitable for using at the gym. The ear buds that come with it have over-the-ear hooks to help keep them in place.

Considering the price and size, Philips has put together a very nice music player that will suit active users very well. It has some idiosyncrasies, in particular the transfer speeds, but it really is a capable player.

I'm a big fan of Kindle e-Readers. We own two of the older generation ones (the last Kindles with keyboard) and for x-mas I bought my mother a Kindle Fire HD 8.9 for x-mas. But, alas, she doesn't seem to have fine enough motor control to hit the small buttons on that device (see my review for that device). So the Fire has been sitting unused on the coffee table for a few months now.

But this is not a review of the Fire HD 8.9. I want to describe my very short experience with the basic Kindle and the Kindle Paperwhite - as they relate to the intended user: my mom. She recently suffered a stroke and one of the side effects is that she now has a constant tremble in her left hand. As she had trouble with the Fire HD 8.9 we went to Staples to see if the more purpose-built Kindles were easier to operate. We were not surprised when she often made mistakes selecting books on the Paperwhite's touch screen. But we were surprised to find that she couldn't even handle the physical buttons on the basic Kindle! From what I could tell, the problems were: the side-buttons (page forward/backward) are much smaller and narrower than they were on our old Kindles (which my mom had no trouble with), so basic navigation among pages became iffy. Similarly, the D-pad is smaller too - and that made selection of books difficult for her. Finally, while I could easily hold my old Kindle with one hand AND operate the page forward button, this is a bit more difficult with the new basic Kindle. My mom could not manage it at all. And since she can't hold the Kindle with her trembling left hand, neither e-Reader was for her. [She is now making do with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9 by laying it on a flat surface and only operating it with her right hand].

I'm still giving the Kindle 4 stars because none of these shortcomings are of interest to the majority of people, but I wanted folks to be aware of the newer devices' potential limitations with those suffering from limited motor skills.

I do a lot with photography and I always keep my eyes open for good lighting solutions that will help me get the lighting effects I want or need for given situations. I saw this one at a reasonable price and decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it. It meets the biggest requirement I have for lighting - it does not strobe.

So many LED lights have an issue with strobing, especially when they’re low-cost. This light is not expensive when compared to a lot of others, so even though it is marketed as a video light I was only cautiously optimistic. To determine this for sure, I set my camera to use the electronic shutter only, sped up the shutter speed as high as I could and pointed directly at the light when it was powered on. Strobing lights always show banding in pictures with higher shutter speeds when using the electronic shutter; this one did not (though the display on the camera sure did but that’s a different problem). This test proved to me that this LED light does not strobe, at least not slow enough for my camera sensor to see it at high shutter speeds.

This is a fairly large LED panel, designed for video use of course but I also can work just fine for photography or even general lighting in the right setting. It comes with a clamp mount and a pole so it can be attached to a desk or shelf, then the mounting head allows for angling the light as needed so it can light a surface at just the right angle desired. The mount is sturdy and there should be no issues with stability when it is set up properly.

The light is super-easy to adjust. There are two dials on the back for tweaking the brightness and the temperature range, and there is a remote included that does the same. The temperature can be adjusted from a warm 2800K to a blistering white 8000K and everywhere in between so you can get the lighting just right.

Power is via an AC adapter and there is no battery. So, this is not a travel light by any means, If you need a light to use in the field, unless you have a power generator with you then this light isn’t it. For a static setting in a studio or room, this light is very good.

I'm a huge Lensbaby fan. I've been using them with my Canon SLRs almost since they first came out, and have assembled a pretty extensive collection of them over the past few years. Yes, I am a lover of blur. It's one of those creative effects that you either love or don't (although I certainly will admit it can be overused with some horrible results). I've recently been playing around with Micro Four Thirds cameras and was thrilled to see that Lensbaby came out with a model specifically designed for the MFT format.

Quick primer for those not familiar with a Lensbaby: it's a very simple device that allows you to tilt the focal plane of the lens to shift focus to any area of the frame and produce a smooth blur effect. It can be in a small or large part of your photo depending on which of the several aperture rings you choose from (all supplied with this Lensbaby) and how much tilt you apply.

This particular version of the lens, called the "Composer" is part of Lensbaby's new Optic Swap System, which allows you to use any one of several optics (plastic, glass, double glass, pinhole/zoneplate) that you can easily swap out of the main body. This comes with the double glass optic - the other optics have to be purchased separately.

The new Composer design allows you to lock the tilt into place for some level of repeatability in your shots. A lot more convenient than earlier versions of Lensbabies, which required you hold the tilt with your fingers. Now it's just pick your aperture and your optic, tilt, and snap away!

This lens comes with an extra you can't get with other Lensbabies for other camera formats - the "tilt transformer." This is an attachment that will allow you to use any Nikon-mount lens as a close approximation of a tilt/shift lens (only close, since you really only get the benefit of tilt and not shift). With this attachment and a "regular" lens, you get a movable sliver, a line of focus, as opposed to the movable point of focus you get with a Lensbaby Optic. Same basic principle, but it produces a slightly different look.

Build quality is good. There's a lot of plastic in it, but my other Lensbabies have performed very well over the years with zero problems. The product comes nicely packaged, but only has minimal instructions. That's not really a problem since the company website has a lot of resources on how to use Lensbabies, plus has photo galleries, forums, instructional videos, and a lot more. Very nice resource if you own one. If you're not sure if a Lensbaby is for you, that should be your first stop to see what type of effects their products can produce. I've spent a lot of time there, and it has been time well spent. The company itself is excellent when it comes to customer service. I've contacted them a couple of times with questions, and they answer emails promptly.

This lens is versatile, and is more convenient to carry (both the Lensbaby as well as a MFT camera itself). I've found with all my gear that convenience of toting it means I'll carry it more often, and thus have more opportunity for taking great shots. The tilt transformer is a wonderful addition - you can play around with a tilt lens at a fraction it would cost you to buy a real tilt/shift lens.

While pricy for a Lensbaby, when you add up all the features it brings to the table, I find it to be a real winner. Highly recommend if you have a MFT camera.

Original review:

Before this, I had two Sony receivers in my living room. My secondary is a much older model - about 12 or so years old - that does not have HDMI and I use it for my whole house audio system. My primary is (was - it just got replaced) a 3-5 year old Sony model that is admittedly in a lower class than this Yamaha receiver (the secondary was in a higher class in its time, I think).

While I usually have all Sony stuff, I was completely willing to try another well-known Japanese brand who specializes in receivers and amps. And - it's just awesome. Totally. Not a single regret about the switch. The RX-A880 gave me back everything I lost going from my older, higher-end Sony to my newer one, AND it gave me so many nice surprises on the way! As anyone can tell you that it sounds good and looks good, I'll concentrate on this little details that I discovered during setup:

1) Besides the seven HDMI inputs, it also has a composite video, a component video, two optical audio, one extra (second belongs to component) coax audio, and two composite audio inputs, not to mention phono.

The great thing is that you can assign different audio inputs to any of the video inputs. So, for example, I decided to keep my Wii around since I now have a component input (and it takes up almost no space), but the cable is component video with composite audio, but the component video input on this has coax for the audio. Bummer. But no, you can change it. Example number two is I have a computer in my telecom closet hooked up to this with both HDMI and line-out audio. For circumstances too complicated to define here, audio does not output via the HDMI. But because of this feature, I can make the audio appear when I select the HDMI input OR when I just want to listen to the audio directly (with no HDMI output). Perfect.

2) 9 Speaker outputs. First, I'm so happy to have the 2-zone thing back (my secondary receiver has it, but my other, newer Sony did not - it only had A/B speakers that shared an amp). But this one you can actually have 7.1 AND a second zone (although you can't play them at the same time. This is really cool if you want the best of both worlds. I don't know if I can find a place for two more speakers in my setup, but ...it's nice to have the option. Supposedly, this all works automatically. I imagine it could work fine, but I am unable to try it at the moment.

3) 2-zone done better. My older Sony had 2-zone, but the controls were - frankly - atrocious. It was always confusing, even for someone like me who can be a super A/V nerd and memorize anything. The way I use it now is just to keep the remote on Zone-2, and do Zone-1 on the unit itself.

This Yamaha, however, has a simple switch on the remote, and you're either controlling one zone or the other depending on that switch. Simple and effective. You can also control it from the unit, unlike the older Sony.

4) 8 custom presets, all controlled directly from the remote. Another 8 for Zone 2?!

The one complaint I read by a reviewer was that you have to scroll through all the inputs from the remote to get to what you want. But that doesn't matter for two reasons: first, you can change the settings to skip anything you don't want. But, second, with 8 custom presets - and each with their own remote button - you probably don't even ever need to scroll through the inputs anyway.

And the custom presets are great. You can turn on and off a bunch of features like whether or not it changes your HDMI out settings, if it uses your YPAO settings, extra bass, which speakers it uses, etc. And it even can link the second zone!

Two great examples:

I can't stand to watch regular background TV with the surround sound on because it makes the commercials that much more obnoxious. But of course I like big booming bass and surround for movies. And it's also annoying to switch the unit off and on all the time, especially if you want to use control for HDMI. So I have one preset for very flat TV sound using just the front speakers that is clearer than-, but no more annoying than-, my regular TV speakers. Then I have another preset for surround sound and big bass for movie watching.

I have one preset for straight music just in zone 1. Then I have another preset for straight music in both zones one and two. It turns on zone 2 automatically. I could not figure out how to make a preset just for zone 2, but it seems that when I am controlling zone 2 on the remote, I can make 8 more presets just for zone 2. You can not adjust these presets via menu, from what I can tell, though.

5) 14 character names on the front of the unit in dot matrix. My other receivers were all limited to 8 characters. You can see all 14 at once, which is great.

6) Much more robust networking. I haven't played with this too awful much yet, but it seems that if you start listening to a playlist or an album on your NAS, then the next time you go back to "server", it will start playing where you left off (well, the song you left off at will start over again, instead of at the exact moment you left at), but at least this way you don't have to turn the TV on just to play some music. I suppose you could create a playlist of all Death Metal, and then you just have a stream going whenever you want it. It also seems like you can actually sign into Pandora and all the other stations and listen to your own account. And all the Internet/Network stuff is a separate scroll-through than the other inputs. I really like how that is set up.

6) The "program up/down" buttons on the remote can be programmed to do about 10 different things. I picked to have the dialogue increased or decreased for when you can't hear what people are saying even though everything else is loud enough. To be clear, I think this depends on if the dialogue is known to the decoder. I haven't tried all the other options yet.

7) Remote is awesome. Besides what I mentioned above, you can also make some changes to the red/green/yellow/blue buttons, but I wish you could really program those completely to your liking. Everything is laid out nicely, and the second zone even makes sense, as I mentioned above.

8) I realize the second HDMI output would be great if you also have a projector or something like that. With it, you can have access to all your devices without having to rewire anything. Haven't used it yet, but am glad to have the extra functionality.

...

There's plenty more, but I'm forgetting some of the details right now. I've only played with this thing for a few days, but I like it more and more. The one thing that is missing is that you can't change all the options via the webpage. You can change some, but I liked with my newer Sony the fact that I could look at and change all my custom presets without having to turn the TV and go through all that. I'm only comparing this to my two Sony units so you get my frame of reference, but realize this Yamaha model is in a higher class than those. Regardless, I love this thing, and it has a lot of great functionality and no serious drawbacks that I've noticed yet. Recommended (obviously).

I use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones all the time and prefer them to normal headphones as I tend to work in noisy environments and I’ve found that with ANC engaged I can play music at lower volumes. I like Sony headphones so I was excited to try these ANC ear buds. They’re a bit unusual in a few ways but they work well and are worth their asking price.

These are truly wireless and have no physical connection between them. Power them both on and they find one another. They pair via Bluetooth to a phone, tablet or PC, and the connection is stable up to about 40’ around corners. This is a good start.

There are several modes to these when it comes to the ANC function and each has its uses. I usually just use full ANC without any of the ambient sound modes turned on as it gives the best music experience. One of the two ambient modes is optimized for speech and voice, the other for more generalized noise. Neither completely cut off noise canceling, but rather they allow different bands of outside noise to come through. In full ANC mode, these are good noise cancellers, though not as aggressive as some others like Bose.

The sound can be adjusted a bit in the app that you can download, as it has an equalizer of sorts that lets you tweak the levels or choose a preset.

Ah, the app… This is the primary downside of these. The method to adjust these is either an Android or iOS app, not a physical piece of hardware and there is no Windows equivalent (for those who want to use these with a PC). The app is a little clunky though fairly self-explanatory and it does do what it’s supposed to do. Given a choice between an app or an additional piece of hardware, I would choose the hardware.

These charge up in the carrying case, which has leads that connect to each bud. Pay attention when you put these in the case – it is possible to reverse them, and while it hurts nothing the charging doesn’t work well… The case has some sort of battery in it and it charges the buds without being plugged in itself, though it does require occasional charging. Charging is fast – I charged them from empty to full in about an hour. One thing that could be improved, though: the buds can be popped in the charger while still powered on, and the act of charging them does not make them cut off. So, you can end up with dead buds and a dead charger too.

These are decent wireless sport buds that have good sound and good ANC functions. They’re comfortable and not overpriced. There are a couple of areas for improvement, particularly in charging but also in the app control, that would make these even better.

I purchased this Panasonic Soundbar in June of 2013. At the time, my requirements were:
- Good sound (can't afford GREAT sound)
- Wireless Subwoofer
- HDMI input and good HDMI-CEC support
- Bluetooth support

In my search, I tested the [[ASIN:B00811NMMI Toshiba SBX4250]] and the [[ASIN:B00BLX9510 Samsung HW-F450]] from my local Costco. My final choice was the Panasonic.

Sound:
- Acceptable sound -- The front speakers are not a big improvement over the built-ins. With the subwoofer turned off, it is easy to mistake the Panasonic sound bar with the speakers from the Television.
- Good subwoofer -- The sub sounds good even at high volumes and fills out the overall sound from the sound bar.
- The Samsung has clearer mid and high ranges so the Panasonic seems slightly muffled in comparison.
- Overall sound better than the Toshiba.
- Wireless range for the subwoofer is short -- especially if placed behind the sofa (interference from people sitting in front of it). Range is about 15 feet with clear line of sight.

Decoders and Passthrough:
- AC3 and DTS Decoder (Toshiba lacks DTS)
- ARC (Audio Return Channel) -- If you use the Netflix app built in to your TV, audio is generated by your TV. Normally, an "optical out" cable from the TV back to the sound bar is necessary. ARC removes that need.

HDMI-CEC (also Aquos Link, Anynet+, Bravia LinkSync, Regza Link, etc):
This is where the Panasonic beats the Samsung. HDMI-CEC allows Televisions to control a connected device -- no matter the brand; The TV remote should be able to turn on a bluray player and send navigation (up/down/etc) and standard playback buttons without the need for a second remote control.

In the case of a sound bar, through HDMI-CEC:
1. The sound bar should turn on when the TV turns on -- Panasonic does this, Samsung does not.
2. The TV should play all sound through the sound bar and volume buttons on the TV remote should control volume on the sound bar -- Panasonic does this.
3. Turning on a bluray player, the sound bar should turn on and switch to the correct input automatically. The TV should also turn on and switch to the correct input -- Panasonic does this. It's then up to your TV do its part.

In conclusion, I chose the Panasonic because it gave me the ability to eliminate a remote control through HDMI-CEC (which Samsung didn't) and it had both AC3 and DTS decoders (which Toshiba didn't). With the added ability to play music from my phone through bluetooth, I'm still happy with my purchase one year later.

Tip: Unlike the Samsung and Toshiba, the Panasonic has a small "receiver" unit that adds another machine to your entertainment center. For me, I use some velcro strips and attach the "receiver" to the back of my TV. It is only 1 ¾" thick which was thinner than my wall mount.

As a child one of my favorite things to do was to look at things under a microscope. I vividly remember gathering a water sample from a swamp near the house and looking at a sample and finding my first paramecium. It has been years since I have owned a microscope, but with this microscope I can see how things have advanced and changed. This one does not have the same magnification as that microscope I had as a child but it is a lot easier to use and I can still see things with it that I cannot see even with a good magnifying glass.

This unit looks more like a drill press than a microscope, in terms of the design. The scope itself fits on a metal shaft and two turning knobs make it easy to raise and lower the scope in relation to the base. The base has two clips for holding down your slides or paper or whatever else you want to look at through the scope. There is no eye-piece on the scope – the image is viewed on a computer screen instead and the connection is made via USB.

Included with the scope is a software CD and this must be installed to use the scope. Installation is quick and painless. I installed under Windows 10 64-bit and had no issues. After installation I launched the software immediately.

The software consists of a view/capture application and a supplemental application for saving your work. The main part of the view & capture app is a live window that shows what is visible through the scope. As the object or slide on the scope base is moved, the image updates in real time. I found it a little awkward to line things up just right at first but I finally did manage to get things in the viewer just as I wanted them.

I started with a gray piece of paper that I thought was solid gray, but I found that the gray is actually a micro dot pattern like magazine print. More interesting was the corner of a $5 bill showing not just the print pattern detail but the fine fibers in the paper. A penny, cat hair and a very close-up view of a microfiber cleaning cloth all proved to be interesting subjects. Attached to this review are some of those detailed images, my favorite being the penny. I have not yet gone to the culvert near the house to gather water samples.

The software allows for two different capture types – photo or video. I have only played with the photo capture so far but it it very straightforward – click the photo button, either on the application interface or on the USB cable where the light level can be adjusted and the image appears in a list on the right side of the application window. If you double click the image you can save the image to the hard drive, zoom in on it and do a few other operations.

Linked to a tablet instead of a computer, this is a great travel scope to take with you. It is well-suited for classroom use as well as for use in the office.

I like this microscope. It is very easy to use, it does a good job of magnification and images are nice and clear. It is very different than the microscope I used growing up, in ways that I like. It's so much easier viewing on a screen than looking through a viewer, making this more fun to use too.

But hey, unlike the photographer at Portrait Innovations, at least I know 'medium format' does not refer to the number of megapixels at which I am shooting. As for my working knowledge, I had three semesters of photography in college. I can process/print both B&W and color film. (Not that that does me any good these days LOL) I can shoot completely 'manual' and I have stood among many pro photographers on the bridge at sunset, waiting for the color to be just right on Half Dome. (My Bogen tripod was way too heavy to be practical for an amateur but it gave me street credit.) So, in a nut shell, I shoot by the 'Sunny 16' rule. I know that opening my f-stop should increase my shutter speed give me a shorter depth of field; and, per the great Ansel Adams, f/8 is a proper exposure for all pictures.

That said, I hate my D3100.

I have had metering issues since I opened the box. I bought the camera so I could take 'even better' pictures of my infant son than I was getting from my D50. Ha. Joke was on me.

The contrast was BLINDING on the factory settings and every shot was over exposed. I have tried every metering option in the menu but the only changes I can achieve are under-exposure, blurred focus and missed shots. It's go high or go without.

I always lower my ISO to 100 when I'm outside because I crave rich color but it's just not there. I have tried Aperture Priority, Shutter Priority and Manual. Nothing. f/16 over my film speed on a sunny day. That's supposed to work! I have used it on many a 'less complicated' camera and achieved photos that make jaws drop. Well, there's no jaw dropping with this camera.

The metering overrides my manual choices every time. It's like I'm having a battle of wits with my camera. :( It reminds me of the days when Kodak was marketing 800-speed film as a universal, never-miss-a-shot solution to all your photo woes. Bleh. Just because there's always an image doesn't mean it's the RIGHT exposure.

I get that being an entry-level/made-for-the-masses DSLR really does mean it's a glorified point-and-shoot but it should preform at least as well as it's predecessors. Honestly, I got far more reliable results from my Canon SureShot and a roll of Kodak 100.

My expectation for a camera is that the image should be very close to perfect when the shutter closes. I know there's always room for improvement before printing but that's the art of photography. The hours I spend working on my photos after the shot should be to make them pop. Instead, my time is spent trying to rescue precious memories.

If you are considering this camera as your first DSLR because you think it will improve your skills, skip it. Invest in an equally expensive point-and-shoot that will give you all the same manual controls and preform much better in low-light situations. The D3100 does not live up to the standards of a Nikon SLR.

This is a standard portable external drive with a USB interface. It's small, easy to handle, and works well. Most external drives use the USB 2.0 interface. This has the newer, and much faster, USB 3.0 interface. (But it works just fine when connected to a computer that has USB 2.0. The speed in that case would be the slower USB 2.0 speed.)

USB 3.0 uses a different connector on the drive, so you need to use the USB 3.0 cable that comes with the drive. A standard USB 2.0 cable won't work because it has a different connector on the drive side. On the computer side, it's a standard USB plug, so it fits both USB 2.0 and USB 3.0 jacks on the computer.

I use this to move many GB's of data from my PC to my Mac laptop. The PC has USB 3.0, so it's blazing fast to move data from the PC to the external drive. My Mac laptop has USB 2.0, so it takes longer to move the data from the drive to the Mac. But it works. Drive capacities are now so large that USB 3.0 is a huge advantage. It takes quite a bit of time to move 1 TB of data at USB 2.0 speed.

Bottom line: while these won't compete with the high end earbuds, they sound quite good, and far better than expected given the price. Comfortable with excellent noise isolation. Some weakness in the mid range, but an overall great value set.

Full review:
I'm familiar with the higher-end earbuds from RHA (such as their model MA-350, which I use almost daily), so I was very interested to see what they could produce for at the lower end of the price scale.

The overall build quality is quite good. They are just as comfortable as the MA-350 in my ear, which is to say they are nearly perfect. They have the right amount of cushion so they don't get tiring but still fit securely so I don't have any problems with them falling out while exercising. The MA150 comes with three sets of ear cushions so you can adjust them to fit what's best for your ear.

The cord is less stout than the MA-350 (it's a conventional rather than woven cord) but still seems durable enough for typical use. I very much like the plug connector - nicely made, and is angled to alleviate stress points (the connection is where many of my buds end up failing).

The sound quality is good. I used them on my Kindle Fire and a SanDisk MP3 player. No, it won't knock your socks off, but it's a lot better than I expected for the price. The bass is clear and more than plentiful for my taste. Where I noticed the most difference between these and the MA-350's is in the mid-range and treble. Definitely less crisp, which I would imagine is due to the fact that these are made of plastic rather than the aluminum construction of the MA-350s. But it didn't cause any significant problems when I used them when movie watching - the dialogue was quite clear.

Noise isolation is excellent. Very little ambient noise leaks in when wearing them.

The biggest miss is the same complaint I have with other RHA `phones - the R/L markings are on the stem in raised black letters on a black background. VERY hard to see. So, the first thing I do is to color in the RHA logo on the right bud with a Sharpie so I can spot L & R easily.

But that quibble aside, these are excellent and a great value. Very good sound, comfortable to wear for extended periods, good noise isolation and nicely made. I also like the packaging - rather than a blister pack with lots of plastic, these come packed in what RHA calls an "eco pack" - minimal thickness and packaging that is mostly thin cardboard. Much easier to recycle and open.

Definitely worth a look if you want a low-cost set that provides a very good music listening experience, and an excellent movie sound experience.

Original review:

Surprise! I actually love this computer.

I mean, I am a bit of a power user, so I have a big gaming laptop and a couple of servers throughout my house, not to mention a few purpose-built niche laptops. So while I was a bit skeptical of this machine before it came since I saw the low price tag, I think it's awesome for the right purpose.

I mean, I totally get what "Chrome Books" are trying to do - be low price, low weight computers that run basically "from the cloud". But who really wants a computer running Android? I mean, there are phones for that. So running Windows 10 is a great idea. (Not that I love Windows 10, but if you install Windows Classic Shell and tweak, tweak, tweak away...turn off all permissions, get rid of all the stupid crap they're trying to sell you, use an offline account, then it is almost as good as Windows 7).

Anyway, you don't get a lot of fancy new stuff, but what you do get is important: 1080p screen, mini-HDMI out (odd choice, would have gone for micro or even full, but whatever), 2 USB 3.0 (No C), a micro-SD card reader, headphone jack, and a M.2 expansion port.

64GB of ROM is pretty small, but they installed so little bloatware (just one program to make the touchpad better - I uninstalled it because I didn't recognize it, am paranoid, and figure I can adjust it with whatever is built into Windows) that you have ~45GB free. Should be enough for stuff like MS office and other junk you may want. But you know what, I have a 36TB NAS, and Windows works flawlessly with it, so if I'm using this as a home machine, it's not a problem. I don't much care for public cloud, so if I want to take this on the road, I can always stream (usually still reach my NAS) or just throw in an SSD (by the way, it only takes the small form factor) or a giant micro-SD card (although admittedly either of these factors takes away the fact that this item is inexpensive to begin with.

6GB of RAM is sufficient for a computer that is not meant to be a workhorse.

It's really thin and light and with a real keyboard is just delightful as opposed to dealing with a tablet; a tablet always disappoints me when I'm trying to get something done quickly. It also boots up fast due to NAND memory. It doesn't even look cheap or anything. It actually looks pretty good.

It has a regular "wall wart" type AC adapter instead of the usual laptop power brick. I like this, but the cord is a little short (on the other hand, it is likely easily replaced with something in my electronics closet) The barrel adapter goes into the right side of the device (which is not abnormal, but less normal than the back or the other side in my experience) and the unfortunate part is that it will partially fit into the stereo mini-plug port for headphones on the same spot on the other side, which is likely to cause some confusion.

The only apparent downside is that the keyboard seems...like it vibrates slightly. Like it's not held in tight enough or something. I mean, it does have nice keys and overall I like it, but it just feels slightly weird, although still much better than a tablet roll-out keyboard.

I actually really like this little machine. Not for my main computer or my only computer, but definitely for easy browsing, or a multimedia machine for a teen, or a school computer, a travel computer, whatever. I'd use it for plenty of things, happily.

If you're cool with the memory - and living off a NAS, an SD card, or the cloud - and you're looking for something small and usable, definitely give this some consideration.

No viewfinder (unlike the A1100. It's not needed all the time, but it is handy)

So, with all of 2 days of experience under my belt:

Update: 4/27/2014 Took a nice long walk, shot 6 min. of 720p x 30fps video and took 101 L-superfine .jpg (4k x 3k pixel) photos. This used up most of a fully-charged Vivitar 1700 mA-h battery. I got a battery warn and shutdown after my walk while reviewing the video at home. The 1000 mA-h stock Canon battery would give proportionately less life. Canon says that the stock battery is good for 210 photos. A 1700 mA-h Vivitar battery should be good for 147 more than that, or 357 photos. That means that 6 min. of 720p video is worth 256 photos! I don't think anyone will be shooting at 1080p x 60fps much.

Another way to look at it is the number of pixels processed per second by any of the 11 modes of the camera. The normal L .jpg picture takes 12.0E+6 pixels/sec (12 megapixels/sec). The least hungry mode S, takes only 0.307E+6 pixels per second. The hungriest mode is the 14 frames per second L multiple shot mode, which takes 168.E+6 pixels/sec. Since this is only in use for a few frames, it's not bad on battery life. The second worst mode 1080p x 60fps takes 124.E+6 pixels per second, 1037% of the normal L photo processing power! I have been interested in a device that can find hidden cameras for a while as we do tend to travel periodically. This device seemed like a good one and I wanted to try it out before I travel again. It seems like a pretty neat device that works fairly well, but it is hamstrung by very poor documentation.

This does more than just find hidden cameras. It is able to pick up Wi-fi signals, wireless phone signals and more. The sensitivity is very much like working with a metal detector - turn it up too high and it becomes nothing more than a sight and sound show; turned too low and it hardly sees anything.

With the unit turned on and set to a reasonable initial detection level I set about looking for devices in my home office. I have several Wi-fi connected devices and I usually have my smartphone there too, and I messed with this detector until I found the level where it was able to find everything. I did not try going near the router which is in another room but I imagine that one would require another sensitivity adjustment.

Most of the functions are self-explanatory, but some took a little trial and error to figure out. This is where good documentation would come in handy, and unfortunately the documentation with this device is poor. It's sufficient to identify the different functions of the device and where to find different components, but the actual descriptions and explanations of the functions are written in very poorly translated English.

Aside from the documentation, it would have been nice to have a carrying case for this device for storage and travel. That's a minor gripe, though.

I am happy with this device, though better documentation would make it much easier to use right away. It has some useful functions that will appeal to wary travelers, and it seems to work well once you figure out the right adjustments.

So, let me start off by saying, this isn't the best quality webcam on the market. But for the price, no one is expecting it to be. And it is FAR from the worst! During the Covid Pandemic, all the regular brand name webcams were sold out so I found myself trying out a bunch of these no-name brands from Amazon. The last one I tried actually had a much harsher fisheye effect in the corners, as well as over-saturated color. This one seems far less cartoony and more realistic in color reproduction, as well as being somewhat more rectilinear (photo speak for straight lines being straight, not as much curved distortion). There is a bit of fisheye curve on the edges, but it is very usable and didn't make my ceiling look concave like my last one I tried. See attached images for examples of the room's wall distortion. It's there if you are looking for it, but not terrible when you're looking at a subject. The microphone is just meh. I have a desktop mic and the sound out of that was MUCH better, especially because you can get it closer to your face than the camera. But the fact that this HAS a mic is a good option in a pinch. I would just strongly recommend an external mic if you want people to hear you clearly. Also something I didn't know before trying this:
It is MANUAL focus! That means it won't follow and focus on you automatically, you have to twist the lens until you're sharp in the view. It actually isn't that hard to nail focus, the depth of focus is pretty deep so once you've set it for your standard sitting distance, you likely won't have to change it ever again unless you walk away from the camera. A fun side effect, however is that the focus lens gear lets you push it to EXTREME MACRO distances! So you can do insane closeups of things if you want to, for example, put a webcam on an ant farm maybe? I tried it out on my desktop speaker, and in one picture you can see the relative size of it compared to my desk and then the closeup you can see the detail of the scratched plastic where it says Harmon / Kardon. Ha, if nothing else this shows me I should probably get new desktop speakers too! These are beat up when up close! A fun and versatile camera for a good price. If you need autofocus tracking, this might not be for you though.

With its huge 64GB file storage capacity, this flash drive can theoretically store the entire contents of a PC's hard drive and its operating system. Since I don't have that many files to store on an everyday basis, I am reserving this flash drive to store high-resolution videos and other RAM-eating monster files.

For $80, this is rather overpriced. There are USB drives that are cheaper and will do the job just as well. To make the USB look like it's worth the extra price, Toshiba made the casing unnecessarily oversized - there's no practical reason why the USB case had to be so wide (you will have trouble sticking another USB drive next to it, which is annoying). It's a gimmick to impress the user, nothing more. However, when you hold it in your hand, it's not as heavy as the metallic finish would lead you to believe - it's actually very lightweight, and to be honest, feels cheap. I have questions of its durability, despite the fancy advertising.

To test, I copied all the videos I had stored in my PC to see how fast it would be to store all of them on this monster drive. I was disappointed that the saving time was not noticeably faster, which may not be the fault of the USB drive but rather my computer. However, I have to say it was a relief that I never got the "you don't have enough memory" message, so you can count on this USB to store tons of videos you can't find room for elsewhere.

The only drawback to this single-USB method of storage is that I don't feel entirely comfortable saving so much stuff on just ONE drive, despite its capacity. It's equivalent to putting all your eggs in one basket - what if you lose that single USB - you're screwed. Though convenient, I'd rather spread out my back-up files, so if you use this USB to save a huge file, I'd buy more than one just to be safe.

The other thing I thought was unnecessary was the included encryption software that's included on the drive. You only see it when you open up the Files folder, and there are two lengthy PDFs with instructions on how to activate the password and security options. Fortunately you do not require to activate them in order to use the drive - I've never found I needed such security measures, but if you plan to store financial data on this USB, it's a good feature.

Lastly, I hate the fact that, unlike my other drives, it has a cap. I am forever losing the caps to my flash drives and have since opted to buy only the retractable ones, where you can slide the connector in or out. Too bad this one doesn't have it, otherwise I would have added a star.

So, in short, a mixed review. Give me a drive that's cheaper, that's big on the inside but small on the outside, capless, and I'd buy more of them.

One thing we have a lot of use for in this household is Bluetooth headphones. Whether it is for work, keeping privacy in the house, using with phones, exercising, running, walking, or other uses, everyone in the house goes through headphones. I was very interesting in these especially for exercising as it is hard to find a good pair that stay in.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These earphones are meant to be used for activities that are rather intense- hence exercising, moving around, etc. These earphones come with a short USB cord for recharging and a few sizes of gel type fittings for different sizes of ear canals.

HOW ARE THESE TO USE?
They hold a charge for six to eight hours depending on how intense the listening time is and if it is consecutive or not. The controls are easy to use on the right ear wire. It does not tell you who is calling, but it does ring in the ear. Answering was easy and the call went through well with decent volume. They do stay in the ears quite well for more intense activity. Once in a while I might knock one out if I am intensely exercising, but most of the time they have been good.

SOUND?
The sound is good, but tends a little toward the flat side compared to other earbuds I have used. We have found that breaking them in by using a lot has helped them to sound better than they did at first, so they are really not bad.

COMFORT?
That is where the stars come off. Yes, they stay in the ears, but after wearing about an hour or so, they really begin to hurt. It is not the size of the cushions, but the hard plastic under them that presses against the ears. Two of us have tried them out and it does it for both of us.

WHAT ARE THESE BEST FOR?
These seem to be the best for exercising, running, walking, or an activity that is limited to an hour or so. They are good as far as sweat and water resistance goes. Recharging time is pretty good it can take from one to two hours to fully charge, depending on the day.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For really cool looking earbuds that stay in the ears during more intense activity, these are a good choice. Any time over an hour, however can be uncomfortable. Music playback is good, but not overly dimensional if that is something you are concerned with. We like them for exercising, walking, or running.

MY RATING

For the price, this is the 3D plasma to own. Panasonic makes the highest rated, best plasma displays on the market for the middle-end consumer and even higher-end sets. The GT30 has taken some hits due to its black-leveling during scene transitions. This seems most notable to those who may not understand or have the know how to alter the video settings properly; I DID notice this occurring when video output is set to "standard", once you tune the display properly, there should be no noticeable or any flickering between darker scenes to brighter transitions. To go into great detail on how to properly set your TV would be worthless, a "good" picture varies person by person but this preliminary issue should not deter one from purchasing this set.

With that out of the way, consider this: you will not see a better high definition plasma display on the market. At the GT30 price, you are not going to get 3D quality, HD quality, feature set and value any where else. If you have not been to any store to view other brands competing with this set/price, do so and do yourself a favor. Once you see a GT30 set up properly, showing the same content as other brands, there should be no questions left to answer. The display owns. From blu rays to PS3 to Wii to regular DVDs, I have not scene until this plasma a more OUTSTANDING visual display. Blu Rays appear as though people are standing in your living room.

the most noticeable attribute of this plasma, at least to me, is the quality and richness of the depth in the display. Its simply amazing. Looks like you can reach your hand into the background and touch things. And no, I am not talking about when 3D is on, that is another story. In pure HD form without 3D, the depth, black, and richness of this display is simply jaw dropping. Your friends will not understand what they are looking at. To note, a HD gaming system looks simply unbelievable. You will be playing your games for the "first time" all over again.

The bad: THE SPEAKERS ARE DOWN RIGHT AWFUL. if you do not have some sort of surround sound system, or at the very least two channels (front left/right) the speakers sound terrible, they may as well sold it without them and saved a few bucks. You will need some sort of sound bar or extra components to get anything other than dialog. And the dialog is barely satisfactory; no bass, tiny highs, bad spacing and underpowered.

3D: Panasonic has the best 3D on the market. Compare it with Samsung or Sony. There is no comparison. View them back to back and you will find that Panasonics 3D technology, although requiring ACTIVE shutter glasses, reproduced 3D images in HD form where as others may not. Samsung for example, 3D reproduction looks like cardboard paper cutouts with no depth and lacking resolution. Not in the GT30 however. The 3D is amazing and even the 2D->3D reproduction (taking standard 2D video and artificially creating 3D images) adds incredible depth to your viewing experience, albeit not so much "pop" off the screen. Worthy to note is that 3D viewing does produce a somewhat dimmer display, not sure if this is due to the glasses tint or how their system works, but overall when 3D is on, expect a less vibrant picture from non-glasses viewing.

Overall, theres not much out there for the GT30 price that offers screen size, content and value. Above all else, picture quality should take the cake here. Please check it out in a store and make your decision. Cant beat this set. On a side note, internet connectivity works flawlessly, I wired the TV with a ethernet cable, which, you should do if you expect the highest speeds and purest connection. The TV synced up with zero glitches and loaded youtube, pandora and amazon with the ease of touching 1 button.

Excellent buy, sound is its largest demerit but can be remedied for a couple of bucks. Good luck!!

This is the no-BS line from Cisco. Enterprise features, but nothing proprietary, no forced contracts, no stupid power port that requires special power cords...

You can hook this up and it will work right out of the box, just like an unmanaged switch, which will make network setup and augmentation very easy. Once I signed into the box, I pretty much had to change my password, but then I had a world of options at my fingertips that I could change at my leisure. There were a few things I wanted to configure right away, and plenty of others I realized I wanted after doing some research. I still have plenty to learn and play with when I have time I want to spend on this.

I do believe you can use Cisco command line to configure these, but it also has a very familiar (to other consumer/business equipment) GUI that is intuitive to use. I will say, though, that the GUI it can be pretty cumbersome if you want to use it to go through and turn on a feature on every single port individually. Part of the problem is that you have to save each port individually and then use the drop-down to do the next port. This switch can be a little slow to respond and therefore frustrating when changing multiple features in a row. I also have a 350 series 10 port switch that does NOT have that problem. I am not sure if it has more resources available or just has less to keep track of because of having fewer ports., but that might be a consideration if choosing between the 250 and 350 series. And if you use command line, you might not care at all...

Oh, and you have to do the "save to running config" thing like you do with the Enterprise stuff. Seems strange, but I guess it more or less makes sense why. But at least in this case you can just click apply...and then go up and click the blinking disk to save (to running config).

I am using this in my telecomm closet, which manages to keep nearly all the ports in my house hot. I'm using ports 25-27 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 350 series switch in my external cabinet, which connects my servers with multi-Gb links. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Here's some random stuff I figured out along the way:

-I am using 10Gbps copper DACs between the two devices. They do negotiate down to 1Gbps, they are cheaper than buying multiple SFPs, and I can use them later when I get 10Gbps ports (so the only reason you'd use fiber is if you needed a >100m link.

-Port trunking works between DAC and regular Cat6 (apparently it won't work with fiber SFPs mixed with Cat6.

-Not sure what I was doing wrong before port trunking on another switch, but I couldn't get anything better than high-error best effort to work as far as speed. On these 250/350 Cisco devices I'm using, all four of my trunks are working perfectly and clearly working at full speed without uncorrected errors (if any at all).

-There are "green features" included, but off by default. The one looks at link length and lowers power on those links if less than 50m. You can only use this if you turn off the Energy Efficient Ethernet standardized protocol, which you might do if the device you are using doesn't work, but I haven't found a case where it correctly reads my link length (and my testers do figure out the correct length, so I don't get this). The other green feature is Energy Detect, which I've turned on across the board, but it's hard to tell if that really saves energy or not, because it just is "on" when the link is down.

-The ports are counted strangely. Port 1 is the top left. Port 2 is bottom left. Port 3 is top second from left, etc. This caused me some brief confusion. The great thing is that you can name all your ports in the GUI so that can make things a lot more clear for you, especially if you keep all ports in your building hot or if you at least keep most of the devices static.

There are a ton of features here, and even more on the 350 series. If you're deciding between the 250 and 350 series, I suggest you do some serious homework to figure out if you actually need the 350 series. Here are just a few of the things I noticed the 350 series has that the 250 does not (not a comprehensive list):

On the 350, you can set link speeds lower on LAGS, use protected LAGS, more LAGS, UDLD, Ethernet tagging, VLAN mapping/private VLAN, lots of VLAN grouping options and more VLAN settings in general, and ISCSI status for QoS.

Oh...worth noting is that the 350 series apparently allows many more trunk groups than the 250 series, which only allows 4, so I would not necessarily want a 250 series for my 24 port switch if I didn't have my servers separate on the 350 (yet it seems unlikely you'd need more than 4 trunk groups on a 10 port 350).

One thing I don't like is that on some rack mounted equipment, you have one set of "wings/ears", but multiple positions/mounting options. These mounting brackets at least are included, but seem like they'd only work with this switch AND you can only put them on in one position, which means the switch will protrude about an inch forward in your cabinet (Well, you can also mount the switch backwards, if you consider that helpful). It would be better to have the option of recessing the switch an inch if you needed to. I also wish they could recess the power supply port on these things since - even with the heatsink on the back of this - the power cord is still the thing making this a tight fit in my closet.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Yes, I can absolutely imagine this to be a great line for a company to use, and I think I could even get a robust network up and running without too much stress or trouble. But there are plenty of other real-world applications for a home network as well: setting restrictions for kids or renters or whoever from getting to all areas of your network. There is all kinds of port security features here, protected ports, and VLAN features, so you should be able to do just about anything you want to do with these switches. Also QoS, traffic limiting, etc. I love having these features at my disposal, even at home!

I first heard about Cobo Vault on twitter from a few of the various people I follow on there. The thought of a new hardware wallet that was open source (something I really like about Trezor) but also air gapped (no Internet connectivity or USB, bluetooth, etc.) was also super appealing to my ultra paranoid side. I figure as Bitcoin and perhaps other cryptos go up in value, security will become even more paramount so the ultra-paranoia is justified.

Anyway, I started with the Essentials version of the product and I was first impressed with the way the product was packaged nicely; nothing loose in the box, everything protected well. Upon removing it from the packaging, the build quality of the device itself was impressive, setup was straightforward as well.

I really like the fact that the Cobo Vault hardware has a sync to the mobile app. Setting this up is part of the initial setup wizard. Doing this allows you to view the balance in BTC, ETH, etc. or fiat equivalent on the mobile app without actually having the hardware wallet. You can also receive via the mobile app through a QR code. It's likely better to use the QR code off the hardware wallet display itself if you're ultra paranoid but, again, it's an option to use the mobile app only. Keep in mind, you can't view the fiat balance on the hardware wallet since it's air gapped.

For sending, you initiate it through the mobile app but you will need the hardware wallet to complete the actual transaction. This is accomplished through a back and forth process of scanning of QR codes between the hardware wallet and your smartphone.

Because I liked the Essential one so much, I bought another Cobo Vault but this time the Pro version. The reason I bought the Pro version is because it has a fingerprint scanner and I found it to be easier to unlock and perform other operations using that method. Without that feature, you have to either type alphanumeric passwords on the tiny keyboard on the touch screen display or draw a pattern on a display (similar to smart phones). Both seem to be difficult for me as it is a little difficult to type the password correctly on the small touch screen display or draw the pattern correctly without going slowly; especially if you have bigger fingers.

To address this, perhaps having an random ordered numeric dial pad for a password might also be a good alternative.

Battery life: Another reason why the Pro version is superior to the Essentials version is that it includes a rechargeable battery as well as the AAA option. The AAA option seems to have inconsistent battery life and seems to drain really fast for me. I brought this up to the Cobo team and they were really responsive to me and explained why the AAA battery life was hard to calculate and inconsistent at times. Still, it'd be nice if there was some way to bring consistency to AAA battery percentage displayed. That being said, the rechargeable battery is the way to go for consistent use but the AAA battery option is great for long term assurance of the device should it outlive the rechargeable battery.
Suggestion would be to allow the device to be powered and/or charged while in use. Right now the rechargeable battery requires the battery to be detached from the device itself in order to be charged.

firmware updates: I'm really impressed with the frequency of the firmware updates as well as the new features being introduced. A+ on that. Performing the updates has been a mixed bag for me. I've found that for some updates, using the rechargeable battery (charging it to full) and then performing the update works best. Other times, most noticeably the update to 1.40 multicoin, I had to use the AAA battery pack with fresh batteries to update both my Pro and Essential; a fully charged rechargeable pack did not work. I'm confident they will work through this as the product continues to mature.

Which brings me to my last point, the thing that impresses me the most about this product is the response from the Cobo team. They are open to feedback and suggestions and both acknowledge it, respond with great detailed answers and work hastily to incorporate new features. I'm really impressed with the support.

I use a mix of different hardware wallets to store my crypto offline and Cobo Vault is probably my favorite to use right now. I'm super excited to see and be a part of this product line as it matures.

This camera is what I call a "subcompact" - the smallest point and shoot cameras that have vertically mounted lenses which allow protection, compactness, and quicker start up times. Normally, you'd expect a small trade off for these features, so I wouldn't compare this directly with a camera endowed by a telescoping lens.

Sony invented the subcompact with the T1 a few years back (at least in my world), and I was able to compare the FinePix Z90 with the one-generation-older 12 MP Sony T90. I'll go the pro/con route...

PROS of the Z90:

-Price is something like half of the latest subcompact Sony.
-Operational costs are cheaper: USB cable is non-proprietary (in case you want a second one or need to replace it) and SD card is cheaper and more universal than Sony's Memory Stick.
-Separate physical buttons to record movies and to take pictures. This is genius to me, because I hate to miss a great video opportunity while fumbling through the menus.
-Does not come with a memory card, BUT cameras that do usually come with one so small that it is worthless. Internal memory is better, because it allows you to copy from one camera card to another, which can be useful.
-Can set it up to take two photos at once, with and without the flash. As an amateur, I often do this manually anyway, but this way you get closer photos (chronologically)to compare in a dynamic scenario, and the subject needs only to pose once.
-The panorama mode works better than in other cameras I've used. They use internal weights alla smart phones (I'm guessing) to help you line up the next picture. Allows you to "pan" a panorama shot in play mode.
-There is a time zone mode that allows you to temporarily change the time (for timestamps).
-The display changes from horizontal to vertical as you move the camera respectively.
-"Touch and track" mode follows a subject.
-Side by side picture compare.
-Search by face, couple, group, favorites, scene, or date, and view a small picture next to thumbnails.
-Charger is smaller with the plug offset to allow it to use only one receptacle on a power strip (as long as it is at the end of said strip).

CONS of the Z90:

-Picture quality was not as good as the Sony 80% of the time (tested in various modes and lighting conditions). That said, a tripod really helps with low light and no flash, where both cameras struggle without it.
-By numbers, it is not much larger than the Sony, but it feels significantly larger.
-Sometimes the "buttons" in the corners of the touch screen need to be pressed more than once.
-Tripod mount has plastic threads, instead of a machined metal insert.
-Cannot take shots as rapidly as on the Sony
-Does not tell you what zoom level you are at. 5x zoom does not appear to make a great difference over 4x.
-"play" and "camera" buttons could be one button used as a toggle.
-Battery can be put in backward, as the slot is not keyed (although the battery is). No big deal, but shows something wasn't thought out thoroughly.

Bottom Line:

The Fuji is trying to deliver everything the market leader has to offer for a much more manageable price tag.
