I have several mp3 players and I had yet to find one suitable for everyday use until I picked this little gem up.

My requirements were:

-LONG battery life with replaceable battery (those embedded batteries are going to need factory servicing after 250-300 charge cycles...you can use rechargeable AA or AAAs and easily replace them)

-Color screen...more than 256 colors.

-USB 2.0 transfer

-Ability to drag and drop

-Ability to play OGG files

-FM tuner

-FM recorder

-Solid construction

I have another unit I use for in-line recording, so that wasn't a big deal to me. I came across this unit for a good price so I gave it a shot. Well, at first, I was upset because I couldn't get the player to be recognized under Windows. I called iRiver and a tech walked me through the steps of setting up the appropriate user account and permission in the registry. After that, I hooked in and updated the firmware.

This syncs with Windows Media Player 10 and does so seamlessly. You can set it to sync up automatically or manually and WMP10 can convert to 64kbps wma files to save space if you want. I updated the firmware and transferred a couple of music files with WMP10-no sweat. I then was able to open up the player and drag and drop files into it (requirement met!) Next came the key part-SOUND.

The sound on this unit is very good, even with the included earbuds. I connected a pair of active noise cancelling headphones with big magnets and the SRS sound was FULL and RICH, even though I was just playing OGG files (remember to put those in the DATA folder, not the MEDIA folder!) There's a lot of tweakability on sound, even though there are no user presets you can save to. The screen is nice, if not really large, and it's easy to get the controls down once you've had a day to get used to them.

The unit came with a sturdy armband and a necklace to connect to the T10's VERY well-secured lanyard clip. Either choice is OK, but I prefer the armband because I am always afraid I'll drink a soda and spill some on the unit if it's hanging right below my mouth.

The T10 has a good tuner and can record FM in nice quality. I also found the voice recording to be good, if a little sensitive to body noise (if you touch the body while you record, it is very audible.) The battery life is projected to be 45 hours (WHICH IS FANTASTIC!), so I use some AA NiMH spare batteries from my digital camera for power and I never have to worry about finding a plug when the power goes out. In a pinch, alkalines work just fine, too.

Let's review my requirements:

-LONG battery life with replaceable battery *CHECK*

-Color screen...more than 256 colors.*CHECK*

-USB 2.0 transfer *CHECK*

-Ability to drag and drop *CHECK*

-Ability to play OGG files *CHECK*

-FM tuner *CHECK*

-FM recorder *CHECK*

-Solid construction *CHECK*

In short, this player has satisfied all my needs and done so with great style to boot. I'd highly recommend it with the following warnings:

-Getting it to connect with Windows initially might require a call to iRiver.

-The unit is sort of chunky (it's kind of like a triangular prism) and will not slip into a pocket like a flat piece of cardboard. You will probably need to use a bigger case or one of the two included carry options.

-The design makes it hard to see the controls when wearing the armband on the left arm. Wearing it on your right will allow you easy access to the controls.

I'd DEFINITELY recommend this unit to ANYONE who needed a great player that didn't need line-in recording.

This crystal-clear screen protector film is very easy to apply. It's pre-cut to exactly fit the Kindle Fire touch screen, and it presses on without any need for additional adhesive. After the film is applied, there is no loss of sensitivity in the touch screen.

The application process is very simple: (1) clean the screen thoroughly, using the included microfiber cloth; (2) use the #1 tab to remove the plastic stiffener/shield from one side of the double-sided film; (3) position the uncovered side of the film on the Kindle Fire screen (holding the film by the #2 tab, starting at one corner, and allowing the film to fall gently onto the screen); (4) use the included smoothing card to get rid of bubbles; (5) use the #2 tab to remove the remaining plastic stiffener/shield; and (6) use the smoothing card again to get rid of any bubbles. The whole process took me less than 10 minutes.

Whenever I apply screen protector film, I usually have to try two or three times to get everything right. With this kit, the first application was successful, because the film adhered properly at the edges, and all but one tiny bubble smoothed out. Now, should I ever need to re-apply the film, I have the second shield in reserve.

It's probably worth noting that the Kindle Fire has a larger screen than an iPhone or iPod Touch or camera viewfinder, so that the risk of getting dust particles under the film during application to the Fire is higher. Also, it may not be necessary to install protective film on the Fire at all, because the touch screen is supposed to be made of particularly tough, scratch-resistant glass.

After doing some research, I read that these headphones are the best "bang for your buck" earbuds and so far, they aren't wrong. This product does some with six different silicon eartips, an small instruction booklet, and a small but durable pouch to put your eartips and buds in. It took me about five minutes find the perfect removable eartips for my ears. It would have been shorter but I was afraid of tearing the silicon tips (so far none have ripped). Everybody's ears are different but my ears prefer the smallest snowman shape ones for both my right and left ear (Pictures of the tips can be found in the 'Wired' only version of this product).

They are easy to clean and the remote is secure (meaning that the remote button or volume slider won't move or activate if it accidentally hits your clothes or something). I haven't used the microphone yet. These things are very secure once you install them in your ears. You can talk, yawn, chew gum, run, jump and drink water and these tips wouldn't budge (you can take them out easily though). The sound quality and noise blocking are great too for when I run. It also works well for people that wear glasses like me.

However I have two small issues with this product. One is that the wire is a little long for me but it usually doesn't get in your way (only once so far but this was my second time using them). You may experience burning in your ears. I did at first when I was trying to find the best way to wear them. For me (using the smallest snowman ones), You just put them before the ear canal so the silicon tips rest comfortably in your ears. Don't push/force them in your ears because that will cause your ears to burn.

In conclusion, if you're looking for the best sleek 'bang for your buck' earbuds that stay secure during rigorous activity who doesn't mind a little burning in your ear canals at first, then I would recommend this product and I'll probably buy it again when/if this product wears out.

Edit: Just after a month of use the the remote button is a little glitchy. Before it could be resting against by chest while running and it would work fine. Now while running, I have to pull it about 5 inches away from my body and point the the top of the headset (where it branches off into two) at about a 45 degree angle in order to pause/skip a song. It's kind of cumbersome and if it didn't do this then I'd definitely rate it higher.

Edit: The sellers were very prompt and understanding with my situation and I got a new pair for free (under warranty). I've been using them for a couple of months and I haven't noticed any problems with them.

This is sort of a mixed review, but it ends in 5 stars because in the end I did end up with an amazing looking product for very cheap.

To start I bought 2 RGB covers for my 2 ram sticks and they worked perfectly fine, and I was going to write a glowing review.

Then I bought 2 more ram sticks and 2 more RGB covers to go with them, and in the pictures you can see that one of the LED's was bad and wouldn't match the rest of the RGB covers.

I asked for a replacement and the next day one was shipped out to me and arrived in a few days, good customer support!

Installed that RGB cover and one of the LED's was significantly dimmer than the rest, (no pictures) so I asked for another replacement.

On the second replacement I got another LED that would not match the rest of the sticks.

3 times the charm right?

On the 3rd attempt I finally got a cover that worked great, and now my pc looks like a light show!

Which is why I say that this product is basically the lottery, you can get great looks for really cheap if your lucky, or a maddening experience of constantly asking for a replacement until you get one that works good.

However I did end up giving this 5 stars as the customer support was amazing. Seriously, within an hour I had one shipped out to me, even the 3rd time, no questions asked.

The product is very easy to install ONLY IF you have bare ram sticks. If you ram sticks have integrated heatspreaders on your ram like mine did, then the installation is significantly hard because you have to take a hair dryer and heat up the sticky glue that holds the heatspreaders and take them off.

Be careful when doing this, I accidentally knocked a small surface mount diode off in the process, luckily I had a soldering iron and just stuck the diode back where it belonged.

However I am not taking off stars for ease of installation since having heatspreaders already on the ram is not this products fault. Once the old heatspreaders are off, installing these is a peace of cake, literally 2 screws and they're on.

This is my second purchase of a Sony Walkman. My first one was for my husband for our anniversary. I bought him an 8g player (NWZ-E438) and once I got that up and running, I realized that 8g really isn't that much when I realized that he has a whole bunch of cd's and videos and pictures. But the reason why I bought the 8g of that model was because it had an equalizer. Now, let's talk about this beautiful S545 model - WOW! It's 16g and what a beauty. the sound quality is A-Mazing, and the picture/video screen is clear and crisp. AND it has an equalizer - 5 settings, plus 2 custom settings = 7 equalizer settings. I bought mine at Walmart, and it was $119. I also got it in red - the red color is a nice color, not faded or pastelie. The sound quality from the exterior speakers will surprise you. Keep in mind that you will not be able to host a large dance party with it, but it is just perfect for a personal experience, let's say in your room or something like that. The sound from the speakers is quite nice, and I would compare it to the speaker from my Motorola RAZR2. My phone can get a lot louder than the Sony Walkman, but the quality of sound is just as good. I was not in any way disappointed with the quality. The only thing I would change on this player is the placement of the speakers - they are on the back, not the front. The picture of this player might fool you to think the speakers are in the front, but they are not. I also learned that this player will not be able to download podcasts. The higher-end Sony Walkmans do.

Another thing is that the software for the player comes loaded in the player, instead of including a cd in the box. It worked really great, it was simple and just way too easy to use. It was much easier to set up on the computer and get going than the one I bought for my husband. With the software, "Content Transfer" all you have to do is drag a song, or a picture or a video right to the Content Transfer window, and POW - it's there, and it knows right where to put it (music, pictures, video). So you don't even have to fuss around and click into the different files. I already have 1,926 songs in WMA format in 48Kbps, 38 videos, and 223 photos, and I have 10g left. Right out of the box, because of the software itself, there is 2g being used for the player, and you get 14g to play with.

This player will also record voice recordings and FM radio recordings (song, advertisement, talk show or whatever). It looks like they give you 99 hours and 59 minutes of recording time.

The FM player will only work if you have either your headset plugged in or your speakers plugged in. The FM won't work with the external speakers - it needs to use the wire as an antenna. And I didn't think the FM was bad - worked and sounded just fine to me.

So, if you are looking for a player, you just might want to consider this one.

I have been wanting a new MP3 player for a while now. I refuse to waste my phone with cluttered songs and use. I have watched everyone else I know blow through phones from constant use. I wanted to have a dedicated MP3 player. Let's see how this worked out.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This comes in a nice box- great for gift giving. It has a cord with it for charging and attaching to computer if you want to download songs to it. This does NOT have any internal memory, however. All songs have to be stored on a microSD card. There is port for headphones, mini USB, and line out port.

HOW TO OPERATE
ON/OFF
The power button is on the top of the unit. It has to be held in for a moment before it kicks in. There is an issue with the power button being on the top pressed down easily. The design of this has a raised edge of the case so that it is harder to press on the power button accidentally.

MENU
The menu button is easy to operate. It takes you around the menus using the forward and backward arrow buttons.

VOLUME
The volume buttons are on the outside edge on the right as you look at the case. The + and - buttons are separate.

BACK BUTTON
This takes you back through the menu and you can replay songs too.

PLAY PAUSE
Is on the front of the case and it is easy to access and see.

SCREEN
This is not a full color screen. It is simple and easy to read, however, without graphic clutter.

BLUETOOTH?
I had a heck of a time with this at first. I was not having it work well with my bluetooth headphones and it frustrated me to no end. I was about ready to give this an awful review when I suddenly realized- it was not the player, it was both sets of headphones that were not working correctly! Once I got the headphones working, the sound is BEAUTIFUL on this.

I have also used this with a few bluetooth speakers with great results. I like the solid feeling of the body- it stays put but does not take up too much room.

SOUND
You can change the sound quite a bit with this to be what you want. There are presets and fine tuning settings you can use. Once I finally got this figured out, the sound is amazing.

READ OUT
Again, this is NOT TOUCHSCREEN nor does it have fancy full color graphics. It is simple and easy to read and use.

STORAGE
Remember, this stores all of the songs on the microSD card. There is not any internal storage in this otherwise.

AM I GLAD TO HAVE THIS?
Once I got the problems worked out, I have to say I really like this. It is not as intuitive as some items, but it is really nice to have and I love to play it. I like shuffler or single CD artist choices, etc.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a really nice MP3 player. It is a bit more rustic than some might be used to with smart phones, but it really works nicely and the sound is great.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. It does what it says, although I would prefer it to have some internal storage as well as microSD, but that is just me. For what this is- it is very nice. I like it and am pleased with the performance.

SanDisk has come out with an extension to their array of MP3 players, beyond the Clip and the View. Their new mp3 player, the Sansa Fuze, is definitely geared towards casual someone who just wants a basic, functional, and well-put together media device for their pocket.

The Sansa Fuze may look like a tiny device at first, but this thing packs some serious features. It has the ability to playback music, video, photos, FM radio, as well as audiobooks. The features for the Sansa Fuze are very impressive to say the least, as it also features a microSD card slot to add extra storage space, content, etc.

The first feature we will focus on is the one which will likely get the most use, the audio aspect. The music menu is organized with artist, album, song, genre, etc. There is also a recently added section which shows the most recent songs added onto the device, as well as a top rated section.

The album menu allows you to see album icons as you are scrolling through the various albums. There is also the ability to form a playlist directly on the player.

The sound quality is very well-done. If you have a great set of headphones you will not be disappointed in the least bit.

The video aspect is definitely not the highlight of the Sansa Fuze. Part of this is due to the low power of the device, and partly due to the screen itself. The supplied Sansa Media Converter does make it easy to convert movies into a format for the device though. A typical movie will take up a little under, or over 1GB. The video looks respectable, but can get a bit choppy at times. One very cool feature about the video is the ability to add a bookmark while watching it.

The photo viewer is very standard as you can view photos from the internal memory of a microSD card. You can set up a slide show with time intervals, and add music as well. The images looked quite sharp.

The FM radio feature is done extremely well on the Sansa Fuze. You get some great reception and the auto program feature picks out crystal clear radio stations. It also has the ability to record radio in WAV format.

This works with voice recording as well thanks to a microphone located right below the microSD slot.

Podcasts and audiobooks are pretty self-explanatory, but one issue with the audiobooks is the lack of a bookmark feature.

The overall user interface for the Sansa Fuze is put together nicely, set up in such a way that a first-time user could pick up this device and feel right at home with it. You have a scroll wheel as well as a home button and a middle click wheel. The scroll wheel can also be clicked up and down, which can make things a bit confusing at times. Overall though, beyond a few hiccups with organizational aspects of the UI, this is one easy device to use.

Getting media onto the Sansa Fuze is extremely simple as you can use any desktop media player to create playlists and such, easily syncing them to the device. It also supports drag and drop without the need for any software. We used Windows Media Player as well as a few other media players to test this all out, and syncing was as simple as can be.

The quality of the device itself is top-notch, as the screen can put out some great contrast and vibrant colors in spots. The screen is extremely clear and does a nice job with photo presentations. Battery life is equally as impressive, as I have been getting around 20 hours on each battery charge thus far. Video playback came in at around 6 hours on a charge.

The package comes with a proprietary USB cable and a pair of earbuds, pretty basic.

Also shipping with the Sansa Fuze is a great bonus, a microSD card which comes with DRM-free music from more than 50 new and emerging artists. This is a great way to immediately test out the music capabilities of the Sansa Fuze, and also adds value to the entire package. Music videos, images, and more are also included on the microSD card.

Overall SanDisk has done a great job with the Sansa Fuze.

Let me begin by saying that I am not gifted in the arena of art. I am more technically oriented and as such I use tablets in different ways than most people. For that reason, this is likely going to be a very different review than that of most others on here.

I use pen tablets for handwriting and as general pointing devices as I find them to be more comfortable than mice and trackballs. I started experimenting with tablets a couple of years ago with a Bamboo small, which worked well but was just too small for me. I then compared a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch to an Intuos4 and it took no time at all to determine that for me, the Intuos4 was a much better choice. With the release of the Intuos5 I jumped at the chance to compare it to the Intuos4, and so far I like it but I have found a couple of things about it that are, in my opinion, less than ideal.

I am using an Intuos5 on a Core i7-based laptop with 8 GB RAM and Windows 7 64-bit.

The very first thing - installation. Installation was about as painless as could be. I plugged in the tablet, installed the drivers and I was able to start using my tablet immediately without any issue. That's a big plus right off the bat. I have had trouble with installs in the past, in particular with the Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, so having a smooth install is a great relief.

There is one thing about the install that troubles me, though. This tablet is capable of left- or right-handed use, so by simply rotating the tablet it is easy for anyone to use it. However, unlike the Intuos4 the Intuos5 only has a USB plug on one side, and it's the edge that always faces away from the computer. This means that the cord will always run above or below the tablet when plugged in unless it's plugged in to a USB hub of some sort. Perhaps that is not a big deal to some, but to me it is a minor irritant. The included USB cable is long enough, though, that I can hang most of it off the far edge of my desk. I suppose it's a good thing that my desk faces the wall.

I immediately grabbed the pen and started writing, and what I have found is that the Intuos5 seems to be a little more sensitive than the Intuos4, which means I can write a little more softly and still get what I want from it. Wacom did a good job of adjusting the sensitivity to the pen and subsequently turning off the touch feature. With my Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch the pen had to be very, very close to the surface of the tablet before touch was disabled, and even then the tablet kept trying to zoom on me as I wrote. Not so with the Intuos5 - the sensitivity to the pen seems to be good up to about an inch from the surface, which is fine for my purposes.

The surface of the Intuos5 does seem to be a little rougher than that of the Intuos4, so expect the nibs to wear more quickly. Though it has more texture it still feels very natural to me and I have no issue with writing on the surface. That said, why make it rougher so that it eats the nibs faster?

While the buttons along the side are configurable, I don't mess with them. I do use the scroll ring though and it works well. It is sensitive to light touch and so far has given me no trouble at all.

For a good graphics test I brought up Corel Painter and did a little doodling. The tablet and Painter work together quite well. Painter was able to determine at what angle I held the pen and it allowed me to make nice strokes and then reverse the pen to erase without any hassle. I really have not tried to push the tablet through all of Painter's features (which would do a great job of showcasing what the tablet can do) but I did enough to convince myself that the Intuos5 is a strong tool for the really artistic individual.

The Intuos4 has a small, no-frills 3-button mouse where the Intuos5 has touch features that make it work like a giant laptop touchpad. This comes down to personal preference. I never use the mouse on my Intuos4 but the touch features on the Intuos5 are very handy and convenient. Others may find the removal of the mouse to be a deal-breaker.

So far, the handwriting recognition seems to be about equivalent to that with the Intuos4. I have had to adjust my writing habits because of my using tablets for this, so a lot of the retraining took place long before the Intuos5 came. The recognition software does a reasonable job of reading my handwriting but it still makes mistakes and requires more patience.

The Intuos5 is a really nice pen tablet. It is comfortable, it is sensitive and it has two modes for accepting input. I question why Wacom placed the USB port on the outside edge of the tablet, and I also wonder why the surface is more rough than the Intuos4, but of all the current tablet offerings on the market right now this one is the best. It's not perfect, but it does try hard. I'm satisfied.

The laptop includes 3 free months of Xbox Game Pass, so I’ve played games available through that library. Games like Moonlighter, Moonglow Bay, Tunic, Sims 4, and Hades. The laptop handled all of those just fine, but many are older games and/or not very hardware intensive.

However, I don’t think 8GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD are enough. In my very first day of downloading games, I filled more than half the hard drive (and only ~236GB is available to start). As for the RAM, my 5-year-old laptop has 8GB of RAM and I’m feeling it. A laptop from 2022 should start with at least 16GB.

The Quad Vent fans vent in the back and on both sides of the laptop. I wish there wasn’t a vent on the right, because it’s right where the mouse sits. After maybe twenty to thirty minutes, my hand gets sweaty, which isn’t great when playing a competitive game.

There are 2 USB-A ports, one on each side. The back has an HDMI port, Ethernet, USB-C, and the power input. I actually really like the power input being on the back, as that way the cable isn’t in the way when using the mouse. But I’d like another USB-A port in the back, because I can see using a hub with this laptop.

The keyboard is not my favorite. On the plus side, it’s a full keyboard. I can’t remember the last time I saw a laptop with a numpad. The keyboard has backlighting, but only one color option: white. The keys are flat on top and somewhat slippery. The keyboard itself feels cramped, especially when gaming with WASD.

The laptop is heavy, about 7 or 8 pounds. It’s not something you’ll want to tote from class to class. The battery lasts about an hour if playing games, and about 3 hours for normal use.

With that said, the GL-AX1800(Flint) WiFi 6 Router is a disappointing product. In the last year, Openwrt has made setting up a mesh network of routers using 802.11r and 802.11s but only if you're running version 19.07 or higher. I wanted this router in the hopes that I can upgrade to WIFI 6 for my custom mesh network but I was sad to find that the variant of the firmware is based off version 15.

While gl.iNet has backported all of the necessary security patches from the newer kernels, it won't help the many power users who have come to depend on the new Openwrt version.

Bottom line is that nothing fixed the problem, despite my reformatting the hard drive, reinstalling Vista, and not installing anything else on the machine. Having outdoor safe speakers is essential for my household. Not only do I have audiophiles who are addicted to headphones and speakers, I have a husband who insists on taking his speakers to outdoor jobs. that is fine except when the job turns out to have a sudden rainstorm or high dust going on. Before giving it to him, I had our daughter put it through the grind at work (food prep) and in town events. Let's see how this speaker performs..

WHAT IS THIS SPEAKER LIKE?
This speaker is gray in color. The housing is very rubbery in consistency. The right side of the speaker has sealed controls under a rubberized pad over top of the buttons. The speaker stays put and is heavier than expected.

ON/OFF BUTTON/PAIRING
Holding down for over a second powers up the speaker. Next to the power button is the PAIRING button. This is not for pairing the speaker to a device but it is for pairing with another speaker just like it. A coworker with my daughter has this speaker and they tested it out- works GREAT so you now get two synced speakers.

CALLS BUTTON
You can send and receive calls with this button. You can also access your voice commands on your phone with this button.

VOLUME BUTTON
This is plus or minus sound controls. You can also skip by holding down- + is forward, - is backward.

PAUSE/PLAY
You can control pausing and playing with this button.

DOCKING
USB for charging, mini USB port (to use to charge a device if need be), and auxiliary outlet for like an old MP3 player or other device that does not have Bluetooth capability.

CHARGING INDICATOR LIGHT
Red when charging and turns white when fully charged. Will indicate when the power is running low so you will know.

SOUND QUALITY
Sound quality with this is very good. My daughter has a coworker with the same speaker so they both have had a chance to experiment with their speakers. So far it has been a great speaker. The balance of the recording of course affects the speaker, but so far it has not been overly muffled, out of balance, etc. Where you put the speaker affects how it sounds too.

When put on the floor, it really does sound better than on, say top of a box, or couch, etc. A very hard surface seems to really make it sound best.

VOLUME
When using the volume controls on the speaker, the sound is better than when you use the volume controls on the device (tablet, phone, etc).

DURABILITY
This speaker was taken to a huge town chicken and biscuit dinner and was dropped and still is working perfectly.

BATTERY
Two 10 hour shifts at full volume, and this speaker kicked through it all before needing to be recharged.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a really nice durable speaker that is dustproof, shock proof, and supposedly water proof, this is a good choice. It is solid, has decent sound , and even can be synced with another speaker if you get two of these for coverage around a room.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is a decent speaker, and I feel more comfortable having my husband use this on his jobs than the other really nice speaker he was beating up.

I have worked with a lot of ANC headphones, and I have a different pair of JVC phones that have served me well. I looked to these phones as a possible replacement for a dead pair of Bose QC-15 phones that finally just wore out. These are good phones that balance sound quality and ANC nicely.

The ANC function is what interested me most about these and I set about testing them. These work very well but they are not as aggressive as Bose or Sony when it comes to actively cancelling out low-frequency noise. This is a good thing in most cases as the aggressive ANC on Bose and Sony is actually uncomfortable when turned on. Where the two bigger players go all-out for maximum ANC function, these go for "good enough for most" and in terms of how they compare against other manufacturers such as Sennheiser, Philips, and other well-known brands they compare well. They cancel out the lion's share of low droning noises such as road noise and fans, enough so that turning on music at low volumes is still workable in noisy environments.

The sound profile is another important consideration and I have seen a wide variance in sound quality, particularly among ANC phones. These get the sound profile fairly close to right which is a refreshing change. The bass is present and strong but isn't pushed forward as with so many other headphones. The midrange is warm and gives music a decent depth. The highs are clear and bright without being shrill. These aren't audiophile quality phones by any means, but they are better than many I have used.

These are over-the-ear phones which is my preference. I also like that these fit snugly and don't slip off whern I look down which is also a personal preference but it's important to me. If you like a very light set of phones these probably are not quite the right fit for you; if you like a set that fits a bit more firmly, these are good in that regard.

These are comfortable too. The ear cups are padded nicely and I can wear them for a couple of hours before I need to take them off for a few minutes. Most headphones I have worn get uncomfortable after a while, and these do also but it is not as quick as with many.

My one complaint is the way these are powered on and off. Instead of a simple on/off button or switch, the cans swivel to power them on and off. I can see the potential for taking them off and leaving them powered on, resulting in reduced useful runtime.

I like these phones and have been working with them quite a bit of late. They're not a complete replacement for more aggressive ANC phones but they get the sound profile right and they are comfortable enough to wear for a long flight. These strike a nice balance between comfort, ANC capability and sound quality.

You should know up front that this extender only works wirelessly with dual-band WiFi routers (routers with both 2.4GHz and 5GHz).

But it will work as a hard-wired range extender for single-band routers (2.4GHz) using an ethernet cable.

If you have a single band router like we do, it will not detect the wireless network or connect wirelessly. If our neighborhood is any indication, this extender won't work with most home routers. Out of the ten or so visible wireless networks in our area, the extender only detected one or two. The two it detected were two of the weaker signals, but I assume were dual band signals the extender would work with.

After several frustrating attempts to get it connected wirelessly, I spent about an hour with customer support before being informed of this limitation on the extender. The product listing says "compatible with all Wi-Fi routers," and it may be compatible with all routers if set up as a wired extender, but apparently it isn't compatible with all as a wirelessly connected extender. If you want wireless connection to your router, check your router's capability and make sure it is a dual-band router before ordering.

As I mentioned, I did get it set up as a wire-connected extender using an ethernet cable. And it works well for that. It puts a good strong WiFi signal all over our house and much of the yard. I'm giving it four stars for that.

I use messenger bags as book bags to take books and tools to and from work every day. I favor canvas bags because they are tougher than nylon and they are a bit more masculine-looking. This particular messenger bag is a little more stylish than some of the others I have seen and so far I am happy with it.

A messenger bag is characterized by the fold-over flap that snaps closed over the main compartment. This particular bag has a very colorful and decorative weave that makes up the entire flap and the result is a softer and more supple flap than if it had been made of the same canvas material as the rest of the bag. That is not a fault or imperfection by any means but needs to be mentioned as a difference. Compared to the flap, the rest of the bag is more coarse and rigid.

Everything about this bag suggests quality. The stitching is very tight and the materials are even and there are no imperfections (nicks and cuts) that I can find on this bag. The stitching used to attach the shoulder strap to the metal loops on the bag, as well as to attach the leather trim to the canvas, is visibly thicker and stronger than what was used to hold the canvas portions of material together. I like the fact that there is some manner of reinforcement on the bottom of the bag (stitched inside so it is hard to know exactly what kind of reinforcement was used).

Instead of actual snaps, the flap is attached to the front of the bag using magnets. These make it a lot easier to open and close the bag.

In the main compartment of this bag are three pockets, one zippered and two smaller pockets that are open on the top. The smaller pockets are ideal for cell phones, small note pads, a calculator and the like while the larger pocket is big enough to accommodate a checkbook or a small book; it is not quite wide enough to handle a DVD case. There is a front pocket that is just barely wide enough to handle a 10” tablet (though I would put a tablet in the main compartment instead). Finally, there is a zippered pocket on the back that is slightly more narrow than the front pocket because of the zipper and is good for papers and maps.

This is a nice messenger bag and I like it. It is made very well, it is spacious enough to handle a couple of technical books and it looks nice.

The build quality as well as the fit and finish of this amplifier board is better than most of the cheap TPA3116 bluetooth boards on eBay and AliExpress. When connected to decent speakers and a 24V switching power supply with sufficient current drive capability, the performance of this amplifier is quite impressive for its size.

Four potentiometers in the front, from left to right are: bass level, treble level, treble volume (volume for the two stereo channels) and overall volume. These pots, as well as the speaker outputs in the back are clearly labeled on the PCB. Tone and volume control circuit appears to use a couple of 072 opamps and an SGM358 opamp. These are not high-grade audio components, simply a low cost solution for a product in this price range. Except for the electrolytic capacitors, most components are SMD.

I tested this amp by connecting it to a pair of Sound Appeal 6.5" 2-way bookshelf speakers for the stereo channels. I did not have access to a passive subwoofer at the time, so I connected the subwoofer output to a 15" bass guitar amplifier speaker cabinet. I used a 24V 5A switching power supply. A 24V 5A power supply may not be sufficient if you are driving 4-ohm speakers and a 4-ohm or lower impedance subwoofer, but all three of the speakers I used were 8 ohms, so 120W of power input was sufficient. With the right speaker setup, the volume output of this set-up can get quite high, even in a big room. Partly due to the efficiency of the 15" bass speaker I was using, it was possible to achieve a quite impressive "thump". Distortion levels are not low at high volume levels, but having the subwoofer output on a separate TPA3116 chip makes it possible to keep somewhat reasonable distortion on stereo channels even when playing bass-heavy music.

Connecting to the bluetooth interface was easy and straight-forward. The amp remembers the previous bluetooth pairing after being powered down.

A few observations about the shortcomings of this amplifier:
- The heat sinks are quite small, and they don't have any mechanical support. Even when driving 8-ohm loads, the heat sinks get really warm at high volume levels. If you are driving 4-ohm speakers at high volume levels, thermal shut-down is possible. If you are using a 18V or lower power supply, you probably won't have any thermal issues.
- There is only a 1000uF 25V filter capacitor at the power input. 25V max rating is a bit too close for my comfort, I would have preferred a 35V capacitor. You really need a well regulated DC power supply to drive this board.
- Bluetooth has a built in antenna on the PCB, but no external antenna interface, making it impossible to mount this board inside a metal case without doing some surgery to the board.
- There are no line level inputs. Bluetooth is the only input option unless you are willing to do modifications on the PCB

Overall, for the current price of $26.99, this is a very nice bluetooth 2.1 amplifier. If you have a couple of decent bookshelf speakers and an old subwoofer lying around, the volume and quality of the sound you can achieve with this amp will be better than any integrated bluetooth system that sells for less than $100.

Update: I recently tested this amp with [[ASIN:B00NOA58RS Dayton Audio B652-AIR 6-1/2" Bookshelf Speaker Pair with AMT Tweeter]]. These speakers are 6-ohms, so it's possible to get a little power out of the amplifier, and especially the high frequencies sound noticeably better.

When it comes to radios, so many of them just don't have the reception that they used to. I came across this one and decided it was worth the try. Unfortunately, the battery choice is annoying, but let's take a look at the radio..

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This is a pretty straightforward radio. It has AM and FM. Each band has a horizontal dial on it. The volume button is large and turns the radio on and off as well. You can adjust the tone from high to low which will either focus on voice or on base tones for what you are listening to.

HANDLE
The handle on this is sturdy and easy to carry.

ANTENNA
The antenna on this is sturdy and easy to pull out and push in.

JACK
There is a standard headphone jack.

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM?
This performs beautifully. The reception is exceptional and I can pull in stations that most other newer radios do not pull in any more. The sound is fabulous with a lot of depth to it.

BATTERIES
I really dislike that this takes 4 D batteries. Those batteries are expensive and tend to run out quickly. I don't normally carry them in the house for emergencies, but it would be worth having some since this radio is great and easy to hear.

WHO MIGHT LIKE THIS RADIO?
Anyone who loves to listen to AM still would love this radio. Many of them don't have it anymore which is frustrating. I also found that it is great for older people to have one of these. I know an older gentleman who has been bed ridden and home bound and he loves this radio. It is easy to operate, see, and great sound.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I like this radio. It is good to have on hand for emergencies or for good listening when internet is down or I just am tired of the internet radio channels and prefer to be local. The sound is great and operation easy. Fabulous reception.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is a perfect gift for older people or those who really enjoy local radio and prefer an easy to use radio that has great reception. Just be sure to have D batteries for emergencies. If it had rechargeable features, it would be perfect!

The Defender GK300- 7M2 Hands Free 2- wire color video intercom system is a relatively inexpensive intercom system designed to provide peace of mind with minimum hassle. This device is simple enough to install and is instantly ready to use with the flick of a switch.

Besides the simple setup, this monitor has some other interesting features that make it useful. I really like the night vision option because it makes visible what would otherwise be difficult to make out. I like the sound- it is easy to tell exactly what is being said- and I like the loud, easily noticeable chime when someone rings the doorbell. The fifty- foot cable is also nice because it is long enough that I was able to place the viewing monitor in my bedroom with no problem.

As for the cons, I can find a few. The video quality isn't the greatest- it is a little fuzzy, even though I can still tell who is on the screen. Then, there is the duration of the video- it displays for only about thirty to thirty- five seconds. After that, the screen goes blank and you have to keep pressing the video button to get it back. This latter feature is one I wish was different. Often, you will want to watch and listen to the person at the door, but because you have to remember to keep pressing the video button, you could easily miss something important.

This is a basic intercom unit, hence the average quality overall. I know there are more sophisticated products on the market, but they all cost several times more than this, the Defender GK300- 7M2 intercom. The plugs have a protective rubber boot guard that protects the clip on the plug - this becomes very important when snaking the cable through walls and tight spaces. Prior to doing this I wrap the boot and plug with a small piece of electrical tape to make sure I don’t unintentionally snag anything.

I love the white PVC shielding on this cable - not only is it durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it can be run along a wall and then painted to match the wall color.

I used this 100 foot cable to run between my router to a PoE switch that branches to several power and transmit data to and from one zone of my security cameras - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

This has proven to be an outstanding, dependable Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love. This is a purchase that you’ll never regret.

I'm a big fan of the Mi Band series of trackers, and this is the first device that finally got me to switch to something else. If you aren't familiar, Xiaomi and Huami aren't big brands in the US compared to other countries, but these are solid high quality products and not your standard fare Chinese junk. I've tried a LOT of different fitness trackers and smart watches- Everything from Google WearOS, Fitbit, Apple, and all the way down to the cheap trackers from Chinese throwaway brands with obscure apps. For a long time I've said I liked the features and quality of the expensive brands, but found they all had major flaws (battery life being a major one- I don't want another thing to charge as often as a phone!). The Mi band from Xiaomi was super affordable and high quality compared to others in that price range, and had a battery that only required being charged once a month.
This is basically the smarter older brother of that band. It is compatible with Mi Fit, so all my data transferred right over, but it is so much nicer than the band. For starters, the notification system is easier to read and keep up with messages, but the benefits go far beyond a larger screen. The music control is a nice touch, I like being able to pause and adjust the volume without taking my phone out of my pocket if playing on a BT speaker while I'm doing dishes, for example. The tracking is pretty accurate compared to other expensive brands, and while it doesn't support apps like Wear OS and Apple Watches, it has all the fitness functions you'd need built in already, including some fun widgets beyond the expected ones like a stopwatch, phone finder and even a compass! And unlike cheap brands, the UI is responsive and smooth. Not the smoothest out there for sure, but more than acceptably smooth considering how much a flagship smartwatch costs compared to this.
It has support for voice commands, but I honestly found that feature kind of gimmicky more than useful. The higher end version of this includes a speaker which might make the command function more useful as sort of a digital assistant, not to mention the ability to take phone calls from your wrist. But the model I got to try out lacks the speaker, which is a fine compromise for a cheaper price tag all things considered. The battery life at first was just OK, a few days on a charge if using lift-to-wake functions, but just as on my Mi Band tracker of old, I found if I turn off auto-wake and rely on using the button to wake the display, the battery life goes from counting in days to counting in weeks. That's the killer feature of this device- the ability to leave it on to track fitness and sleep habits without having to charge it so often. I'll have to charge it more than my old Mi Band's monthly top up for sure, probably at least 2x a month, but that's still very manageable.
So that's it, after years of loving my Mi Bands and considering it the standard by which all practical fitness trackers should be judged, I'm finally moving on to an Amazfit watch. This is a difficult value to beat.

Our antenna rotor broke and for 3 years we have been waiting for new chips to come through so we could get another one. It has taken WAY too long. I got this to help with the problem in the meanwhile. What I got was MORE problems.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes in a blister pack. It has a long cord and a double tail plug on it. The idea is that you put the plug into the antenna spot on the TV and the other is a USB port that you put into your TV. There is a sticker to put this on the wall and instructions.

HOW THIS WORKS
I have had no end of frustration with this thing. We do not have an OLD TV but we do not have any USB ports in this that work with the antenna. The outlets are such that I can not fit ANY adapters into the plug to use an adapter for the USB. The cord from the USB to the intersection where the antenna cord is is very short- only 13 inches. Put that together with the other cord for the antenna which is also about 13 inches and you can not spread them tightly so you only have about 22 to 24 inches tops to get from the TV on the wall down to a USB outlet if you don't have USB on your TV.

I TRIED TO MAKE THIS WORK
I have tried many different USB adapters to get this to work and none of them will work with this unit. I am frustrated and have spent so much time on this, I am giving up. I really wanted this to work, but despite this being an HDTV, it just isn't working out with this unit. I guess we will have to go without antenna TV on that TV longer.

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you have USB available on your TV and an antenna hook up, this might work for you. If you don't have a USB port that will work with this unit, you will have to have an available plug that has USB conversion in it, or USB on a power strip that is not more than 24 inches away from the antenna jack on the TV to make it work. You can also use an extension cord and adapter, but honestly, it is a lot of expense for a unit that might or might not work as you like.

MY RATING
THREE STARS. I can not give this a terrible rating like I want to in my frustration. To be fair, three stars is about right. I do not like that it does not come with adapters or alternatives for TVs. Most people who watch antenna TV do not always have the newest equipment. We happen to have this TV that needs the hookup. We have another TV which is newer but the picture is not that great and we already have it set up with another antenna hookup.

I would like this a LOT better if it came with a streamlined USB plug adapter for the power outlets.

UPDATES
If by some miracle, I can find a USB adapter that will fit in this situation and actually WORK, I will update this review and reconsider the rating. For now, it stays as it is. I have put enough time and resources into trying to make this work.

I have a Fuji X-T3 and I have not shied away from third-party lenses at all. I have been looking for good wide-angle lenses and I have been aware of TTArtisan for a while. I was curious how well this lens would perform and I decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it though I am still working with it and learning that it can do.

This lens is a brick! Right out of the box I was startled at the overall weight. It has a lot of glass in it, but it also is all metal - very little (if any) plastic. Even the front lens cap is metal. In spite of the price, this is a solid little lens.

It is probably the tightest fit lens I have used. It requires a little pressure to get it to click into place and to remove it later when mounting on the camera body. I was a little concerned at first, thinking I could potentially damage the camera. However, it does fit and does not harm the camera in spite of how tightly it fits.

Optical quality seems to be good, though that varies a little with the aperture setting. At the widest settings (and f/1.4 in particular) there is a little softness in the corners and a slight vignetting. As the aperture is closed more the image gets sharper at the edges. This is not unusual or unexpected for wide-angle large-aperture lenses, and it is actually slightly better than I was expecting.

I have not yet had a chance to get out and determine the coma with this lens. I am waiting for a clear night so I can get a starry sky shot with the aperture wide open, which will highlight not only the coma but also the chromatic characteristics. If it is particularly bad I will come back and update.

As a portrait or landscape lens this one works very well. Initial exposures have worked out well, but I am still learning what this lens can do.

Are there better wide-angle lenses out there? Sure - and they cost a lot more too. For the price this lens is far better than expected and I am looking forward to working with it more. It is good enough that I am staring to look at other TTArtisan offerings.

I ordered the iHome Alexa Built-in Bluetooth Speaker Portable Wireless Waterproof Rechargeable Lights Up to Music, with Speakerphone, Passive Subwoofer, Carry Strap, Durable Shockproof Floatable Design (IBT158) to replace an old sub par portable speaker that I’ve had for years. The iHome is quite the upgrade with the built in Alexa, better sound and being waterproof. I’ve had this product now for several weeks and would like to share my thoughts.

I must say that the sound is pretty good and packs a punch in such a small size. It’s much better than the much smaller and several years old portable wireless speaker that I have been using. In fact there really is no comparison at all. Let’s just say that it is the best sounding portable wireless speaker that I personally have ever owned. My daughter who “borrowed” the older speaker some time ago (and she never gave it back) keeps asking to "borrow" the new iHome as she says, “it’s louder and sounds WAY better”. I absolutely agree with her. Plus the lights on this thing are a nice touch, and there are options (via a button on top) to cycle through and change the color options or turn them off.

Setting up the iHome for Bluetooth and Alexa was easy and very straight forward, and there has been no issues whatsoever. We are mainly an Android household however my oldest daughter uses an iPhone and everyone has had the same great experience. So far my only complaint is that the Bluetooth connectivity distance isn’t the greatest but with that said, none of my Bluetooth devices really have much range in our home so I am not going to knock points off for that. The sound out of this little guy makes up for the Bluetooth short comings and the bonus of Alexa being packed into this as well as the waterproof features make this a great value for the selling price.

One thing worth mentioning is that to use Alexa, you can’t just say “Alexa” to activate her. You do have to physically press a button on the iHome speaker to access her, which isn’t a huge deal breaker, but because of this, you can’t use other Alexa devices to make an announcement and have it broadcast to the iHome speaker. Being fairly new to the Alexa and smart home world, I am not going to hold this shortcoming against the iHome device. It actually makes sense that with this being portable, you wouldn’t want to have Alexa always listening and drain the battery while on the go. Speaking of Battery life, it's decent but not spectacular by any means. This is pretty subjective however as usually when I use the iHome, I'm listening to it at a pretty high volume ;)

Another observation is that this uses micro USB to charge, and I really would like to see more devices using the newer and better USB C charging capabilities.

As far as the “waterproof” capabilities go, I must report that I have yet to float the device in a pool or let the kids play with it outside while running through the sprinklers. I know that it says it’s waterproof and it absolutely looks like it would hold up to getting wet as it is very well built, rugged and quite solid, but I don't want to risk ruining this new toy that the whole family has been enjoying so much.

That's great because the thermal paper is super cheap, you can buy any brand that fits physically in the machine- although this camera comes with plenty of rolls to get you started (which is more than some of the big brand insta-cams offer! It says it fits a Nikon D800, but when mounted, the D800 is too tall, barely fitting under the overhead grip arm.

The overhead arm does not extend forward enough to allow the camera to balance, even with the camera mounted all the way to the rear of the baseplate. Thus, even when I'm holding just the front two inches under the hot shoe mount, the camera when mounted with a heavy zoom lens like the 24-70 f/2.8, tilts down. A lighter, shorter lens works better, but you still cannot hold the unit by the foam grip handle without your knuckles scraping the camera's hot shoe mount.

The entire device is of molded ABS plastic and is somewhat flexible in a "springy" way. It appears strong, but remember, your multi-thousand dollar investment is hanging by that little joint in the back of the base plate. If it breaks, it's curtains. You might want to have a safety lanyard attached to a neck strap lug that attaches to your wrist, just in case.

The sleds on the bottom are nice. When you put it down, it's stable, although I had to re-superglue one of the padded inserts on one of the sled rails.

The camera mounting screw is well designed and easy to use, but for some reason, is too long. The threads bottomed out in my camera and would not hold the camera tight. I had to remove the thumb screw and add a washer on the underside of the base effectively shortening the threads. I could have ground off 1/16" or so, too. Not a big deal, but out of the box it didn't work.

One thing's for sure: you need a strong arm to hold this for any amount of time if you have a heavy lens attached. If you are working with a lightweight SLR and a lightweight lens, it's much easier. And seeing the viewfinder is a real problem. And forget about focusing. If you mount a remote electronic viewfinder on the upper hot shoe, it's much easier to see what you're shooting, but now you've added even more weight and your arm will die. (True steadicams went with vests and spring-assisted arms for this reason years ago.)

Overall, the sled is a simple, inexpensive method to hold a camera from above and does smooth out motion well. It's a worthy gizmo to have in your bag.

UPDATE: I attached my Canon HFS-100 HD camcorder to this sled and have never taken it off. It is absolutely the best accessory ever! Perfectly balanced. The overhead handle allows excellent control and fabulous low angle positioning when capturing kids or animals on the floor. The camera's flip-out viewfinder is the key, something the D800 sorely lacks.

This case was recommended in several build guides, and seemed to be highly rated on Amazon, but I must say I'm quite disappointed.

Pros:
(1) It does the job. It's roomy -- in fact, it's really big. There's room for a really big graphics card without taking out any drive cages.
(2) Comes with four quiet fans (2 intakes in front, one large intake on the side, one exhaust on the back), and room to add more on the top.
(3) Having a couple of usb3 ports and audio/mike ports in the front is very convenient. Having the power supply at the bottom (in the back) also worked well for me.
(4) All the bits come apart and back together without too much trouble.

Cons:
(1) I had a lot of trouble getting my EVGA power supply to install, because the screw holes didn't line up nicely. Finally managed it by using a combination of power and adapting to what the case gave me.
(2) The 5.25 drive bays go in the conventional way, with the backs near the mobo for easy connections. But the 2.5/3.5 drive bays go in sideways, which might seem convenient at first, but now you have their connectors on the other side of the box -- so you're threading your power and sata cables around, and creating a bulge of cables etc. And that extra wiring room that the case promises? It doesn't extend all the way to the front, apparently the artists overcame the engineers (or they fought and the users lost). This arrangement also means that it's harder to share your sata power cables, depending on what you're trying to do with your setup.
(3) As others have pointed out, those nice intake fans aren't standard, they would be hard to replace individually. I'd have to replace all of them with standard case fans, I think.
(4) I wasn't as impressed with the cable management as many others were -- while it was useful to be able to run some wires on the back, that also made some of the shorter ones trickier to connect. Also, I find it easiest to place the box down on the side to work on the inside. Having to flip it over or keep it standing vertical wasn't my idea of convenience during assembly, and it made things really tricky when I wanted to add another hdd.

Neutral:
(1) An inexpensive mini-speaker (for POST beeps) would have been a good idea to include with the box.

All in all, I'm not unhappy enough to curse it, but I'm also far from recommending it. I'd look around more the next time, so 3* seems about right.

This review covers two different models of the Arctic fan:

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>Model with USB hub:
I have been using the original ARCTIC Breeze for a while and have been very pleased with its performance, and especially pleased with how quiet it runs. The Pro model builds on that and adds a few more useful features.

Unlike the original model which had a bendable stem with a USB plug on the end, the Pro has a base so the fan can be positioned away from the USB port on the PC. The attached power cord is a little over 5 feet long, making it possible to put the fan on my desk and plug it into the PC on the floor.

The base also has 4 USB input ports, so it works as a USB hub. It has a 5V power input jack if you want to turn this into an active hub. The power adapter to do so is NOT included.

Unlike the single-speed original version, this has a knob so you can vary the speed. It's not precise, but there is a somewhat noticeable difference between low and high. It's a continually variable speed - you can turn the dial to whatever speed you like.

Best of all, it's just as quiet, if not quieter, than the original model. That's the biggest plus for me by far, since the cheap USB fans make a racket. This just makes a low-pitched hum. The build quality is solid - the base is sturdy, and the bendable arm holds its position well.

One negative: the packaging. It's in a clam shell package that is a major, major pain to open!

While it's more expensive than the original, the added benefits of being able to position it on a desk and use it as a hub makes the upgrade worth considering. Highly recommend.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>USA EDITION:
I've have (and use) a couple other Arctic USB fans and have been 100% satisfied with them. This new version (their "USA Edition") has a couple of improvements over past designs.

The base is a metal plate which increases the fan's stability when you're bending the stem to point the fan. The on/off/speed dial switch no longer has a lit LED ring around it. I never found the lit LED ring to be bothersome on the other Arctic fans, so having or not having it is not a big deal to me.

The base also does away with the USB hub connections that other models have. That's keeps the base more streamlined and allows it to have a lower profile. It also does away with the clam shell packaging, instead using a very easy to open box.

The build quality of this, like the other Arctic fans I have, is excellent. The stem is bendy by stays put where you want it; the operating sound is pretty hushed; the on/off/speed control works well. The overall design is attractive, with a red/white/blue color scheme and graphics.

It moves a surprising amount of air. No, it won't blow your hair back as a Vornado fan will, but this makes a noticeable difference in circulating air. The size makes it very easy to find a spot on your desk to position it.

While I can't speak to the long-term reliability of this as of yet, I expect it will last for some time. I have an Arctic fan similar to this that I've been using almost daily for the past 1+ years, and it still works as good as it did when new.

Looks good, works well, and easy to use. Highly recommend.

I’m a big fan of the Roar since it provides me with two key benefits: great sound and is easy to use. The Roar 2 retains those two benefits and adds one more: a smaller footprint. I’m going to try my best to not overuse the words “outstanding” and "impressive" in this review, but it’s going to be a challenge. This is an impressive speaker.

The out-of-the-box experience is nicely done. As expected at this price point, it comes in upscale packaging. More important, it comes with a pretty decent user guide. That’s significant since the Roar 2 has a lot of features – to call it just “a speaker” really shortchanges it. It’s also a recorder, a power bank, an MP3 player, an SD card reader, a speakerphone – it will even lull you to sleep with Bedtime Mode where it gradually decreases the volume and then powers off. My only complaint about the manual is that it’s physically small, which means the type size is also small. I do wish manufacturers would realize that those of us with aging eyes still like loud music!

And loud music is this product’s forte. I’m able to get room-filling sound while maintaining crisp highs, clear midrange and solid but not muddy bass. I can even go past room-filling to the “let’s annoy the neighbors” levels and still maintain impressive fidelity. Using the Tera Bass option boosts the bass response to the point where you would swear there was a separate subwoofer on the floor. You can see the end plates resonate to help drive the bass (plus it just looks really cool as well).

Day to day usage of the Roar 2 is straightforward even though there are so many features. All the buttons are labeled fairly clearly, albeit at times with small type. I would also have preferred a greater contrast to the labels since sometimes they are hard to see unless the Roar 2 is under a bright light. There are voice prompts for many key features which I found helpful. Normally I don’t care for voice prompts, but these were done in a natural sounding voice at a low volume making them not at all irritating. But, if you don’t like them at all, you can turn them off. There are small, but clear indicator lights to keep you apprised of battery charge level, settings, and other criteria.

The build quality is excellent. This feels as good as it looks, with a solid heft to it, an excellent quality metal grill, and quality plastic case components. All the buttons have a good tactile feel to them. I have it in white, which looks very nice with the gray contrast control pad. My only quibble is that some of the buttons/levers are on the small side. However, those tend to be the lesser used function. The main function buttons (on/off, volume, pairing, Tera Bass, etc.) are larger and easy to use.

The Roar 2 is not inexpensive, but the performance, build quality and features make it an excellent value. If you enjoy great sound and need to keep to a small footprint speaker, these should absolutely be on your short list (and at the top of it by a wide margin). Highly, highly recommend.

First of all, these speakers sound just great, they really do. I'll echo the comments that the cords are an awkward design, depending on where you place them in relation to your sound source and listening position.

The power on-off button is on the top of the subwoofer, but the volume up-down control is on one of the satellites. And the sub's level control is on the sub itself. Aside from just plain being a bit weird, it means you're going to have to keep both the sub and one of the satellites within easy reach. Also, the cord that connects to your sound source is attached to the sub (as is the power cord); combined with the controls on the sub, this is just plain awkward. I'm using these speakers at work, and I have the sub on the floor under my desk. I'm controlling the volume from iTunes, so that's cool. But it would be very annoying if I had to be using the speaker's controls all the time.

A minor annoyance is the shape of the metal legs for the satellites. They are sturdy and look nice, but they take up much more space on my crowded desk than I'd like. Other speaker systems use more vertically shaped satellite stands, which take up half the space. These satellites are much more squat.

I also have one of the better Logitech 2.1 systems, which also sounds great. But Logitech puts all the controls on a little control unit that you can keep in easy reach. (And also has a headphone output too.) That's a much more convenient design. But between the two, the sound of these Altec Lansing speakers is superior.

Here's the dealmaker for me -- the bass control on the subwoofer can be turned all the way down, so the sub isn't putting out any sound at all. This is a great feature because it lets me play just the satellites late at night, and I'm not disturbing my housemate in the adjoining room.

I am specifically using these to step up 3v to either 5v (for USB devices) or 12v (for a strip of LEDs). I've set up two so far, and they work pretty well. The pot is very sensitive, so that you can bump it up by tenths of a volt or less. The pads are pretty easy to solder to. The power delivery is relatively clean, I have some flicker on the LED strip, but that seems to resolve itself fairly rapidly - for sensitive applications you might want to run through a capacitor to clean things up a bit.

The unit is moderately efficient, but becomes quite warm - when converting from 2xAAA Lithium batteries (3v) to 12v, with an approximate draw of 200mA the converter (both the top of the transformer and bottom of the board) temps at about 116F within three minutes or so of operation. Pretty warm, warmer than I would typically like. I might try hooking up a 9v instead to see if this knocks the temps down a bit, or if that fails, adding a thermistor to mitigate the risk of a thermal event.

Would recommend for general experimentation though.

Every other speaker sounds like pillows are blocking the sound. lol. I have had friends say that same line to me a few times. The sound is very different from other speakers. Looks like I have the privilege of being the first person to review the BA M25 speakers. I picked up a pair of these on Christmas Eve and have been playing them constantly over the past 2 weeks. My focus has been on 2 channel stereo recordings instead of movies. My set up is through an older Denon AVR 610 receiver that I have had for almost 20 years. I was initially impressed with the smooth, balanced feel of these speakers. Good mid range, nice high end, but not too bright, and a very strong bass response. The M25s defy their size in producing bass tones. Give them some break in time before making a final assessment. These speakers excel at producing music performed on real instruments. The do a great job on jazz, blues and acoustic folk styles of music. Vocals come across nicely as well.
Boz Scaggs "But Beautiful" CD of standards sounds great. Upright bass, piano and vocals make you feel like you are in a small jazz club. Diana Krall "Live in Paris" also plays very well. Nice piano, guitar & vocal reproduction. Jorma Kaukonen's "Blue Country Heart" CD showcases some great finger style acoustic guitar. Very natural acoustic guitar tones. Linda Ronstadt's "Winter Light" CD has some of the most powerful vocals you will ever hear and the M25s reproduce Linda's voice and backing instrumentation extremely well. The sound is never strained or harsh. Initially, I was a bit more apprehensive on some CDs with lots of bass. They sounded like they were trying to overcompensate on bass, but this has evened out over the past week. Eric Clapton's "Pilgrim" CD has come serious bottom end and the M25s produce very deep, tight bass response. Peter Gabriel "So" is a similar story. Deep, tight bass response that does not bottom out. Paul Rogers "Muddy Waters Blues" is a treat on the M25s. The opening track features some acoustic delta blues guitar, followed by a chorus of female backup singers and later some nice Strat blues guitar tones. It all sounds great on these speakers.
The look and finish on the speakers is impressive also. They are finished in a polished black exterior with a leatherette finish on the top, back & bottom. They look like a piece of fine furniture that would fit into a modern style of home décor. These speakers are very expensive though. I got a demo pair at less than half of the $399 per speaker list price. I don't think I would have bought them at full price. I have been listening to Boston Acoustics speakers for over 20 years. I still own a pair of A60s and a pair of A120s that have served me well over the years. The M25s have replaced the A120s as my primary speakers in my living room due to their sonic capabilities and their stylistic good looks.

Update 6/24/14 - After listening to these speakers for 6 months, I continue to be even more impressed by the Boston M25s. I bought these thinking they will do until I can find better. While there are better speakers out there, I have concluded, after many demo sessions, that I would need to spend at least $1500-$1800 or more to get some form of improvement over the M25s. Short of stepping up to KEF R300 @ $1800, B&W CM5 @ $1500 or Aperion Verus Towers, the M25s deliver the goods with very balanced & neutral sound, great detail in the upper register and sold bass. Highly recommended.

Like most of the other reviewers I received this as a review sample along with a [[ASIN:B00N38TQJC Sabrent Premium 4 Port Aluminum USB 3.0 Hub]]. This will actually work with just about any of Sabrent's hubs as well as most other 5 volt (DC) devices on the market that require up to 4 Amps of current.

The barrel connector comes with an adapter to a larger size barrel connector to cover Sabrent hubs. I have checked every source I could find to get the barrel connector specs, but none are to be found. This is frustrating to say the least because this is truly a multi-purpose power supply that can be used on non-Sabrent products. Since it is not claimed to be universal I am giving it five stars because it works perfectly with the hub with which I tested it.

One feature that I particularly like is the fact that the cable is heavy duty with good strain reliefs on both ends. This is not your typical, flimsy power supply cable. Another thing I like is this runs cool even with constant use. I am using it to power a hub with a disk drive and both the hub and this power supply are running cool even after a twenty-four hour period.

This is capable of providing up to four Amps, but will only 'push' what the device requires. What that means is if you are powering four devices that draw .6 Amps each this supply will only push 2.4 Amps, so there is no worry about overloading. On the other hand if you are attempting to power a hum that requires over 4 Amps this is not the proper power supply and will not work.

If you own a Sabrent powered hub this is a safe choice, Do make sure you know the total current draw of the devices into the hub and make sure that the total does not exceed four Amps.

I've been using both, and the main difference in usability is that the beanbag mount has a lower initial stability and higher reserve stability than the fold-flat mount.
In other words, the fold-flat will stay put better - until it breaks free, when it becomes completely free with no holding power. The beanbag is a little easier to get to shift on a bounce, but then it has enough mass to settle stably in its new position.
On the whole I prefer the beanbag as I'd rather have my GPS move around a little bit more than have it stay put better but then fly around uncontrolled.
Other differences are that the fold-flat mount is lighter and folds up smaller, much better suited to stowing away or traveling.
The fold-flat also lets the GPS vibrate more, the beanbag dampens vibrations, but this can be overcome by pushing the GPS down in the fold-flat mount until it stays in contact with the base.
These are great for projects where you are disconnecting items. Use them to mark hoses/connections, etc.

In order to try the over burn feature, I would need the appropriate disks that can normally hold 8.5 GB (DVD+R).  These disks are not too difficult to find online, but the office supply stores only seem to stock 4.7 GB disks.  I guess you either have to special order or buy online.  Most everything that I need to burn can either fit on a 4.7 GB DVD or can be compressed (without much loss of quality) to fit.  It may be false economy to buy the higher capacity disks, as they are nearly double the price of lower capacity.  With burnable media prices being so low anyway, you don't gain much by squeezing as much as you can on a particular disk.  So why did I get this drive?  I like to have a drive on the shelf if one goes bad (and they do sometimes), and then I don't have to wait for one to arrive.  I assumed it was probably good to have one that can burn to maximum capacity as this isn't much more expensive than a regular DVD burner.  Since I haven't actually installed or used the drive yet (waiting for disks), one should not pay as much attention to my review as some other reviewers.  I just wanted people to be aware that you can't insert a 4.7 GB disk and expect to over burn to 8.7 GB.  You need to understand the differences in available media and get the appropriate blank media. Update:  I finally received the appropriate media to test the drive.  It seemed to work good for the first 6 or 8 disks, but then 3 disks in a row had burn errors.  Bad media?  I don't think so; it appears the drive is failing already.  I'll test on another computer and see if it is the media or the drive and update the review again, but right now I can't recommend this drive at all.  UPDATE 2:  I tried this again after rebooting my computer and it now seems to work fine and does indeed overburn, so you can squeeze a lot on one disk.  When I had 3 bad burns in a row, I thought it was the burner, but it may have been bad media.  On the other hand, I suspect something flaky on my PC, as I have had bad burns before occasionally (not recently) and then after a reboot everything was fine again.  I may have too many programs loaded when I try to burn.  That's not the fault of the DVD drive.  Most likely the fault of the burning program (and I am using a major well-know program.)

This time I experimented to see if I could get Debian Linux distro running on the NVME on my older workstation.

It took a few tries. Getting the OS to boot directly from the NVME was a no-go. Since the NVME is mounted on an adapter card, I had hoped it would trick the system into thinking it was just an ordinary SATA drive and boot from it. But that didn't happen.

So what I did was installed all the Linux OS EXCEPT for the boot folder on the NVME, and put the boot folder on the SSD HDD. So it boots from the SSD but the entire OS is on the NVME and runs from it.

Step one:

The partition manager in the Debian installer didn't want to partition the NVME at first.

So I bailed out of it and used GParted (Gnome disks utility couldn't do this) to "create partition table" and selected msdos as type. That wiped everything and turned the whole drive into unallocated space. From that point the partition manager worked.

Step two:

From the linux bootable USB installer I partitioned the SSD (not the NVME) with a primary partition labeled (to be mounted) as /boot. (You can make this partition most any size from a few GB on up---the boot files don't require a lot of space.) The remaining space I manually labeled as /msc.

I partitioned the NVME so the installer would put everything else on it, starting with / (root). You can simply make the whole NVME / root and the installer will take care of putting everything else on that drive, or you can do what I did and set up size-defined partitions for /home, /usr, and so on.

After installing the system, the installer asks where you want the bootloader GRUB installed. I selected the SSD.

It worked. The SSD does the booting to the NVME, which then runs the OS. And it did improve speed.
