I use this to connect my MP3 player to a 3.5mm jack I installed in my car's center console. The low-profile 3.5mm connector was very important to me because I wanted to make the connection as slim as possible to avoid accidentally torquing it, catching things on it, or applying pressure to the jack when moving things in and out of the console.

It works quite well for this purpose. the connector is slim - about as slim as they come, such that it basically clamps right up against the side of the player and the wall of the console. The plug itself feels solid and has a small snap when connecting to things. The cable is soft and almost as flexible as a woven cord, even if it does prefer some orientations to others. Sound quality is typical - which is to say, as good as every other cable I've owned.

The only thing I didn't like about the cable was the colors - it really doesn't go with the car interior and stuck out as a result, a bit distracting. So I used a Sharpie Pro - the big chisel-tip type - to turn it black. It is cotton sheathing, so this is quite viable. I was careful - after inking the entire cable and letting it dry, I washed it in warm water, then dried it and ran a soft, clean rag over it about a hundred times, until it came away basically clean. After the fact, while you could tell the original black bits from the inked threads, it's just different shades of black, rather than looking blotchy. I imagine using something like RIT black dye would be about equally effective, if you heated it and let it soak for a good long while.

So I would recommend it. The braided cable looks premium and is much easier to work with than its equally-thick rubber counterparts. This makes it easy to handle the MP3 player while it is still plugged in.

This item is one version of the OSSC, and turns out it is not case-compatible with the official one, having several different components populated on the board, so it will not fit in the normal OSSC cases.

It is not at all confidence-inspiring that the manufacturer here deviated from the official board layout and component selection. The PSU is extremely cheap, and some things are just incorrect.

Some of the components I noticed were different are:

- the screen: The height of the screen is quite a bit lower than what's shown in pictures of the official OSSC, and on closer examination, it appears the screen was soldered to the wrong side of the board because of layout issues.
- the buttons: the buttons here have yellow nubs on top, but the official one has low profile tactile buttons. This is another point where 3D printed cases made for this (such as those sold by Laser Bear) will interfere with this OSSC, preventing the case from closing.
- The audio select switch: the switch is mounted to the bottom of the PCB instead of the top. There appear to be traces for the switch on the top of the PCB, but it's not clear why they were mounted to the bottom of the board. Again, this is an issue because cases will have allowance for this switch, and expect the switch to be located on the top of the PCB.

Given that these components were swapped or moved, I can't be certain about the rest of the component choices, and given how cheap the power supply is, I'm not confident at all that the manufacturers here prioritized quality over price in any way whatsoever.

Then, somehow, after a few weeks of being in this mode, suddenly it "got well" again and the battery would show its charge and charge correctly for a few months. This is the first Logitech keyboard I've gotten, and now I see why Logitech is considered to be a proficient manufacturer in keyboards and other computer-related paraphernalia.

Without installing any such programs or software, either from the website or from the included disc, I plugged in the USB receiver right out of the box, followed the easy-to-setup instructions engraved on the back of the keyboard, and away I went. I was able to type flawlessly at the office, and the keys are very smooth and quiet. Even though it's just a keyboard, I kept opening up different programs to test out the typing. Pure joy! (For a nerd like me, at least.)

I guess the only gripes I have, and I noticed it almost immediately, is that there are no lights to indicate locks for the numbers, caps, or scroll. It's a minor gripe, but a gripe nonetheless since I have to utilize the Caps Lock every so often at work.

When I used the extra buttons for various computer software, I found that the respected programs opened up right away. There was some stall, but that was the result of my slow, crunching computer.
The mouse worked just as it should.

Now, I have to admit, what I really wanted to get this keyboard for was my Wii at home. I know, it sounds nerdy.
But the keyboard I was using before was an old office wired one that was given to me. That one worked fine, but I wanted a wireless one. So, I took home this MK300 keyboard and USB receiver, plugged in the latter into the back of my Wii console, opened up the Internet Channel and found, to my delight, that the keyboard worked flawlessly.
There was some range betwixt the keyboard and receiver--about ten feet or so--but it made no matter: my sitting spot isn't too far from the console, so it's not like I'm going to be typing in a completely different room.

Since this keyboard works so well, I was hoping to use it on a Mac. I've yet to buy the MacBook Pro--which is why I'm stuck with the Wii's Internet Channel for now--and since the specifications for this certain keyboard doesn't include Apple's OS, I'm assuming that there is simply no way around hardware setups (ever tried?) and will have to resort to something else, when the time comes.

All in all, though, if you're looking for an excellent wireless (not Bluetooth) keyboard at a relatively inexpensive price tag for any PC machine or Wii, look no further. The MK300 works like a charm.

For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

A seller replaced a different defective FM transmitter unit with this one for me (mine has the Kollea brand name on it, but this is the identical unit, private-labeled). This is a better product than what it replaced, but is not without it's flaws. I have three (*UPDATE: now four, and the fourth one is a deal-breaker--see below) complaints with this unit:

1) It will not automatically reconnect to my phone about 75% of the time. I have to manually shut Bluetooth off and turn it back on on the phone, sometimes a few times before it pairs successfully. This is a hassle--a PITA. Every time I get in the car, I have to go through this process--every time power is cut from the transmitter, actually, so if your passenger knocks it and it pops out of the 12V socket, it will have to be re-paired, which is supposed to happen automatically, but does not, and you then have to go through the process. Frustrating.

2) Charge output is only 1.0A. this is why I returned the first one--phone gives a "slow charging" warning when charging from this unit, regardless of what USB cable I use (I tried four different cables, all of which I know for certain can carry 2.1A).

3) Callers have occasionally complained they cannot hear me well when using this unit, and I occasionally (but not often) encounter FM interference. I believe Bluetooth itself is part of the problem, and anyone who has used a few Bluetooth headsets or units like this knows audio quality is terrible. Period. We just deal with it. Add to that the burden of having to transmit your signal via FM to a car stereo and the user-side audio (what you will hear in your car) is always going to be craptastic.

4) (*UPDATE) When paired, voice recognition on my phone, which is usually quite good, becomes severely impaired. This is also likely the culprit for complaint #3, above. I suspect this is because when paired, it tries to use the built-in microphone for voice recognition instead of the microphones on my phone (of which there are 4). It is disabling the extremely good microphones in my phone (Nokia lumia Icon which is well known for having incredible audio input) and using the unit's crappy microphone instead. This microphone is located in the unit, which is attached to the center console of my car near the shifter, and thus picks up all the vibrations and related road and engine noise transmitted through the structure of the car as I drive. This approach is terrible. I have stopped using the unit for anything requiring voice input, including telephone calls. In other words, this is just a big awkward charger now, and one that charges painfully slowly (see complaint #2). If it were possible to disable the onboard mic, and use the mics in my phone instead for calls and voice recognition, this would be a much more serviceable unit As it is now, it is just a piece of junk.

Cannot recommend this item. There are definitely worse products out there. I have not tried them all, but of those I have used, this is the best one so far. I will likely keep using it until the lack of automatic pairing pushes me over the edge with it one day and I get something else. I am usually not a fan of ear bud-style headphones as I have trouble finding sets that are either comfortable or have good sound. More often than not, buds have been tuned to have the bass either too strong or too weak and they sound very unnatural. Sony did a good job with these and got them sounding very balanced. They’re not perfect when it comes to comfort but there are ways to remedy this.

These are not active noise canceling (ANC) phones. Sony offers another model that is ANC-capable and they’re excellent but an order of magnitude more expensive. If you need ANC, this particular set of buds cannot do that so consider other options but be prepared to spend more.

These are sport-style ear buds in that they come on a neck harness and they are wireless. They connect easily via Bluetooth though they come with an adapter so they can be corded and used with devices that cannot work with Bluetooth. One concern with this type of phone is that often the cord is a little short between the harness and the buds, meaning a turn of the head pulls the cord a bit and can dislodge the buds from your ears. This particular set has some extra play in the cord so I have not had this issue as of yet. The cord on either bud can be “shortened” on either side by pulling the slack through tensors on the harness to reduce play in the wire.

In terms of use for sports and exercise, these feel a bit more fragile than most and I would caution against using them for doing anything much more active than running. They might hold up just fine, but these are a bit more pricey than most and are not ruggedized. This is probably my main complaint with these.

Comfort-wise, these are not bad. I have had better success with these than most, though I still greatly prefer over-the-ear headphones most of the time. The inserts are relatively soft and pliable and they do fit well, and the set comes with multiple sizes so adjustments can be made to get them to fit just right. In researching, I found that there are plenty of replacement tips; so, they can be swapped out if need be to find something that fits better or is more comfortable.

The main consideration about any set of phones, regardless of price, is the sound. In my mind, Sony has always had good quality products that do a fine job of balancing the sound. These ear buds are very much in line with my previous experiences. The sound profile is very balanced and even and the result is natural sounding playback. The tendency with the majority of manufacturers is to heavily push the bass. The bass in these is present and you can definitely hear it but it is not so pronounced as to dampen or overpower the rest of the profile. The midrange sounds good (particularly for ear buds) and had the right depth, meaning music sounds warm and not like it’s coming out of a tunnel or barrel. The highs are bright and clear but not piercing. I would stop short of saying these are audiophile quality, but the sound is much better than most bud-style earphones.

These are not your typical, cheap set of ear buds. These are better than the average and they are designed to be more comfortable and useful in an active lifestyle. They sound great. My only complaint is the construction - the harness in particular feels fragile. If you don’t need ANC and you don’t anticipate using your phones for heavy physical activity, these are a great choice. If you need something a bit more rugged, you might consider other options.

Other reviewers will probably cover the wi-fi setup, but I got this for another reason. I hate wi-fi because it can be slow, too many things can interfere with the signal (such as microwaves) and there is always a security concern. In addition to being a wi-fi extender, this works great for extending the range of your router's wired connections, which is how I am using it. There are two parts to this; one is the sending end, which you plug into your router via included ethernet cable and then into an electrical outlet. The receiving end of this has 3 ethernet ports and you can connect up to 3 devices by ethernet cable. If you use it this way, there is no setup at all. It truly is plug and play and worked immediately for me. The setup sheet doesn't make it clear that it can function this way, but there is a picture on the box showing it. Also, I was very pleased with the fact that both pieces included a pass-through outlet, which is a great feature. It would seem that this would keep you from losing an outlet. Maybe and maybe not. Here's why. Both pieces are quite long. If you plug them into the top outlet of a typical 2 part outlet, the devices will cover the second outlet. So just plug them into the bottom outlet, right?; then the top outlet is free. Maybe. The problem is that the devices are just a little too tall and you cannot fit a 3-prong gounded plug above them. You can use a 2-pronged plug and it will mostly likely fit. You would think someone would have tested this when they designed the product. It's that slight design flaw that caused me to knock one star off my rating. Other extenders of this type that I have seen are small enough to fit with another 3-prong cord above them when plugged in to the bottom of a 2-part outlet.

If you have a large house, it is possible you might have more than one main electrical circuit running through your house. This only works if you plug both devices into the same master circuit. Of course that is not the fault of the device; that will be true of any range extender of this type.

These power plug range extenders have been on the market for a while, but nice someone finally decided to include a pass-through outlet, but too bad that the device isn't just a little smaller so that it doesn't partially block the second plug in a 2-plug outlet when plugged in at the bottom. Note these do need to be plugged directly into a wall outlet; can't be used off a power strip. That could be an issue if you are short of outlets, as I am.

The connection speed wasn't quite as good as I expected, but it is adequate. The units heated up a little, which I didn't like, but not uncomfortable to the touch. I also have experience with standalone extenders that don't use the powerlines in your home; they work just about as well and some of them also have ethernet ports; the only difference being that you are going Wi-Fi to the extender and then going back to ethernet if you want to use a cable, whereas with a powerline extender, you are going through wires all the way. Those standalone extenders only require one outlet too.

I have some cognitive impairment and mobility challenges from lupus, and I was able to set up Fire TV really easily. The batteries go in the remote; the hdmi cable goes where it goes, and the power plugs in where it plugs in. The only painful part for me/my hands was logging into my wireless network via the onscreen qwerty keyboard.

The screens are responsive with virtually no latency, thanks to the quad core processor and 2 gb ram. And video streaming is also very smooth. I have only been using this a day, but I haven't had it pause to buffer yet. I have a Chromecast in my son's room, a recent model Mac Mini in the living room, an older C2D Mac Mini in my room with Boxee on it, and a Raspberry Pi, and they all buffer at some point during just about every movie. I stayed in a vacation home with a Roku 2 last summer, and it was great, but it also had to buffer a lot. We also have three game consoles that have streaming video apps, and they buffer, too. I think the Fire's secret may be its wifi card. I am sure that, at some point, my ISP will find a way to slow it down.

So, yeah, I am giving the Fire TV four stars for doing exactly what I need it to do. I had come to Amazon to get another Chromecast, but I saw this and thought it would probably be better suited to what I need in my bedroom (I need my husband to be able to watch a tv show without my help - he is completely tech-challenged and cannot work the Dish remote - too many buttons).

The reason it doesn't get five stars is that there aren't yet enough content apps. There is a manga channel, a documentary channel, an art house channel, along with Crackle and Flixter and Plex (Plex is a for pay service that lets you stream your home content). There is plenty to watch if you are a Prime member (I am - and I appreciated having that already set up on my Fire TV - Thank you, Amazon!) I am also a Dish subscriber, with HBO and a Hopper. I have apps for those directly on some of my devices. I can get them on the internet on the tbs I have hooked up to computers. I can even blast them over to my Chromecast from my tablets. But they aren't on Fire TV, and none of my tablets will screencast to Fire TV. Soon as they are, this is a five star device for me.

I read in Entertainment Weekly that HBO and Amazon Prime have come to an understanding that will make lots and lots of HBO shows available through prime, which will also make them available through Fire TV. For the ones that are not, HBOGO will have an app for this. Between that news and my son's enjoyment of an eight dollar (as opposed to 40 to 60 dollars) platformed on this thing, I am adding a star.

Had a 45 inch Sharp Aquos in the living room for over three years, and always thought it delivered wonderful HD output. On my PC, I own a Nvidia 3D Vision Set for the past two years for my PC gaming. The 3D Vision uses shutter technology, and definitely works beautifully with a 120HZ Monitor. Being a huge fan of all things tech, I've been watching the 3DTV market for the past few years, and finally it happened: Passive 3D! An affordable option which can feed 3D to a group of four+ without making you bankrupt.

I transferred the Sharp to the bedroom, and plugged all peripherals (PS3, 360, HDDVR and Roku) into the LG. Fired it up and immediately noticed how the colors popped. It actually ran rings around my Sharp Aquos! I transferred some 3D tech demos I saved on my PC to a USB drive, then ran them on the LG and was blown away by the 3D quality. Clean, bright and wonderful depth! Next, I popped in a BluRay movie (Monsters vs. Aliens) and again, my jaw dropped. I understood that the passive tech on the LG is suppose to have one drawback: horizontal resolution is decreased in 3D mode, but I'll be damned if I can see any difference. The TV arrived the day after Thanksgiving, so we still had the Thanksgiving Day Parade saved on our DVR. We used this to test the 2D to 3D on the fly conversation and it worked out pretty nicely. It definitely adds depth to any 2D broadcast, but nothing compared to true 3D.

As for gaming, the PS3 recognized I had a 3D TV from the start, and the few games I quickly tried (Wipeout, Uncharted 3 & Super Stardust) were mind-numbinlgy gorgeous. I didn't get a chance to try any 3D gaming on my 360 yet, but that's next!

Overall, I couldn't be happier with my decision to go for this LG!

Some quick notes:
- Unlike my 3D Vision PC shutter set up, the LG Passive does not darken the screen; colors remain bright and vibrant!

- My eyes were able to handle much longer periods of 3D viewing with the passive glasses. The 3D vision shutter would screw me up for the night if I played a long gaming session wearing them.

- The LG uses the same glasses they give out in theaters; go see Hugo and keep the glasses! :-)

- Get access to YouTube on your TV, and search YT3D! The LG Passive supports a number of different 3D formats which work brilliantly with most of YouTube's 3D showings'; there's TONS to see on there!

- The only ghosting I noticed was when you were not watching the TV from a normal viewing angle. For instance, if you stand up and move a bit close, you'll see overlapping images, but who watches TV like that?

- The two negatives: LG supplies a set of two orange and two white glasses. Orange and White? Really? What happened to the black glasses shown on the box and in a zillion ads? No big deal though, glasses are cheap. I found an eBay vendor selling a lot of 10 Movie glasses for $15.00! Try doing that with shutter technology. The USB input does not support DTS sound, so if you have a movie stored on a USB drive, it has to be converted or you will have no sound.

I bought two different brands of drive recorders for my vehicles. I bought this one, and I bought the Apeman C420D. Granted it costs a couple more dollars, I am blown away by how vastly superior the Kingslim D2 is compared to the Apeman.

Firstly, the video/picture quality is outstanding on the Kingslim. It’s crystal clear on both the front and rear cameras. Even when moving at high speeds, there is no blur or bounce to the recording. At night, the Kingslim is still amazingly clear compared to the Apeman. The Apeman records terrible footage in low/no light. I have angled my rear camera upwards rather than facing the ground (as a back-up camera would be angled) so that I can record license plates/road ragers of vehicles behind me, and I am able to read the license plates/see the driver almost as clearly as I am able to see from the front camera.

Secondly, the setup was fairly easy, and I think anyone could do it themselves. All you have to do is run the wires through your trim to the lighter socket and back of your vehicle, and depending on if internal or external mounting your rear camera, through the back of your vehicle. You can also splice the wire to your reverse light wire, which will turn the camera system into a back-up camera. I decided not to do this because you can just instead change the front camera’s screen to the rear camera’s feed and use it that way temporarily.

Lastly, and most importantly, the customer service. I had an issue with the parking sensor and headlight sensor on my Apeman C420D and contacted support about it. All they could tell me was that those features were made that way and were functioning properly, and that if I didn’t like it to just turn them off.

I’ve had zero issues with my Kingslim so far, so the only interaction with their customer service was a letter that they sent me (I was surprised by that, as it’s usually just an email), thanking me for my purchase. This shows me the difference between how Apeman sees their customers and how Kingslim appreciates us.

All in all, you will not be disappointed in this camera. It is exactly as advertised!

However, for Windows PCs this is also optimum because it has Windows keys.

It comes with a brief, but well-written user guide.

I received these as a free review sample. I want to point out that these are hard-wired only. They use a 3.5mm connector and ARE NOT bluetooth. If you want phones for critical listening and transcribing music (or listening to a raw feed before mixdown) these are perfect. Bluetooth always entails some loss of sound quality, but these, and other direct connect phones, do not.

They are neutral enough to pass for high end in-ear monitors (IEMs), but there is a little bias on the low end. As long as you take that into account you can mentally compensate when listening to raw feeds.

One of the things that I found impressive is I could not detect any bias towards the mid range frequencies, nor do the high end frequencies sound compressed. For me this means that I can listen to acoustic jazz and hear the music as originally recorded. This is especially important for a lot of mid 1950s recordings before engineers started playing games with the mix. For these phones I sampled tracks from [[ASIN:B00CJYWUM6 At the Showboat / See What I Mean? / Settlin' In]] and [[ASIN:B000QQV5FM Dorothy Donegan Live]], and listened to the entire two hours and forty-eight minutes of Erroll Garner's [[ASIN:B00ZJ5QXDO The Complete Concert By The Sea]]. That test proved that these phones are absolutely superb for folks for love music.

While this is claimed to be for Android, I tested it on an iPad Air 2 and a ThinkPad T61 - it worked beautifully on both. In fact, on the ThinkPad I was playing from CD instead of an MP3 file and the sound quality was better than a direct connect from my Note 4 phone.

A few notes about the physical characteristics and features: I tested out the control block using my Note 4 phone and found it to be less than intuitive. I prefer controlling functions using those integrated in my Note 4 (including EQ.) I love the tangle free cord, and the comfort of the phones though. Everything about the construction and sound are of the highest quality.

Bottom line: if you are fanatical about sound quality these phones are ones that I highly recommend. I own other IEMs that cost twice as much that are close to these. Granted the expensive ones have completely neutral low frequency response, but if you are not mixing down these are as good in the overall scheme of things.

The sound is very soft.

Again, this is an inexpensive camera, but it does every thing it's supposed to do.

My mom ordered 2 of these thinking she'd be able to play music out of both of them at the same time from her iPhone. They come in the mail and we cannot figure out how to do this at all, and the instructions that came with them were unclear, as well as what we found online.
After a few hours of trial and error, this is what we figured out:
Pair both of the speakers to the iPhone
Make sure *one* of the speakers in connected (the other may not show anymore/doesn't have to be connected)
On the *connected* speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (a sound will play)
On the other speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (the same sound will play with some additional beeps)

Play music and they should work! This worked best for us when only one iPhone was connected/paired with the speakers at a time.

Hope this helps someone else!

This is a handy little item if you need power backup for a phone or tablet, when you expect to have an extended period away from a power source. I'm planning to carry it with me when travelling, for example, and it might be handy on a hike as well.

I plugged in my regular micro-usb phone charger (the specs call for 2.1A at 5V) to fully charge it. Then I tested it on a phone (Samsung S4) and a tablet (Tab S), and found the results quite satisfactory. The specs say that the two USB ports will provide 2.4A at 5V simultaneously, and I was certainly able to charge my two devices at the same time without problems.

There's some discussion in the instructions about "smart charging", but I can't verify if that makes any real difference. (The idea seems to be that you can tell the charger to dialog with your device to select an optimal charge profile. Nice idea, but I didn't see a difference after I did what they asked. Maybe it was optimal already ...)

The flashlight is a nice touch, but I don't know that I'd ever use it. I'd carry a flashlight if I think I might one, rather than depending on one charger to provide backup power as well as a light source.
